Thermostat miswiring is a top cause of no-heat/no-cool calls and fried control boards. Know the standard terminals and the equipment behind them.

### Standard 24V Terminal Map

- **R / Rc / Rh** — 24V power (Rc cooling, Rh heating; jumper if single transformer).
- **C** — common (24V return) — **required** for Wi-Fi stats (**Ecobee**, **Nest**, **Honeywell T-series**) to power themselves.
- **W / W2** — heat stage 1 / stage 2.
- **Y / Y2** — compressor/cooling stage 1 / stage 2.
- **G** — indoor fan/blower.
- **O/B** — heat pump reversing valve (**O** energized in cooling = most brands; **B** energized in heating = Rheem/Ruud).
- **AUX/E** — auxiliary/emergency heat (heat strips on heat pumps).

### Common Configurations

- **Conventional AC + gas furnace:** R, C, W, Y, G (+ Y2/W2 for two-stage).
- **Heat pump:** R, C, Y, G, O/B, plus **AUX** and **E** for backup heat. Set the thermostat to heat-pump mode and correct O/B logic.
- **Dual-fuel (heat pump + gas furnace):** Needs a thermostat that supports a **balance point** to switch from compressor to gas below a set outdoor temp.

### The C-Wire Issue

No C-wire? Options: run a new conductor, repurpose an unused wire, or use a **Fast-Stat / add-a-wire** adapter. Nest's power-stealing can cause intermittent faults on some systems — a true C is best practice.

### Zoning Systems

Zoning uses a **control panel** (Honeywell TrueZone, Ecobee SmartSensor logic, or panel-based) driving **motorized dampers** per zone.

- Each zone gets its own thermostat feeding the panel.
- The panel manages dampers and staging, and uses a **bypass damper or modulating/variable-speed equipment** to relieve static when only one zone calls.
- Best paired with **variable-speed/inverter** equipment (Carrier Greenspeed, Trane) so airflow modulates instead of dumping into a bypass.

### Commissioning

1. Power off at the disconnect before wiring.
2. Match wires to terminals; configure stat for the equipment type and stages.
3. Test each call: G (fan), Y (cool), W (heat), AUX/E, and O/B reversing.
4. Verify damper operation per zone and confirm static stays in range.

### Pro Tips

- Always land a **C-wire** on smart stats — it eliminates power-stealing gremlins.
- Label wires before pulling the old stat; photograph the terminals.
- Wrong O/B setting = heating when you want cooling — verify reversing-valve logic per brand.

title: Diagnosing Low Cooling, Frozen Coils, and No-Heat Calls
content:
## Systematic HVAC Troubleshooting

Three of the most common service calls — weak cooling, iced coils, and no heat — share overlapping root causes. Diagnose with measurements, not guesses.

### Low / Weak Cooling

Measure the **temperature split** (return-air temp minus supply-air temp) — should be **16-22°F** at the coil under normal humidity.

- **Low refrigerant charge:** High superheat, low subcooling, low suction pressure — find and fix the **leak** (electronic detector/bubbles), recover, repair, evacuate, recharge to spec. Never just top off.
- **Dirty condenser coil:** High head pressure, hot condenser — wash with coil cleaner.
- **Restricted airflow:** Dirty filter/evaporator, high static — clean, fix ductwork.
- **Failing compressor/capacitor:** Test the **run capacitor** (within ±6% of rated µF) and compressor amps vs. RLA.
- **Metering device (TXV)** stuck — erratic superheat.

### Frozen Evaporator Coil

Ice forms when coil temp drops below freezing — almost always **airflow or charge**.

1. **Low airflow** (most common): dirty filter, dirty coil, undersized/blocked returns, weak blower, closed dampers. Restore airflow.
2. **Low refrigerant charge:** undercharge drops suction pressure/coil temp below freezing.
3. **Low ambient operation** or stuck blower relay.

**Fix steps:** Shut off cooling, run **fan-only to thaw** completely, then diagnose the root cause before restarting — don't just restart into another freeze.

### No Heat (Gas Furnace)

Follow the ignition sequence with a meter:

1. **Call for heat:** 24V at W? If not, check thermostat/C-wire/transformer (3A fuse on board).
2. **Inducer runs?** No → bad inducer or board.
3. **Pressure switch closes?** Check for blocked vent/intake or **clogged condensate trap** (condensing units trip the switch).
4. **Igniter glows / spark?** Cracked **hot surface igniter** is common — test resistance (~40-90Ω).
5. **Gas valve opens / flame?** Verify gas on, manifold pressure.
6. **Flame sense:** Weak/dirty **flame sensor** = furnace lights then drops out after a few seconds (microamp reading too low). Clean it — the #1 no-heat fix.
7. **Limit switch open** from overheating → check airflow.

### No Heat (Heat Pump)

- Verify reversing-valve **O/B** logic, defrost board, and that **AUX heat strips** energize. Check for iced outdoor coil (failed defrost).

### Pro Tips

- Carry a **multimeter, manometer, and gauges** — measure don't guess.
- A clean flame sensor and clean filter resolve a huge share of calls.
- Always find the leak before recharging — refrigerant doesn't disappear on its own.
code_references: manufacturer service facts / sequence of operation

title: Refrigerant and Carbon Monoxide Safety: A2L Handling and Combustion Hazards
content:
## Refrigerant and CO Safety on the Job

HVAC techs work around asphyxiants, flammable refrigerants, high pressure, and combustion byproducts. These hazards are invisible — respect them.

### Refrigerant Hazards

- **Asphyxiation:** Refrigerants displace oxygen in low areas (basements, pits). Ventilate; never service in unventilated confined spaces.
- **Frostbite:** Liquid refrigerant boils at sub-zero temps — wear **safety glasses and gloves**; flares and connections can spray.
- **High pressure:** R-410A operates ~400+ PSI on the high side and far higher under fault; R-454B is similar. Use **rated gauges/hoses**, never overheat a charged cylinder, and never exceed cylinder fill limits.

### A2L (R-454B / R-32) Flammability

New low-GWP refrigerants are **mildly flammable (A2L class)**:

- Use **A2L-rated** recovery machines, gauges, vacuum pumps, and **leak detectors**.
- **No ignition sources** — no smoking, no open flame, no sparking tools near a charged/leaking A2L system.
- Equipment may include **refrigerant detection sensors (RDS)** that trigger fans — don't defeat them.
- Respect **maximum charge per room volume** limits and ensure ventilation.
- Brazing on an A2L system: recover fully, then purge with nitrogen before applying heat.

### EPA 608 / Legal

- **Venting refrigerant is illegal** (Clean Air Act §608). **Recover** before opening systems.
- Hold **EPA 608 certification**; use DOT-approved recovery cylinders and track refrigerant.

### Carbon Monoxide (Combustion Side)

CO is colorless, odorless, and deadly. Sources: cracked heat exchangers, backdrafting furnaces/water heaters, blocked flues.

- **Always run a combustion analysis** on furnace startup/service — target **CO air-free < 100 ppm**, ideally near zero; investigate anything elevated.
- Inspect the **heat exchanger** for cracks — a leaking exchanger sends CO into the supply air. Shut down and red-tag if cracked.
- Verify proper **draft** and that vent/flue is clear and correctly sloped.
- Install/test **CO alarms** near sleeping areas; recommend low-level CO monitors for clients.

### Electrical & General

- **Lock out/tag out** at the disconnect before servicing; verify 0V with a meter.
- Discharge **run/start capacitors** before handling — they hold a shock charge.
- Watch for spinning condenser fans and hot surfaces.

### Pro Tips

- Keep a **personal CO monitor** clipped on during combustion work.
- Transition to A2L tools now — new equipment is shipping with R-454B.
- If a customer reports headaches/nausea that improve when they leave home, treat it as a CO emergency.
code_references: EPA 608 — Clean Air Act refrigerant handling

title: Wall Framing Layout: Plate Marking and Stud Spacing at 16" and 24" OC
content:
## Wall Framing Layout

Accurate layout is what separates a wall that drywalls and sheathes clean from one that fights you every panel. Start by snapping chalk lines on the slab or subfloor to locate the **inside edge** of the bottom plate per the floor plan.

### Plating and Crowning

Cut your top and bottom plates from straight `2x4` or `2x6` SPF/DF #2 stock. Lay them edge-to-edge (this is **ganging the plates**) so you mark both at once. Always frame exterior walls in DF #2 or SPF #2 — crown every stud and orient crowns up consistently.

### On-Center Spacing

- **16" OC** is standard for load-bearing walls and walls receiving `1/2"` drywall on ceilings/walls per **IRC R602.3(5)**.
- **24" OC** is allowed for many non-bearing and single-story bearing walls with `2x6` studs (advanced framing / OVE), saving lumber and improving insulation cavity.
- Pull your tape and mark **15-1/4"** for the first stud center so the leading edge of the first `4x8` sheet of sheathing lands on stud center at 16". Mark with an **X** on the side the stud sits. Continue at 16" increments: 31-1/4", 47-1/4", etc.

### Openings

Mark king studs, then trimmers (jack studs), then the rough opening. Standard interior door RO is door width + 2" for jamb/shim. Use a **Speed Square** and a sharp pencil or a **DeWalt** layout marker.

### Assembly

- Nail through the plate into the stud end with **2) 16d** nails (`3-1/2"`) per **IRC R602.3(1)** — end nail, 2 each end.
- A **Paslode** or **Hitachi/Metabo HPT** framing nailer with 3-1/4" paper-collated nails speeds this dramatically.
- Stand the wall, plumb it, and brace with `1x4` or `2x4` diagonals before releasing.

### Pro Tips

- Keep layout consistent across the whole floor so plumbing/electrical and HVAC stack between bays.
- Mark **C** for cripples and **T** for trimmers to avoid confusion.
- Double-check your **first stud offset** — getting it wrong throws every sheet of sheathing and drywall off module.

A disciplined layout pays off through the entire build: sheathing, drywall, and trim all reference the same 16" module, so panels break on framing and fasteners land where they should.

title: Header Sizing and Spans for Bearing and Non-Bearing Walls
content:
## Header Sizing and Spans

Headers carry roof, floor, and wall loads across openings. Undersizing causes sag, drywall cracking, and sticking doors. Size from **IRC Table R602.7(1)** for exterior bearing walls and **R602.7(2)** for interior bearing walls, or use engineered lumber tables.

### Sawn Lumber Headers

Common built-up headers use two or three `2x` members with `1/2"` plywood spacer to fill a 3-1/2" stud bay (a `2x` is 1-1/2" thick; 2 plies + 1/2" ply = 3-1/2").

- **(2) 2x6 DF #2**: spans roughly **4'-0"** supporting roof + ceiling, one story.
- **(2) 2x8**: approx **5'-0"** to **6'-0"** depending on building width and snow load.
- **(2) 2x10**: approx **6'-6"** to **8'-0"**.
- **(2) 2x12**: approx **8'-0"** to **9'-6"**.

Spans drop as building width (20', 28', 36') and ground snow load increase — always check the actual table column.

### Engineered Lumber Headers

For longer or heavily loaded spans, use **Weyerhaeuser Trus Joist Microllam LVL** (1.55E or 2.0E) or **Parallam PSL**. A `(2) 1-3/4" x 11-7/8" Microllam LVL` header readily spans garage door openings of **9'-16'** depending on load. **Boise Cascade VERSA-LAM** LVL is an equivalent product. Always defer to the manufacturer span tables or an engineer for garage and great-room beams.

### Jack and King Studs

The number of **jack (trimmer) studs** per side increases with span/load — `1` jack for short openings, `2-3` jacks for wide LVL headers per the manufacturer detail. **IRC Table R602.7.5** gives minimum jack/king counts.

### Connections

- Nail built-up sawn headers per **IRC R602.3(1)**: 16d at 16" OC each edge, staggered top and bottom.
- For multi-ply LVL/PSL, follow the **Trus Joist** nailing/bolting schedule (e.g., 2 rows 16d at 12" OC, or `1/2"` through-bolts at 24" OC for 3+ plies and side-loaded conditions). **GRK RSS** structural screws are an approved alternative to nails for many multi-ply built-ups — check the connector and beam manufacturer details.
- Use **Simpson Strong-Tie** column caps (**CC/ECC** series) or face-mount hangers (**HUC/HGUS**) where beams frame into posts or carry girder loads.

### Header Bearing and Cripples

- Provide full bearing under each header end onto the jack studs; crush at the bearing point signals an undersized condition.
- Above the header, fill with **cripple studs** at the same OC as the wall studs to carry the top-plate load down to the header.
- A continuous **rim/band** over the opening keeps the top plate aligned.

### Key Rule

Non-bearing interior walls can use a flat `2x4` or single `2x6` header for openings up to ~8'. Never assume bearing vs. non-bearing from the floor plan alone — verify the **load path** from roof and floors all the way to the foundation before sizing. When in doubt on garage beams, great rooms, or anything carrying a girder truss, get a **stamped engineered design** rather than guessing from a span table.

title: Floor Joist and TJI Layout: Spans, Spacing, and Squash Blocks
content:
## Floor Joist and TJI Layout

Floor systems must meet **L/360** live-load deflection for finished floors. Layout drives squeak-free, flat floors.

### Sawn Joist Spans

From **IRC Table R502.3.1(2)** (40 psf live, 10 psf dead, #2 grade):
- `2x8 DF #2 @ 16" OC`: ~ **12'-7"**
- `2x10 DF #2 @ 16" OC`: ~ **15'-5"**
- `2x12 DF #2 @ 16" OC`: ~ **18'-0"**

Going to 24" OC or southern pine/SPF changes spans — verify the species column.

### Engineered I-Joists (TJI)

**Weyerhaeuser Trus Joist TJI** joists outperform sawn lumber for long, flat, quiet floors. Common series: **TJI 110, 210, 230, 360, 560**. A `TJI 230 @ 16" OC, 11-7/8" deep` spans roughly **17'-19'** at residential floor loading. Deeper `16"` TJIs reach well past **24'**. **Boise Cascade BCI** joists are a direct alternative.

### Critical TJI Rules

- **Never cut, notch, or drill the flanges.** Web holes only, per the manufacturer hole chart.
- Install **web stiffeners** (filler blocks) at hangers and concentrated loads where the detail requires.
- Use **squash blocks** (1-1/16" taller than the TJI) beside the joist under bearing walls/posts to carry vertical load around the I-joist — the flange alone won't take point loads.
- Provide **rim board** (Weyerhaeuser TimberStrand LSL rim, `1-1/4"` min) at all ends for lateral support and load transfer.
- Use approved hangers — **Simpson Strong-Tie ITT/IUS** series face-mount hangers sized to the I-joist, or **MiTek/USP** equivalents.

### Layout Procedure

1. Lay out rim/plate at **16" OC** matching wall studs above for stacked framing.
2. Set joists crown-up (sawn) — TJIs have no crown.
3. Glue and nail the subfloor — `3/4" T&G` Advantech with **PL Premium** construction adhesive and `2-3/8"` ring-shank nails or screws at 6" edge / 12" field.
4. Block at supports; add bridging/strongbacks for long spans to reduce bounce.

### Deflection and Bounce

Meeting the span table satisfies strength and **L/360** deflection, but occupants notice **vibration** long before structural limits. For long open floors, add a **TJI strongback** (a `2x6` on edge through the web knockouts mid-span) or tighten spacing to **12" OC** or **19.2" OC**. A stiffer subfloor (`23/32"`–`7/8"` Advantech) and full glue coverage also reduce perceived bounce.

### Bottom Line

Follow the **Weyerhaeuser Trus Joist Specifier's Guide** for hole locations, hanger selection, web stiffeners, squash blocks, and blocking — engineered floors are only as good as their details. Mixing a sawn rim with TJIs, point-loading a flange, or skipping squash blocks under a bearing wall are the failures that produce sagging floors and callbacks.

title: Selecting and Nailing Simpson Strong-Tie Connectors
content:
## Simpson Strong-Tie Connector Selection and Nailing

Connectors only achieve their rated load when you install **every specified fastener** in **every hole** with the **correct nail**. The most common field failure is short nails or empty holes.

### Joist Hangers

- **LUS28** — face-mount hanger for a single `2x8`. **LUS26**, **LUS210** size to 2x6/2x10. Fill round joist holes and the double-shear angled holes.
- Use **10d x 1-1/2" (N10)** joist nails into the joist and **16d (N16)** into the header where the table calls for them. Do not substitute drywall or deck screws.
- For I-joists use **ITT/IUS/MIU** series; for heavy beams use **HUC/HGUS** concealed/heavy hangers.

### Hurricane/Seismic Ties

- **H2.5A** and **H1** ties tie rafters/trusses to the top plate to resist uplift. Install per the truss-to-plate connection schedule, typically **5) 8d x 1-1/2"** each.
- **LSTA21 / LSTA24 / MSTA** strap ties splice plates and provide continuity across openings.

### Hold-Downs

- **HDU** series (HDU2, HDU5, HDU8, HDU11) bolt to a post and anchor to a **Simpson SSTB or PAB anchor bolt** in the foundation for shear-wall overturning. Use the specified **SDS screws** (e.g., HDU5 = 14) **SDS25300**) into the post and torque the anchor nut to spec.
- **PHD/HD** bolted hold-downs are used for heavier conditions.

### Fastener Discipline

- Simpson connectors are designed for **Simpson Strong-Drive SD/SDS structural screws** or specified common nails. **GRK RSS/structural screws** are excellent for general structural fastening but use Simpson-approved fasteners in Simpson connectors.
- **MiTek/USP** offers cross-referenced equivalents — do not mix a USP hanger with Simpson load values.
- Galvanize/stainless (**ZMAX / HDG**) in exterior, treated-lumber, or coastal conditions — ACQ pressure-treated lumber is corrosive to standard zinc.

### Post Bases and Caps

- **ABU/ABA** adjustable post bases and **CBSQ** column bases hold posts off concrete (1" standoff) to prevent rot and anchor to the foundation. **BC/BCS** post caps tie posts to beams.
- Match the base to the post size (`4x4`, `6x6`) and the anchor to the concrete (cast-in **PAB** or post-installed **Titen HD**).

### Verification

Use a connector that is **fully nailed off** — an inspector counts holes. A `LUS28` with two empty nail holes can lose a significant fraction of its rated capacity. **Fill them all** with the **correct length and diameter** fastener. Common red-tags: drywall/deck screws in hangers, 1-1/4" roofing nails where N10 joist nails are required, short nails that don't penetrate the supporting member, and skipped double-shear angle nails. Keep the **Simpson Strong-Tie connector catalog** or app on site to confirm the fastening schedule for each model before you hang it.

title: Wall Sheathing and Nailing Schedules per IRC R602.3
content:
## Wall Sheathing and Nailing Schedules

Structural wood sheathing braces walls against wind and seismic racking. The **nailing schedule** is the difference between a code-compliant shear panel and a wall that fails.

### Panel Selection

- **7/16" OSB** (APA rated, e.g., **LP**, **Weyerhaeuser**, **Norbord**) is the standard exterior wall sheathing. `15/32"` (1/2") plywood is used where higher capacity or moisture durability is needed.
- Orient panels with the strength axis (long dimension) across studs; stagger vertical joints.
- Leave a **1/8" gap** at panel edges and ends for expansion (use a nail or spacer tool).

### Standard Nailing — IRC Table R602.3(3)

For `3/8"`–`1/2"` wood structural panels on walls:
- **8d common (0.131" x 2-1/2")** nails
- **6" OC at panel edges**, **12" OC in the field** (intermediate supports).
- Keep nails **3/8" from panel edges** to avoid blowout.

### Braced Wall / Shear Wall Nailing

For engineered shear walls, the schedule tightens dramatically:
- **6" / 4" / 3" / 2" OC** edge nailing increases shear capacity per the engineer's schedule.
- Use **blocking** at all horizontal panel joints when the design calls for blocked shear walls.
- Mark the shear-wall schedule on the panel so the inspector and crew can verify.

### Tools and Pressure

- A **Hitachi/Metabo HPT NR83A5**, **Paslode**, or **Senco** framing nailer set to flush — **do not overdrive**. Nails countersunk past the OSB face lose shear value. Set depth on a scrap and adjust regulator (~90-100 psi).
- Hand-nail or palm-nail the last row where the gun can't reach flush.

### Continuous Load Path

Sheathing ties studs to the top and bottom plates and, with proper nailing into the **rim/sill**, transfers shear to the foundation. Combine with **Simpson** anchor bolts, hold-downs, and **mudsill anchors** for a complete braced-wall line per **IRC R602.10**.

### Panel Layout

- Run the first course with the bottom edge lapping the **mudsill/rim** so sheathing ties the wall to the foundation — this is critical to the braced-wall load path.
- Stagger vertical end joints by at least one stud bay between courses (running-bond pattern) for better diaphragm action.
- Block all unsupported horizontal joints when the shear schedule requires **blocked panels**; many engineered designs do.

### Quick Reference

- Field nailing forgotten? It's the most common red-tag — **12" OC in the field is mandatory**, not optional.
- **Over-driven nails** (sunk past the OSB face) and **edge blowout** both reduce shear capacity — set the gun on a scrap first and keep nails 3/8" from edges.
- A **WRB** (weather-resistive barrier such as **Tyvek HomeWrap** or **CertainTeed**) goes over the sheathing, lapped shingle-style, with all windows, doors, and penetrations flashed and integrated.
- For shear walls, **photograph and mark** the panel with its nailing schedule so both the crew and inspector can verify edge spacing at a glance.
code_references: IRC R602.3(3) — wood structural panel nailing

title: Diagnosing Squeaky Floors and Racking Walls
content:
## Troubleshooting Squeaks and Racking

### Squeaky Floors

Squeaks come from wood moving against a fastener or against another piece of wood. Common causes:
- **Subfloor not glued** to joists — nails work loose as lumber dries and the panel rubs the nail shank.
- **Smooth-shank nails** instead of ring-shank or screws backing out.
- **Gaps** between subfloor and joist (crowned or twisted joists) leaving the panel unsupported.

**Fixes:**
- From below: drive a **GRK or Simpson SDS screw** up through a `2x` cleat snugged tight under the subfloor where the gap exists. Do **not** pull the subfloor down onto a joist if a gap exists at a different joist — shim first.
- From above (finished): use a **Squeeeeak No More** scored-screw kit through carpet, or face-screw with **trim-head screws** into joists, then fill.
- New construction: always **glue** subfloor with **PL Premium** and fasten with ring-shank nails or subfloor screws at **6" edge / 12" field**. Use `3/4" Advantech` for dimensional stability.

### Racking and Out-of-Square Walls

Racking is lateral lozenging of a wall, usually from inadequate bracing during or after construction.
- **During framing:** walls left un-sheathed and un-braced rack in wind. Always install temporary `1x4` let-in or `2x4` diagonal bracing until sheathing is on.
- **Permanent:** racking resistance comes from **wood structural panel sheathing** nailed per **IRC R602.3(3)** or engineered shear walls per **R602.10**. Metal **let-in T-bracing** or Simpson **WB/RCWB** portal frames are alternatives.

**Diagnosis:**
- Measure diagonals corner-to-corner; equal diagonals = square. A difference indicates racking.
- Check **drywall cracks at door corners** and **sticking doors** as symptoms of seasonal racking or header sag.
- Verify **hold-downs (HDU)** and **anchor bolts** are present and tight at braced-wall ends — missing overturning restraint lets shear walls rotate.

### Twisted and Crowned Lumber

Green dimensional lumber moves as it dries. A twisted joist or a crowned-down member leaves the subfloor unsupported and creates squeaks and uneven floors.
- Always install joists and studs **crown up** and consistent.
- Block and bridge long joist spans to keep members from rolling/twisting.
- For chronic movement, switch to **engineered lumber (TJI, LSL studs)** which stays straight and stable.

### Prevention

Glue + screw subfloors with **PL Premium** and ring-shank or subfloor screws, fully nail sheathing per the schedule, brace walls until sheathed, and confirm the **continuous load path** from roof to foundation including hold-downs and anchor bolts. Let framing **dry/acclimate** before drywall to minimize shrinkage-driven cracks and pops. Most callbacks — squeaks, racking, cracked drywall corners, sticking doors — trace back to a single skipped fastening, bracing, or moisture-management step, so build the discipline in from the first wall.
materials_required: GRK or Simpson SDS structural screws

title: Ladder, Scaffold, and Fall Protection on the Frame
content:
## Fall Protection While Framing

Falls are the leading cause of death in construction. **OSHA 1926.501** requires fall protection at **6 feet** in residential construction. Plan it before you leave the ground.

### Ladders

- Maintain the **4:1 ratio** — base out 1 foot for every 4 feet of height.
- Extension ladders must extend **3 feet (3 rungs)** above the landing and be tied off at the top.
- Inspect for cracked rails, bent rungs; use **Type IA (300 lb)** rated ladders for framing loads (tools + body).
- Never stand on the top two rungs of a stepladder. Keep **three points of contact**.

### Scaffold and Pump Jacks

- Fully plank platforms; provide **guardrails at 39"-45"** with mid-rails when 10+ feet (or 6 ft for some scaffolds), and **toe boards**.
- Base plates and mud sills on firm, level ground; plumb and brace frames.
- Pump-jack poles must be braced to the wall every 10 feet.

### Personal Fall Arrest (PFAS)

Where guardrails aren't feasible at heights ≥6 ft (roofs, walls, openings):
- **Full-body harness** + **shock-absorbing lanyard or SRL** + anchor rated **5,000 lb** per worker.
- Use a **roof anchor** (e.g., **Guardian**, **Malta Dynamics**, **DBI-SALA**) screwed into rafters/trusses with the specified lag/structural screws.
- Calculate **total fall clearance** — free fall + deceleration + harness stretch + safety margin — so you don't strike a lower level.

### Floor and Wall Openings

- Cover floor holes with secured, marked covers rated for **2x the load**.
- Stair openings, shaftways, and skylights get guardrails or covers immediately after framing.

### Nailer and Saw Safety

- Sequential-trip triggers reduce double-fire injuries on **Paslode/Senco** guns. Keep the nailer pointed downrange; disconnect air before clearing jams.
- Eye and ear protection always; the **DeWalt** or **Makita** worm-drive saw demands guards intact and full attention.

### Working at the Wall and Eave

- When standing walls, keep crew clear of the swing path and brace immediately; an unbraced wall can topple in a gust.
- Setting trusses and rafters at the eave is high-exposure work — use a **harness tied to a roof anchor**, a **scaffold at the eave**, or a guardrailed work platform. Plan anchor points before the first truss flies.
- Cover or guard the **stair opening and floor openings** the moment the deck is sheeted.

### Housekeeping and Daily Routine

Clear cut-offs, coil cords and air hoses out of walk paths, and pick up spent nail strips and collation paper. A clean deck prevents the trips that turn into falls from height. Conduct a **daily inspection** of ladders, scaffolds, harnesses, lanyards, and anchors — tag out anything damaged. **Document** the inspection and hold a brief toolbox talk; OSHA expects a competent person overseeing fall protection on the site. Plan the fall-protection method **before** the crew leaves the ground each morning, not after someone is already 12 feet up.

title: Roof Rafter and Truss Basics: Layout, Bracing, and Tie-Downs
content:
## Roof Rafter and Truss Basics

### Stick-Framed Rafters

Rafters are sized from **IRC Table R802.4.1** based on species, snow/dead load, and spacing.
- `2x8 DF #2 @ 16" OC` rafters span roughly **13'-16'** depending on load.
- Cut a **plumb cut** at the ridge, a **bird's-mouth (seat cut)** at the wall plate (depth ≤ 1/4 the rafter depth per **IRC R802.7.1**), and a **tail/plumb cut** at the eave.
- A structural **ridge beam** is required when rafters can't form a triangle (cathedral, no ceiling ties); a non-structural ridge board is allowed when **ceiling joists/rafter ties** resist outward thrust per **IRC R802.4.5**.

### Roof Trusses

Engineered trusses arrive with a stamped layout and **truss design drawings (TDDs)**. The contractor must follow the **BCSI (Building Component Safety Information)** bracing guide.
- Set trusses at **24" OC** (typical), spread by the layout, and align with stacked wall studs.
- Install **temporary bracing** as you go — diagonal and lateral — to prevent the dominoes-style collapse that injures crews.
- **Permanent bracing**: top chord braced by sheathing, bottom chord and webs braced per the TDD.

### Tie-Downs and Uplift

Wind uplift must be resisted at each truss/rafter-to-plate connection:
- **Simpson Strong-Tie H2.5A**, **H1**, or **H10** hurricane ties — installed with the full nail count (typically **5) 8d x 1-1/2"** plus plate nails).
- High-wind zones use heavier **META/MGT** straps and a continuous load path down to the foundation hold-downs.

### Sheathing

- `7/16"` or `1/2"` OSB/plywood, strength axis across rafters, **8d at 6" edge / 12" field** per **IRC R803**.
- Use **plyclips (H-clips)** at unsupported panel edges between rafters at 24" OC.
- Leave a **1/8"** gap at panel edges.

### Ceiling Ties and Collar Ties

- **Rafter (ceiling) ties** near the top-plate level resist the outward thrust that would otherwise push walls apart — required for non-structural-ridge assemblies per **IRC R802.4.5**.
- **Collar ties** in the upper third resist ridge separation under wind uplift; install per **IRC R802.4.6**, typically `1x4` min at 4'-0" OC.
- Where a structural ridge beam is used, rafters bear on the beam and ties may not be required — but the ridge beam and its posts must be sized and supported to the foundation.

### Verification

- Confirm **heel height, overhang, pitch, and bearing** match the plans and truss layout before sheathing.
- Verify every truss/rafter has its **uplift connector** fully nailed before the roof is loaded.
- **Never cut, notch, or modify a truss** (top chord, bottom chord, or web) without **written truss-engineer approval** and a repair detail — field alterations void the engineered design and create life-safety hazards.

Get the bracing, ties, and tie-downs right; the roof is the structure's hat against gravity and wind alike, and the most-watched assembly in a wind event.

title: Hanging Drywall: Screw Spacing, Ceilings First, and Type X Fire-Rated Board
content:
## Hanging Drywall Correctly

### Board Selection

- **USG Sheetrock 1/2"** regular for most walls and ceilings at **16" OC**.
- **1/2" sag-resistant (USG Sheetrock UltraLight Ceiling)** for ceilings at **24" OC** — standard 1/2" sags at 24" OC.
- **5/8" Type X** fire-rated for garages, ceilings, party walls, and any rated assembly (**IRC R302**). **National Gypsum Gold Bond Fire-Shield** and **CertainTeed Type X** are equivalents.
- Run sheets **perpendicular** to framing to bridge more members and stagger butt joints.

### Hang the Ceiling First

Always hang **ceilings before walls** so wall sheets support the ceiling edges. Use a **drywall lift** or a deadman `T-brace` and a helper. Push tight to framing — gaps cause screw pops and cracks.

### Screw Spacing — IRC R702.3.5

- **Ceilings:** screws at **12" OC** in the field (7" OC if nails).
- **Walls:** screws at **16" OC** in the field.
- Keep fasteners **3/8" from edges**.
- Use **#6 coarse-thread drywall screws** for wood framing (`1-1/4"` for 1/2", `1-5/8"` for 5/8"). **Fine-thread #6** for steel studs.
- Set screws to **dimple** the paper **without breaking it** — a **DeWalt** or **Makita** drywall screw gun with an adjustable nose-cone sets perfect depth every time. A torn face paper has near-zero holding power.

### Cutting and Fitting

- Score the face paper with a utility knife, snap, cut the back paper.
- Use a **rotary cut-out tool (RotoZip / DeWalt)** for outlets — measure twice; over-cut boxes are a finishing headache.
- Maintain a **1/4" gap** at the floor (kept off the floor with a foot lifter) so the board doesn't wick moisture and so panels seat tight to the ceiling.

### Fastening Strategy

- Fasten from the **center of the sheet outward** to avoid bowing.
- Don't fasten within 1" of an untaped edge that meets another sheet — let the joint compound and tape do their work, but support both edges on framing.
- **Glue + screw** (construction adhesive bead on studs) reduces screw count and pops on walls.

### Field Tip

Butt joints are the hardest to finish flat. Place them on a **back-blocked** location or center them on a stud and feather wide. Minimize butt joints by buying the longest boards that fit (`12'`).

title: Taping and Finishing: Levels 0-5 and the Three-Coat System
content:
## Taping and Finishing to Levels 0-5

The **GA-214** finish levels define how smooth a wall must be for its final finish. Spec'ing and hitting the right level avoids callbacks and overwork.

### The Finish Levels

- **Level 0:** No taping/finishing — temporary or unfinished.
- **Level 1:** Tape embedded in joint compound; fire/smoke barriers above ceilings, plenums.
- **Level 2:** Tape + one coat over fasteners; garages, behind tile.
- **Level 3:** Two coats over joints/fasteners; medium/heavy textures.
- **Level 4:** Three coats; flat paints, light textures, most residential walls.
- **Level 5:** Level 4 + a **skim coat** of joint compound or high-build primer over the entire surface; required for **gloss/semi-gloss paint** and **critical raking light** (large windows). Use **USG Sheetrock Tuff-Hide** or a thinned **Plus 3** skim.

### The Three-Coat System

1. **Embed coat (tape coat):** Apply **USG All-Purpose** joint compound into the joint, embed **paper tape** (or self-adhesive **FibaTape mesh** on flat joints with setting-type compound). Wipe to bed the tape with a `5"-6"` knife; squeeze out excess. Mesh tape must be used with **setting-type (hot mud)** like **USG Durabond/Easy Sand** to prevent cracking.
2. **Fill coat:** After dry (24 hrs for All-Purpose, faster for setting types), apply a wider `8"-10"` coat, feathering edges. Coat screws again.
3. **Finish/skim coat:** A `10"-12"` final feather with **USG Plus 3** (lightweight, sands easily, low shrinkage). Feather butt joints out **16"-24"** each side.

### Sanding and Inspection

- Sand between coats only as needed with **150-220 grit** on a pole sander; final sand with **220**.
- Use a **drywall sander with HEPA vacuum (Festool Planex / DeWalt)** to control dust.
- **Light test:** Sweep a halogen/LED work light across the wall at a low angle to catch ridges and pinholes before primer.

### Compound Types and When to Use Them

- **All-purpose (USG All-Purpose / green lid):** good adhesion and crack resistance for embedding tape; dries slow (~24 hrs), shrinks more.
- **Topping / lightweight (USG Plus 3 / blue lid):** low shrinkage, sands easily — ideal for second and finish coats. Don't embed tape with topping; it bonds weaker.
- **Setting-type (USG Easy Sand / Durabond 20-45-90-210):** chemically hardens in the named minutes regardless of humidity. Use for first coats, mesh tape, deep fills, and same-day recoats; **Durabond** is very hard to sand (use Easy Sand for sandable setting mud).

### Pro Notes

- **Setting-type compound** (Easy Sand 20/45/90) for first coats speeds same-day recoating and resists shrinkage; **lightweight all-purpose (Plus 3)** for final coats sands easily.
- Don't over-sand into the tape — **three thin, wide coats** beat one thick coat every time.
- Box and tube tools (**auto-taper, flat boxes, angle heads**) dramatically speed production work and lay a more consistent crown than hand-finishing.
- Always **prime with a dedicated drywall primer-sealer** before topcoat to equalize the suction difference between paper and compound.

title: Corner Bead and Inside/Outside Corners Done Right
content:
## Corners: Inside and Outside

Corners are where drywall jobs are judged. Straight, chip-resistant corners read as quality.

### Outside Corners

Protect outside corners with **corner bead**:
- **Metal (galvanized) bead** — nailed/screwed/crimped every **8-9"**. Classic and durable but dents.
- **Paper-faced metal bead (USG Sheetrock Beadex)** — bedded in joint compound with a corner roller/applicator; superior bond, fewer pops.
- **Vinyl bead** — won't rust; good for high-moisture areas.
- **No-Coat (Trim-Tex/No-Coat) flexible bead** — for **off-angle and arched** corners and bullnose; sets ultra-straight and resists cracking. **Trim-Tex** vinyl beads are a pro favorite.

**Installation:**
1. Set the bead plumb and straight — a bowed bead telegraphs through every coat.
2. For paper-faced: trowel **USG All-Purpose** on both walls, press bead in, wipe both flanges. For metal: fasten then coat.
3. Three coats, feathering **6", 9", 12"** off the nose. Run a knife along the bead nose as a screed.

### Inside Corners

- Fold **paper tape** along its center crease; embed in compound on both walls with a `5"` knife or a **corner trowel / inside corner roller**.
- Wipe each side to bed, leaving no trapped air or wrinkles. Trapped air = bubbles that telegraph and crack.
- Apply a fill and finish coat to **one side at a time** (let dry between) so your knife rides clean against the adjacent dry side.

### Bullnose and Specialty

- **Bullnose corners** use specialty bead (**Trim-Tex Bullnose**) with matching transition/adapter pieces at intersections.
- **Archways** use flexible vinyl bead snapped to the radius.

### Common Mistakes

- Starving the bead of compound (it pops off).
- Over-flexing/cracking metal bead at the fold.
- Not checking the corner for straight with a **4' level** before mud sets.

### Choosing the Right Bead

- **High-traffic outside corners** (hallways, garages): rugged **metal** or **paper-faced metal (Beadex)** for impact resistance.
- **Off-angle walls** (cathedral ceilings, bay windows): **Trim-Tex / No-Coat** flexible beads bend to any angle and won't crack.
- **Wet/exterior-adjacent areas:** rust-proof **vinyl** bead.
- **Decorative:** bullnose and chamfer beads with matching transition fittings at inside/outside intersections.

### Three-Coat Schedule for Corners

1. **Set/bed coat** to install the bead (compound for paper-faced, fasteners for metal).
2. **Fill coat** with **USG All-Purpose**, feathering ~9" off the nose.
3. **Finish coat** with **USG Plus 3**, feathering ~12", screeding off the bead nose for a razor-straight line. Sand lightly between coats only as needed.

### Tools

A **corner roller + corner finishing tool (flusher)** speeds inside corners dramatically on production jobs and lays a consistent, centered crown. Keep blades and rollers clean of dried mud, and check every corner for straight with a **4' level** before the compound sets — a crooked corner telegraphs through every coat and the paint.

title: Cement Board and Wet-Area Substrates: Durock for Tile
content:
## Cement Board for Wet Areas

Gypsum board — even moisture-resistant **greenboard** — should **not** be used as a tile substrate in showers/tub surrounds per **IRC R702.4.2**. Use cement board or an equivalent.

### Substrate Options

- **USG Durock Cement Board** (`1/2"` and `5/8"`) — the standard. **CertainTeed** and **National Gypsum PermaBase** are equivalents.
- **HardieBacker (James Hardie)** fiber-cement board — smoother face, lighter.
- **Foam tile backer (Schluter KERDI-BOARD, USG Durock Brand Foam)** — lightweight, waterproof by design.

### Installation

1. **Framing:** studs at **16" OC** max; blocking behind board edges. Tub/shower flanges integrated with the **moisture barrier**.
2. **Moisture management:** Install a **vapor barrier (6-mil poly)** behind the board **OR** a **surface waterproofing membrane** over the board — **never both** (avoids trapping moisture). **USG Durock** with **RedGard** or **Schluter KERDI** surface membrane is a common waterproof system.
3. **Fastening:** Use **1-1/4" or 1-5/8" cement board screws** (corrosion-resistant, e.g., **Rock-On / Durock screws**) at **8" OC** for walls, **6" OC** for floors. Keep **3/8"** from edges. Pre-drilling isn't needed with self-embedding heads.
4. **Gaps:** Leave **1/4"** at the tub/pan and **1/8"** between sheets; do not jam tight.
5. **Seams:** Embed **2" alkali-resistant mesh tape (FibaTape cement-board tape)** in **thinset mortar** — not joint compound — across all seams and corners.

### Floors

- For floor tile, set the board in a **full bed of thinset** over the subfloor (don't just screw it) and stagger joints; this prevents flex and cracked grout.

### Do / Don't

- **Do** waterproof penetrations (valve, spout) with membrane/sealant.
- **Don't** use drywall screws or drywall mesh tape on cement board.
- **Don't** use cement board as a finished surface — it's a substrate for tile/thinset only.

### Cutting Cement Board

- **Score and snap** with a carbide scoring knife for straight cuts — far less silica dust than power-cutting.
- For holes (valves, drains), use a **carbide hole saw** or jab saw; if you must power-cut, do it **outdoors with HEPA dust extraction** and a respirator (cement board cutting releases respirable crystalline silica).

### Greenboard vs. Cement Board

**Moisture-resistant gypsum (greenboard)** is acceptable behind tile in **non-wet** areas (e.g., a powder-room backsplash) but is **prohibited as a direct tile backer in showers and tub surrounds** per **IRC R702.4.2**. Wet areas require **cement board, fiber-cement, glass-mat gypsum (DensShield), or a foam backer board** with proper waterproofing.

### Why It Matters

Water behind tile rots framing and grows mold inside the wall where you can't see it until it's expensive. A correctly fastened, properly **waterproofed Durock** assembly — board on chairs of thinset at the floor, mesh-taped seams in thinset, membrane over penetrations, and the right corrosion-resistant screws at 8" OC — is the foundation of a shower that performs for decades rather than failing in a few years.

title: Cracks, Nail Pops, and Joint Banding: Causes and Repairs
content:
## Troubleshooting Drywall Defects

### Nail/Screw Pops

A pop is a fastener pushing the compound off the face, usually from **lumber shrinkage** as framing dries from ~19% to ~8% moisture content.
- **Repair:** Drive a new **#6 coarse drywall screw** about **1-1/2"** from the pop to re-anchor the board to the stud, then reset or remove the popped fastener. Dimple, **three thin coats** of **USG Plus 3**, sand, prime, paint.
- **Prevent:** Use **screws not nails**, glue + screw, and let framing dry/acclimate. Don't overdrive.

### Cracks

Causes and fixes by type:
- **Joint cracks (along seams):** Often from **paper tape not bedded** (trapped air) or **mesh tape with all-purpose mud**. Cut out, re-tape with **paper tape in setting compound (Easy Sand)**, three coats.
- **Corner cracks (door/window corners):** **Stress concentration** from framing movement/racking and butt joints landing on the corner. Repair and consider a flexible **No-Coat/Trim-Tex** bead. Best prevention: don't break drywall joints at opening corners — use an **L-cut** so no seam aligns with the corner.
- **Ceiling/truss cracks at wall-ceiling junction:** **Truss uplift** (seasonal). Fix with **floating corner / drywall clips (Simpson DUC)** and back-blocking so the ceiling board isn't fastened within ~16" of the wall. Use a crown molding or a flexible caulk joint as a relief detail.

### Joint Banding / Photographing

Visible joints under paint, especially in raking light:
- **Cause:** Uneven suction (paper face vs. compound) and inadequate feathering — a **Level 4** finish under **gloss paint** or big windows shows every joint.
- **Fix/Prevent:** Upgrade to **Level 5** — full skim coat or **high-build primer (USG Tuff-Hide / drywall primer-sealer)** over the whole surface to equalize porosity. Always **prime before topcoat** with a dedicated drywall primer.

### Diagnostic Tips

- Use a **raking light** at low angle to map all defects before repair.
- Identify **why** it cracked (shrinkage, movement, bad tape) — repairing the symptom without the cause guarantees a callback.
- For recurring movement cracks, a **control joint (USG #093/zinc)** relieves stress in long runs (>30 ft walls / >50 ft ceilings).

### Bubbles and Blisters in Tape

Bubbles under paper tape come from **insufficient compound behind the tape** (the knife squeezed it all out) — the tape has nothing to bond to. Slit the bubble, work fresh compound under it, re-bed, and recoat. Prevent by leaving an adequate bed and wiping at a moderate angle.

### Sanding Scratches and Ridges

Visible swirl marks or knife ridges under paint come from coarse grit or over-aggressive sanding. Final-sand with **220 grit** on a pole sander or a **HEPA-vac drywall sander**, then check with a **raking light** before primer. Catch ridges now — they are far cheaper to fix before paint than after.

### Root-Cause Discipline

Every one of these defects has a cause: lumber shrinkage, trapped air, wrong tape/mud pairing, framing movement, or skipped priming. Identify and fix the **cause**, not just the cosmetic symptom, or the same defect returns as a warranty callback.

title: Drywall Dust and Silica: Respiratory and Lift Safety
content:
## Drywall Dust, Silica, and Lifting Safety

### The Hazards

Joint compound sanding creates fine respirable dust. While gypsum dust itself is a nuisance/irritant, **some joint compounds historically contained crystalline silica**, and cutting **cement board (Durock)** releases **respirable crystalline silica (RCS)** — a known cause of **silicosis** and lung cancer. **OSHA 1926.1153** sets the silica PEL at **50 µg/m³** (8-hr TWA) and requires an exposure control plan.

### Dust Control

- Use a **drywall sander with integrated HEPA vacuum** — **Festool Planex LHS**, **DeWalt DCE800**, or a pole sander connected to a **HEPA dust extractor (Festool CT, Bosch VAC)**. This is the most effective engineering control.
- **Wet sanding** with a sponge eliminates airborne dust for small areas (slower, leaves more texture).
- For cement board, **score-and-snap** instead of power-cutting; if you must cut, use a **HEPA-vac-attached saw** and cut **outdoors**.
- Seal off the work area with poly and a **negative-air machine** in occupied remodels.

### Respiratory Protection

- Minimum **NIOSH N95** for nuisance gypsum dust; **P100 / half-face respirator (3M 6000 series)** for silica-generating tasks (cement board, heavy sanding) per your control plan.
- Fit-test and don't rely on a respirator alone — engineering controls (HEPA) come first in the hierarchy of controls.

### Eye, Skin, and Housekeeping

- Safety glasses/goggles; dust irritates eyes and skin.
- **Never dry-sweep** silica dust — use **HEPA vacuum** or wet methods. Dry sweeping re-suspends RCS.

### Lifting and Material Handling

Drywall is heavy: a `4x12 x 5/8"` board weighs **~95-100 lb**.
- Use a **drywall cart, panel hoist, or lift** for ceilings — never muscle ceiling boards solo.
- Two-person carry on edge; bend at the knees, keep the load close.
- Use a **drywall lift (Telpro PanelLift)** to set ceiling sheets safely and reduce shoulder/back injury.

### Hierarchy of Controls

OSHA expects controls applied in order: **elimination/substitution** (score-and-snap instead of cutting; pre-cut panels), then **engineering controls** (HEPA extraction, wet methods, local exhaust), then **administrative controls** (limit exposure time, schedule sanding when others are off-site, wet cleanup), and **PPE last**. A respirator alone is not a compliant program — engineering controls must come first.

### Housekeeping

- **Never dry-sweep or use compressed air** to clean drywall/silica dust — both re-suspend respirable particles. Use a **HEPA vacuum** or wet wiping.
- Bag and dispose of dust; don't track it through the house in a remodel.
- Change and launder dust-laden clothing separately so you don't carry silica home.

### Bottom Line

HEPA extraction + correct respirator + no dry sweeping protects lungs; lifts and carts protect backs. Build the **written silica exposure control plan** into the job **before** sanding or cement-board cutting starts, designate a competent person, and make HEPA sanding the default — not the exception — so the crew's lungs are still working at retirement.

title: Slab-on-Grade Pour: Base Prep, Vapor Barrier, Thickness, and Reinforcement
content:
## Slab-on-Grade From the Ground Up

A durable slab is built before any concrete arrives. The base and prep determine whether it cracks, heaves, or lasts 50 years.

### Subgrade and Base

- Strip topsoil/organics; compact the **subgrade** to **95% Standard Proctor** with a plate compactor.
- Place **4"-6" of compactable granular base** — `3/4" minus crushed stone` (Class 5 / road base) — and compact in lifts. This provides drainage and a uniform bearing surface.

### Vapor Barrier

- Install a **10-15 mil vapor barrier** (e.g., **Stego Wrap**, or minimum **6-mil poly** per **IRC R506.2.3**) directly under the slab for living/conditioned spaces.
- Lap seams **6"** and tape; seal penetrations. Place concrete directly on the barrier (current ACI 302 guidance) unless a blotter layer is specified.

### Thickness and Concrete

- Residential slabs: **4" minimum** (`R506.1`); garage/driveway often **5"-6"**; loaded areas thicker per design.
- Mix: **3,000-4,000 psi** at 28 days. **Quikrete 5000** (5,000 psi) for high-strength flatwork; ready-mix is preferred for any slab over ~1 cubic yard. Target **4"-5" slump** for hand-placed flatwork.

### Reinforcement

- **6x6 W1.4xW1.4 welded wire mesh (WWM)** or **#3/#4 rebar grid** at **18"** for crack control — keep it in the **upper third / mid-depth**, never lying on the ground. Use **chairs/dobies** to hold position (mesh pulled up with hooks is unreliable).
- **Grade 60 #4 rebar** for thickened edges and turn-downs.
- **Fiber-reinforced** mixes add secondary crack control but don't replace structural rebar.

### Forms and Screeds

- Set **2x form boards** to grade with a slight slope for exterior slabs (1/8"-1/4" per foot for drainage).
- Establish screed grade with a laser level; **wet-screed** or use screed rails.

### Edge and Isolation

- **Thickened edges** (turn-down) at perimeter and under bearing walls.
- **Isolation/expansion joint** material (1/2" fiber) where slab meets foundation walls, columns, and footings so the slab can move independently.

### Sequence

Base compaction → vapor barrier → reinforcement on chairs → forms/screed grade → pour → screed → bull float → finish → cure. Skipping compaction or floating the mesh up to the bottom are the two most common slab failures, and both are entirely preventable with chairs and a plate compactor.
code_references: IRC R506 — concrete floors on ground

title: Footings and Foundation Walls per IRC R403 and R404
content:
## Footings and Foundation Walls

Footings spread structural loads to the soil; foundation walls retain earth and carry the building. Both are code-governed life-safety elements.

### Footings — IRC R403

- **Width and thickness** come from **IRC Table R403.1** based on load-bearing value of the soil and number of stories. A typical **1-story footing** on 1,500 psf soil is **12" wide x 6" thick**; 2-story commonly **15"x7"**; verify the table.
- **Minimum thickness 6"**; footing **projection** beyond the wall = wall thickness each side, max equal to the footing thickness.
- **Depth below frost line** per local frost depth (**IRC R403.1.4**) — e.g., 42"-48" in cold climates. Monolithic/frost-protected shallow foundations (**FPSF, R403.3**) are an alternative.
- **Pier/column footings:** form round piers with **Sonotube** fiber tubes (8", 10", 12" dia.) set on a spread footing or bell, with **#4 vertical bars** and a **Simpson ABU/CBSQ** post base cast or set in the top.
- Place on **undisturbed or properly compacted soil**. Step footings on slopes per **R403.1.5** (max 1:2 slope, vertical steps formed).

### Reinforcement

- Continuous footings: typically **2) #4 Grade 60 rebar** longitudinal, supported on chairs, **3" clear** from the bottom (soil) and sides per **ACI 318** cover requirements.
- **Dowels** tie the wall to the footing — **#4 vertical** dowels bent into the footing and lapped to the wall steel.

### Foundation Walls — IRC R404

- Wall thickness and vertical reinforcement come from **IRC Tables R404.1.2(x)** based on wall height, unbalanced backfill height, and soil class.
- An **8" cast-in-place wall, 8' tall, with 7' backfill** may require **#4 vertical at 48" OC** or tighter — read the exact table for your soil.
- **Minimum concrete strength f'c = 2,500 psi** (**R402.2**); 3,000 psi typical for walls/footings, higher for severe weathering exposure.

### Anchorage and Waterproofing

- **Anchor bolts:** `1/2"` min, embedded **7"**, max **6'-0" OC** and within **12"** of each plate end (**R403.1.6**). **Simpson Strong-Tie** mudsill anchors or **titen HD** anchors are common.
- **Damp-proofing/waterproofing** below-grade walls (**R406**) and **drainage (R405)** — perforated drain tile in gravel.

### Drainage and Backfill

- Install a **perforated foundation drain (drain tile)** in clean gravel at the footing, sloped to daylight or a sump, per **IRC R405**.
- Damp-proof or waterproof the exterior wall face (**R406**) before backfill.
- **Do not backfill** until the wall has cured and is **braced top and bottom** (floor framing or temporary bracing) — backfilling against an unbraced green wall is a classic cause of cracked and pushed-in foundation walls.

### Concrete Placement

- Place walls in lifts and **consolidate with a concrete vibrator** to eliminate honeycomb and voids around rebar — under-vibrated walls leak and expose steel.
- Keep the mix to a placeable but not soupy slump (**4"-5"**); don't add water to make it flow.

### Inspection Hold Points

Footing **trench depth/width**, **rebar size/cover/laps**, **dowels**, and **anchor-bolt spacing/embedment** are inspected **before the pour**. Never pour over **uninspected, saturated, or frozen** subgrade — frozen ground heaves when it thaws and saturated soil loses bearing. Confirm forms are plumb, braced, and tied so they don't blow out under the hydrostatic pressure of fresh concrete.
materials_required: 1/2" anchor bolts or Simpson Titen HD

title: Rebar Placement, Cover, and Lap Splice Lengths
content:
## Rebar Placement and Lap Splices

Reinforcing steel only works when it's the right grade, in the right position, with adequate cover and proper laps.

### Grades and Sizes

- **Grade 60** (60 ksi yield) is standard for residential/commercial — marked with **"60"** or a single grade line. **#4 = 1/2"**, **#5 = 5/8"**, **#3 = 3/8"** (ties/stirrups).
- Bar number = diameter in eighths of an inch (#4 = 4/8 = 1/2").

### Concrete Cover (ACI 318)

Cover protects steel from corrosion and fire:
- **3"** when cast against and permanently exposed to **earth** (footings).
- **1-1/2"** for formed surfaces exposed to weather (#5 and smaller).
- **3/4"** for interior slabs/walls not exposed to weather.
- Maintain cover with **chairs, dobies (concrete bricks), and bolsters** — never let steel sit on the ground or rest on the form face.

### Lap Splices

Where bars are continued, they overlap so load transfers through the concrete (a **tension lap splice**). A common field rule of thumb for Grade 60, 3,000-4,000 psi concrete, uncoated bars:
- **Class B tension lap ≈ 40-48 bar diameters (db)** — verify against **ACI 318** development tables and the structural drawings.
- `#4 bar`: db = 0.5", so a 48db lap ≈ **24"** (commonly specified as a min **24"** lap for #4 in residential footings/walls).
- `#5 bar`: 48db ≈ **30"**.
- **Stagger** splices in adjacent bars; don't lap all bars at the same section.

### Tying and Support

- Tie intersections with **16-gauge annealed tie wire** using a **bag tie/snap tie** pattern or a **Makita/Max rebar tying gun** for speed and consistency.
- Support grids on **chairs at 3'-4' OC** so they don't sag under foot traffic or the weight of fresh concrete.
- Bend corners with proper radius (use a **hickey/rebar bender**) — sharp 90s crack; corner bars must lap into both walls.

### Don'ts

- Don't substitute smooth bar for deformed where deformed is specified.
- Don't "hook and pull" mesh up after pouring — it ends up on the bottom and does nothing.
- Don't reduce cover to clear formwork — it leads to corrosion and spalling.

Verify size, grade, spacing, cover, and lap length before the inspector arrives and before any concrete is ordered.
tools_required: Makita or Max rebar tying gun

title: Mix Design, Slump, and PSI Selection for the Job
content:
## Choosing the Right Mix: Slump and PSI

Matching the mix to the application controls strength, workability, durability, and cracking.

### Compressive Strength (PSI)

- **2,500 psi** — minimum per **IRC R402.2** for footings/walls in mild climates.
- **3,000-3,500 psi** — typical footings, foundation walls, interior slabs.
- **4,000 psi** — exterior flatwork, driveways, garage slabs; better freeze-thaw durability. **IRC Table R402.2** requires **3,500-4,500 psi** for slabs/foundations exposed to **severe weathering**.
- **4,500-5,000 psi** — heavy-duty/commercial slabs. **Quikrete 5000** and **Sakrete 5000 Plus** are bagged 5,000 psi options for small pours/posts.

### Slump (Workability)

Slump measures consistency (a slump cone test per **ASTM C143**):
- **2"-3"** — stiff, low water/cement ratio, high strength (formed walls with vibration).
- **4"-5"** — typical flatwork; placeable and finishable.
- **5"-6"+** — wet, easy to place but **weaker and more prone to cracking/shrinkage**. Never add site water just to ease placement — it lowers strength dramatically (each extra gallon per yard can cost ~200-300 psi).
- Use a **mid-range or high-range water reducer (superplasticizer)** to increase slump **without** adding water when you need flow.

### Water-Cement Ratio

Lower w/c = higher strength and durability. Target **≤0.50** for exterior/freeze-thaw, **≤0.45** for severe exposure.

### Air Entrainment

- **Exterior concrete in freeze-thaw climates must be air-entrained** — typically **5-7%** entrained air (**ACI 318 / IRC R402.2**). The microscopic bubbles relieve internal freeze pressure and prevent scaling.
- **Do not air-entrain interior slabs that will be hard-troweled** — air causes blistering/delamination under power trowels.

### Admixtures

- **Accelerators (non-chloride, like W.R. Meadows / BASF)** for cold-weather pours.
- **Retarders** for hot weather/long hauls.
- **Fiber** (poly or steel) for secondary crack control in slabs.

### Aggregate Size

Maximum aggregate size should not exceed **1/3 the slab thickness**, **3/4 the clear spacing between bars**, or **3/4 the cover**. Common flatwork uses **3/4"** or **1"** max aggregate; smaller aggregate (**3/8"**) for thin or heavily reinforced sections.

### Bagged vs. Ready-Mix

- **Bagged mixes** (**Quikrete 5000**, **Sakrete 5000 Plus**, fast-setting post mixes) suit small pours, footings for posts, and repairs — typically usable up to roughly a yard before mixing labor and consistency favor ready-mix.
- **Ready-mix** is the right call for any slab, wall, or footing of meaningful volume — consistent batching, controlled w/c ratio, and tested air content.

### Ordering Ready-Mix

Specify: **strength (psi), max aggregate size, slump, air content, and admixtures**. Confirm the **batch ticket** on delivery (it lists the mix design and any water added), note the **time batched** (place within ~90 minutes / before initial set per **ASTM C94**), and **never exceed the allowed retempering water** — adding site water to ease placement quietly destroys strength and durability. The right spec and discipline up front prevents weak, scaling, or cracked concrete that no amount of finishing can fix later.

title: Finishing and Curing: Float, Trowel, Broom, and Cure
content:
## Finishing and Curing Flatwork

Finishing develops surface durability and appearance; curing develops strength. Both are timing-critical.

### Placing and Screeding

- Place and consolidate (vibrate formed sections), then **screed** to grade with a straightedge in a sawing motion, pulling excess.
- **Bull float** immediately after screeding with a **magnesium bull float (Marshalltown)** to embed aggregate and cut high/fill low spots. Float **before bleed water** appears — never overwork.

### Wait for Bleed Water

The single most important rule: **wait for bleed water to evaporate** before edging/jointing/troweling. Finishing while bleed water is on the surface traps water under the cream and causes **scaling, blistering, and delamination**.

### Edging and Jointing

- **Edge** the perimeter with an edger for a rounded, chip-resistant edge.
- Cut **control joints** (see jointing article) with a groover or saw at the right time.

### Floating and Troweling

- **Magnesium/wood float (hand or fresno)** opens the surface and brings up a working paste — a floated finish is slip-resistant.
- **Steel trowel** for a hard, dense, smooth interior finish — make multiple passes as the slab stiffens, raising the trowel angle each pass. **Power trowel (Marshalltown / Allen)** for large slabs.
- **Do not steel-trowel exterior air-entrained concrete** — it densifies the surface and causes blistering/scaling.

### Broom Finish (Exterior)

- After floating, drag a **concrete broom** perpendicular to traffic/drainage for slip resistance on walks, driveways, and patios. Time it so the broom leaves a clean texture without tearing.

### Curing — Critical for Strength

Concrete needs **moisture and temperature** to hydrate. Cure for a **minimum 7 days** (3 days for high-early mixes):
- **Wet cure:** keep surface continuously wet (burlap, soaker hoses, ponding) — best result.
- **Plastic sheeting** to retain moisture (may cause mottling).
- **Curing compound:** spray-applied membrane like **W.R. Meadows 1100-CLEAR / SEALTIGHT** or **Quikrete Acrylic Cure & Seal** — convenient and effective; apply right after finishing.
- **Cold weather:** protect with blankets/heat, keep above **50°F**; **hot weather:** fog, evaporation retarder, shade.

Proper curing can add **30-50% to ultimate strength** versus a slab left to dry out. Skipping the cure is the most common, most damaging finishing mistake.

title: Control, Construction, and Expansion Joints
content:
## Joints: Where and When to Cut Them

Concrete **will** crack as it shrinks during curing. Joints control **where** it cracks so you get a straight line instead of a random one.

### Control (Contraction) Joints

Control joints create a weakened plane so shrinkage cracks form below the joint, hidden.
- **Spacing:** roughly **24-36 times the slab thickness** in feet — for a **4" slab**, joints every **8-12 feet**; keep panels as **square as possible** (length:width ≤ 1.5:1).
- **Depth:** cut **1/4 of the slab depth** minimum (a 4" slab → **1"** deep).
- **Timing:**
  - **Tooled (grooved)** joints during finishing while plastic.
  - **Saw-cut** joints with an **early-entry saw (Soff-Cut)** within **1-4 hours**, or a conventional **walk-behind saw** within **6-18 hours** — late enough that the saw doesn't ravel the edge, early enough to beat random cracking. In hot weather this window shrinks fast.
- Don't run reinforcement continuously through a control joint if it's meant to fully open (or use smooth dowels).

### Construction (Cold) Joints

Where a pour stops and resumes:
- Form a clean bulkhead; install **smooth dowels (greased on one side)** or a **keyway** so load transfers but the slab can move.
- Roughen/clean the joint and use a **bonding agent** if a monolithic bond is desired; for slabs, dowels at the joint are standard.

### Isolation (Expansion) Joints

Isolation joints separate the slab from fixed elements so each moves independently:
- Place **1/2" preformed fiber (asphalt-impregnated) joint filler** where a slab abuts **foundation walls, columns, footings, equipment pads, and at the garage-to-driveway interface**.
- Around penetrations (posts, pipes) use isolation board or a circular isolation detail to relieve stress risers.
- True "expansion" joints are less critical for normal-temperature exterior slabs than isolation/contraction joints, but long exterior runs benefit from periodic expansion provisions.

### Sealing

- After curing, **seal active joints** with a flexible **self-leveling polyurethane sealant** over a **backer rod** to keep water/debris out (prevents freeze-thaw spalling at joint edges).

### Common Mistakes

- **Cutting too late** — random cracks beat you to it.
- **Joints too shallow** — crack ignores the joint and wanders.
- **Panels too large or rectangular** — interior cracking. Keep panels square and within spacing.

Plan the joint layout on paper before the pour; mark lines for the saw crew.

title: Cracking, Scaling, and Cold Joints: Diagnosis and Prevention
content:
## Troubleshooting Concrete Defects

### Cracking

Identify the type to find the cause:
- **Plastic shrinkage cracks** — short, random surface cracks appearing **within hours** of placement, from rapid surface evaporation (hot, windy, dry). **Prevent:** fog spray, evaporation retarder, windbreaks, sunshades; place in cooler hours.
- **Drying shrinkage cracks** — develop over days/weeks as the slab loses moisture. **Control** with proper **joint spacing/depth** and adequate **reinforcement**; lower water content.
- **Settlement cracks** — over rebar or poorly compacted subgrade. **Prevent** with compaction, proper cover, and consolidation.
- **Structural cracks** — wide, through-depth, from overload or inadequate footing/rebar. Requires engineering evaluation.

### Scaling and Spalling

Surface flaking/peeling, common on exterior flatwork:
- **Causes:** finishing over **bleed water**, **steel-troweling air-entrained** exterior concrete, **no air entrainment** in freeze-thaw climates, **de-icing salts**, or **inadequate curing**.
- **Prevent:** specify **air-entrained 4,000+ psi** mix, **broom finish** (don't hard-trowel exterior), **wait for bleed water**, **cure 7 days**, and **don't use de-icing salts the first winter**. Apply a penetrating **silane/siloxane sealer** for added protection.

### Cold Joints

A cold joint forms when fresh concrete is placed against concrete that has begun to set, with no proper bond.
- **Cause:** delays between truck loads, placing too slowly in hot weather.
- **Result:** a visible line and a plane of weakness/leakage.
- **Prevent:** place continuously, **vibrate/consolidate** across the interface while the previous lift is still plastic, schedule trucks tightly, and use **retarder** in hot weather to extend working time. If a planned stop is needed, form a proper **construction joint with dowels/keyway**.

### Crazing and Dusting

- **Crazing** — fine cosmetic hairline web on the surface from rapid surface drying; mostly aesthetic.
- **Dusting** — soft, powdery surface from finishing bleed water in, low strength, carbonation, or poor cure. **Prevent** with proper finishing timing and curing; remediate with a densifier/hardener.

### Curling and Delamination

- **Curling** — slab edges lift as the top dries/shrinks faster than the bottom. Controlled by lower-shrinkage mixes, good curing of the top surface, proper joint spacing, and adequate slab thickness.
- **Delamination** — the troweled top skin separates from the concrete below, usually from **sealing the surface (early troweling or air entrainment) while bleed water/air is trapped underneath**. Prevent by not hard-troweling air-entrained exterior concrete and waiting for bleeding to finish.

### Repair Materials

- Fine cracks: low-viscosity **epoxy or polyurethane crack injection**.
- Spalls/scaled areas: clean to sound concrete, prime, and patch with a **polymer-modified repair mortar**; topical overlays for large areas.
- Protect repaired and new exterior slabs with a penetrating **silane/siloxane sealer (W.R. Meadows)**.

### Diagnostic Approach

Document crack **width, depth, pattern, and timing**; review the **batch ticket** (psi, air, water added) and the **weather** at placement. Most defects trace to a short list of process failures: **water added on site, finishing with bleed water still present, missing air entrainment in a freeze-thaw climate, joints cut too late or too shallow, or no curing**. Fix the **process** — not just the surface — or the next slab fails the same way.

title: Concrete Silica, Chemical Burns, and PPE
content:
## Concrete Safety: Silica, Burns, and PPE

Concrete work carries two distinct chemical hazards plus the usual heavy-material risks. Both can cause permanent injury.

### Respirable Crystalline Silica

Cutting, grinding, drilling, and dry-sawing concrete release **respirable crystalline silica (RCS)** — causing **silicosis**, lung cancer, and COPD. **OSHA 1926.1153** mandates a **PEL of 50 µg/m³** (8-hr TWA), an **action level of 25 µg/m³**, and a written **exposure control plan**.
- **Engineering controls first:** use **wet cutting** (water-fed saws/grinders) or **tool-mounted HEPA dust extraction** (e.g., **Bosch**, **DeWalt**, **Milwaukee** dust shrouds + HEPA vac). Table 1 of the standard lists compliant control methods.
- **Respirators:** when controls aren't enough, **N95** minimum; **P100 half-face (3M)** for heavy grinding/cutting per the plan and fit-test.
- **Never dry-sweep** concrete dust — HEPA vac or wet methods only.

### Cement Chemical Burns and Dermatitis

Wet concrete is **highly alkaline (pH ~12-13)** and contains **hexavalent chromium**:
- Prolonged skin contact causes **severe chemical burns** (third-degree burns reported from kneeling in wet concrete) and **allergic/irritant dermatitis**.
- **PPE:** **waterproof gloves (nitrile/rubber)**, **waterproof boots**, long sleeves/pants. **Alkali-resistant kneepads** — never kneel directly in wet concrete.
- **Eye protection:** sealed goggles — a splash of wet concrete can cause permanent eye damage. Flush splashes immediately with water for **15+ minutes** and seek medical care for eyes/burns.
- Wash skin promptly with **pH-neutral cleanser**; don't let concrete dry on skin.

### Material Handling and Equipment

- An **80 lb bag** of mix is a back hazard — lift with legs, use a cart/hand truck.
- **Pump lines** can whip under pressure — clear the discharge zone; never look into a line.
- **Power trowels and saws** — guards in place, secure footing; trowel arms can spin and injure.
- Hearing protection around saws, vibrators, and compressors.

### Heat and Site

- Concrete crews work in sun and heat — **hydrate, shade, rotate** to prevent heat illness.
- Watch for **trench/excavation collapse** when forming footings — slope, bench, or shore per **OSHA 1926 Subpart P** for trenches **5 ft+**.

### Bottom Line

Wet-cut or HEPA for silica, waterproof PPE and goggles against caustic burns, and lift/handle smart. Build the **silica control plan** before the saw or grinder comes out.

title: Installing Architectural Asphalt Shingles: Exposure, Nailing, and Layout
content:
## Overview
Architectural (laminate) asphalt shingles are the workhorse of residential steep-slope roofing. This procedure covers GAF Timberline HDZ, Owens Corning Duration, and CertainTeed Landmark — all dimensional shingles with a 5-5/8" exposure and a self-sealing strip.

## Slope Requirements
- Standard application: **4:12 and steeper** per IRC R905.2.2.
- Low-slope (2:12 to 4:12): permitted only with **double underlayment** and cemented laps.
- Below 2:12: shingles are prohibited — switch to a membrane system.

## Starter Course
Never cut field shingles for starter. Use a dedicated starter strip (GAF Pro-Start, OC Starter Strip Plus) with the factory adhesive bead **1" up from the eave edge** to bond the first course and resist blow-off.
- Overhang the drip edge by **1/4" to 3/8"**.

## Nailing Pattern
Fastener placement is the #1 warranty-defining detail.
- **4-nail standard**: nails 1" and 13" from each end, in the nail zone (the reinforced **StrikeZone** on HDZ).
- **6-nail high-wind / >130 mph**: add two intermediate nails. Required in HVHZ and most coastal zones.
- Drive nails **flush**, never overdriven (cuts the mat) or underdriven (tents the tab). Use 1-1/4" galvanized roofing nails, longer over decking + existing layer.
- Nails must penetrate **3/4" into deck or fully through** thinner sheathing.

## Exposure and Offset
- Maintain **5-5/8" exposure** — chalk horizontal lines every few courses to prevent drift.
- Stagger joints per the manufacturer's pattern (HDZ uses the **LayerLock** racking for a 6" offset minimum between courses).

## Hip and Ridge
Cap with matched ridge product (GAF Seal-A-Ridge, TimberTex). Maintain **5" exposure** on caps, fasten with 2 nails per cap **above the exposure/sealant line**, and seal the final cap nail heads with asphalt plastic cement.

## Workflow Tips
- Bundle-load the ridge, not the eave, to balance the deck.
- Pneumatic coil nailers (Bostitch RN46, DeWalt DWMC150) speed production but **must** be pressure-tuned and depth-checked hourly.
- Hand-seal in cold weather (<40°F) since thermal sealing won't activate.

## Common Mistakes
- High-nailing above the nail line voids the wind warranty.
- Skimping starter at rakes — rake starter prevents wind uplift on gable edges.
- Inconsistent exposure telegraphs across the roof in raking light.
tools_required: roofing coil nailer (Bostitch RN46 / DeWalt DWMC150)

title: Underlayment and Ice-and-Water Shield Requirements (IRC R905.1.1)
content:
## Purpose
Underlayment is the secondary water barrier beneath shingles. Code defines minimum types, laps, and ice-barrier placement based on climate.

## Standard Underlayment (IRC R905.1.1)
For slopes **4:12 and greater**, a single layer of underlayment is required:
- ASTM D226 Type I (#15 felt) or Type II (#30 felt), or
- ASTM D4869 / D8257 synthetic underlayment (GAF FeltBuster, OC ProArmor, CertainTeed RoofRunner).

**Lap requirements:**
- Horizontal (head) laps: **2"** minimum.
- End laps: **4"** minimum.
- Synthetics: follow printed overlap lines (typically 4" side / 6" end).

## Low-Slope Underlayment (2:12 to 4:12)
Per R905.1.1, **two layers** of underlayment are required: start with a 19" starter strip, then full 36" sheets lapped 19" so every point is double-covered.

## Ice Barrier (IRC R905.1.2)
In regions where the average January temperature is **25°F or colder** (or where ice damming has a history), a self-adhered ice-and-water membrane is required:
- Must extend from the eave edge to a point **at least 24" inside the exterior wall line** (measured along the slope).
- On low slopes and around valleys, penetrations, and skylights it is strongly recommended even outside cold zones.

**Products:** Grace Ice & Water Shield, GAF WeatherWatch / StormGuard, CertainTeed WinterGuard.

## Membrane Installation Best Practices
- Apply to **clean, dry decking** above 40°F (or use HT/high-temp formulas).
- Roll out, peel release film, and broom-press to eliminate air and fishmouths.
- Lap upper sheets over lower by **3-1/2"**; side laps **6"**.
- Seal around pipe boots and in valleys before shingling.

## Valley and Wall Detailing
- Line open and closed valleys with ice-and-water full-width (36") centered on the valley.
- Run membrane **up sidewalls and headwalls** behind step flashing.

## Inspection Checklist
- Verify ice-barrier coverage past the warm-wall line.
- Confirm underlayment laps shed water (upper over lower).
- No staples exposed in water channels; cap-nail or plate-fasten synthetics per manufacturer.
tools_required: cap-nailer or hammer-tacker with cap staples

title: Flashing Systems: Step, Valley, and Pipe Boot Detailing
content:
## Why Flashing Matters
Most roof leaks originate at transitions and penetrations, not in the field. Per IRC R903.2, flashing is required at wall and roof intersections, valleys, and projections. Do flashing right and the roof outlives the shingles.

## Step Flashing (Sidewalls)
Use individual **bent step flashings** — never continuous flashing — along a sloped roof-to-wall junction.
- Standard piece: **4" x 4" x 8-10" long**, bent 90 degrees.
- Install **one piece per shingle course**, woven so each step laps the course below by the shingle exposure and the piece above laps it.
- Fasten to the **roof deck**, not the wall, with one nail high in the vertical leg.
- Counterflashing or siding/housewrap covers the vertical leg; never rely on caulk alone.

## Headwall Flashing
Use continuous apron flashing where a slope meets a vertical wall head-on. Extend **4" onto the roof and up the wall**, tuck behind WRB/siding, and hem the leading edge.

## Valley Flashing
- **Open valley**: metal W-valley (painted steel, aluminum, or copper) over ice-and-water. Trim shingles back **6" each side** of centerline, clip the upslope corners, and embed the cut edge in a 3" bead of cement. Hold field nails **at least 6"** from valley center.
- **Closed-cut valley**: shingle one plane through, then cut the other 2" off-center; embed cut shingle edge in cement.

## Pipe Boot / Penetration Flashing
- Use a one-piece boot (neoprene or lead) sized to the pipe.
- Shingle **up to the bottom** of the boot, slip the boot flange **under** the upslope shingles and **over** the downslope shingles.
- Set the flange in cement; fasten only the top and sides above the boot.
- For neoprene boots, expect UV failure in ~10-15 years — spec **lead** or add a storm collar in harsh sun.

## Drip Edge and Kickout
- Drip edge along eaves goes **under** underlayment; at rakes it goes **over** (R905.2.8.5).
- Install a **kickout flashing** where a roof edge meets a wall to divert water into the gutter — its absence is a classic cause of wall rot.

## QA Tips
Water-test or hose-test penetrations before final. Never substitute sealant for proper lap geometry; flashing should shed water by gravity alone.
code_references: IRC R905.2.8 — flashing for asphalt shingles

title: Low-Slope Roofing: TPO and EPDM Membrane Basics
content:
## When to Use Low-Slope Membrane
For slopes **below 2:12** (and commonly up to 3:12 on commercial decks), single-ply membranes replace shingles. The two dominant systems are **TPO** (thermoplastic) and **EPDM** (rubber). Major manufacturers: **Carlisle SynTec, Holcim/Firestone (UltraPly TPO, RubberGard EPDM), GAF EverGuard, Johns Manville**.

## TPO vs. EPDM
- **TPO**: white, heat-reflective (high SRI), **heat-welded** seams. Common thicknesses **45, 60, 80 mil**. Spec 60-mil minimum for commercial; 80-mil for high-traffic/hail.
- **EPDM**: black (or white), highly flexible, excellent UV/ozone life. Seams are **tape-adhered (seam tape)** or, older systems, liquid splice adhesive. Thicknesses 45-90 mil.

## Substrate and Insulation
- Mechanically fasten or adhere **polyiso insulation** (R-6/inch) to the deck; stagger board joints, then a **cover board** (DensDeck, SecurShield HD) for puncture/walk resistance.
- Slope to drains at a minimum **1/4" per foot** (tapered iso) to avoid ponding.

## Attachment Methods
- **Mechanically attached**: fasteners + plates in the seam, membrane rolled out and welded.
- **Fully adhered**: bonding adhesive (Carlisle CAV-GRIP, water-based) to cover board for high wind uplift and a smooth look.

## TPO Heat Welding
