- Use a robotic welder (Leister Varimat) for field seams; hot-air hand welder + silicone roller for details.
- Target **welder temp ~1,050-1,150°F** tuned daily for ambient conditions; run a **test weld** each morning and **probe** the cooled seam.
- Minimum seam weld width: **1-1/2"**.

## EPDM Seaming
- Clean mating surfaces with seam cleaner, apply **6" seam tape**, roll firmly with a 2" steel roller, lap-seal the exposed edge.

## Flashing and Terminations
- Flash penetrations with pre-molded pipe boots and uncured/cured membrane corners.
- Terminate at walls with termination bar + water-cut-off mastic, then counterflash.
- Set drains with target sumps and clamping rings; pitch-pan only as a last resort.

## QA
Probe **100% of seams** with a cotton-tipped probe once cooled, flood-test where feasible, and document fastener pull-tests for the wind warranty.

title: Attic Ventilation: Balancing Intake and Exhaust
content:
## Why Ventilation Matters
Proper attic ventilation removes heat and moisture, extends shingle life, prevents ice dams, and is a warranty condition for GAF, Owens Corning, and CertainTeed. Imbalanced systems cause condensation, mold, and premature deck rot.

## The 1/300 Rule (IRC R806.2)
Provide **1 sq ft of net free ventilation area (NFA) per 300 sq ft** of attic floor when intake and exhaust are balanced (vapor retarder or balanced vents present). Otherwise the ratio is **1/150**.
- Example: a 1,500 sq ft attic needs **5 sq ft total NFA** — split ~50/50 intake and exhaust.

## Balance Intake and Exhaust
- Aim for a **50/50 split**, or slightly **more intake than exhaust** (never more exhaust than intake).
- Exhaust-heavy systems pull air from the path of least resistance — often another roof vent — short-circuiting the attic and starving the system.

## Intake (Low / Eave)
- **Continuous soffit vents** are the gold standard. Keep insulation off the soffit with **rafter baffles (proper vents)** to maintain the air channel.
- Verify NFA printed on the product; many decorative soffit panels deliver far less than they appear to.

## Exhaust (High / Ridge)
- **Ridge vent** is preferred: GAF Cobra (Cobra Rigid Vent 3, Cobra SnowCountry), OC VentSure, CertainTeed Ridge Vent.
- Cut the deck slot back **1" from each side** of the ridge board (leave solid at the ends); cap with matching ridge shingles.
- **Do not mix** ridge vents with powered/box vents on the same attic — they short-circuit each other.

## Powered and Specialty Vents
- Powered fans and gable vents can work but must not undercut a ridge-and-soffit system.
- In cathedral/vaulted assemblies, maintain a continuous baffle from soffit to ridge.

## Verification Checklist
- Calculate NFA both sides; confirm intake >= exhaust.
- Confirm baffles installed at every rafter bay.
- No bath/dryer ducts terminating in the attic — vent them through the roof.
- Snow-country: use baffled ridge vent to resist wind-driven snow infiltration.
materials_required: GAF Cobra Rigid Vent 3 ridge vent

title: Diagnosing Roof Leaks: Tracing Water to the Source
content:
## First Principle: Water Travels
The interior stain is rarely below the actual entry point. Water enters high, runs down rafters, sheathing, or felt, and drips where geometry stops it. Diagnose by ruling out penetrations and transitions before blaming the field.

## Highest-Probability Sources (in order)
1. **Flashings** — step, headwall, valley, chimney counterflashing.
2. **Penetrations** — pipe boots (cracked neoprene), HVAC curbs, satellite mounts.
3. **Valleys** — debris dams, undersized cut-back, nails too close to center.
4. **Ice dams** — water backing up under shingles at eaves (cold climates).
5. **Field defects** — overdriven/high nails, wind-lifted tabs, mechanical damage.
6. **Condensation** — misdiagnosed as a leak; check ventilation and bath fans.

## Inspection Procedure
- From the attic, trace the stain **uphill** along the rafter; look for daylight, rust around nails, and water tracks on the underside of the deck.
- Mark the suspected area and measure to the ridge/eave/rakes to translate to the exterior.
- On the roof, inspect the corresponding area for the source list above.

## Controlled Water Test
Work **bottom-up** with a helper inside:
- Wet the eave/lowest suspect area first for several minutes; if no leak, move up.
- Isolate one variable at a time (boot, then valley, then sidewall). Rushing the hose up the roof makes the test useless.

## Common Culprits and Fixes
- **Cracked pipe boot**: slip a new boot or a EPDM retrofit collar; reseal flange under upslope shingles.
- **Failed chimney counterflashing**: re-cut reglet, install new counterflashing with sealant, don't rely on tar.
- **Exposed/high nails**: dab with roofing cement or seal with a compatible flashing tape.
- **Ice dam**: add ice-and-water at eaves, improve insulation and ventilation; the membrane treats the symptom, ventilation treats the cause.

## When It's Not a Leak
Frost in the attic that melts on warm days mimics a roof leak. Check for unvented bath/kitchen/dryer exhaust and inadequate NFA before tearing into the roof.

## Documentation
Photograph each suspect, log the water-test sequence, and note the fix — critical for warranty and callbacks.

title: Roofing Fall Protection and OSHA Compliance
content:
## The Rule You Cannot Skip
Under OSHA 1926.501(b)(13), workers on residential roofs **6 feet or more** above a lower level must be protected by **guardrails, safety nets, or a personal fall arrest system (PFAS)**. Conventional fall protection is the default; a written, site-specific fall-protection plan is required only when those are proven infeasible.

## Personal Fall Arrest System (PFAS)
A complete PFAS (1926.502(d)) has three parts, the **ABCs**:
- **Anchorage**: rated for **5,000 lb** per worker (or engineered 2:1 safety factor). Use a ridge anchor lagged into rafters/trusses, not just sheathing.
- **Body harness**: full-body, snug, dorsal D-ring (no body belts).
- **Connectors**: shock-absorbing lanyard or **self-retracting lifeline (SRL)**. Verify total fall distance (free fall + deceleration + harness stretch + safety margin) clears the next level — free fall limited to **6 ft**.

## Slope-Specific Rules
- **Low-slope roofs** (4:12 and less): warning lines + safety monitor permitted in some operations, but PFAS or guardrails preferred near edges.
- **Steep roofs** (>4:12): PFAS or guardrails with toeboards required.

## Ladders (1926.1053)
- Extend the ladder **3 ft above** the landing/eave.
- **4:1 pitch ratio** (1 ft out per 4 ft up).
- Secure top and bottom; maintain **3 points of contact**; never stand on the top two rungs.

## Hazard Controls
- **Skylights and roof openings**: cover and label, or guard — they are leading killers. Covers must hold **2x the load**.
- **Weather**: stop work for ice, frost, wet membrane, or wind gusts that compromise footing/material handling.
- **Heat**: water, rest, shade; rotate crews on hot TPO/asphalt.
- **Electrical**: maintain clearance from service drops; locate overhead lines before raising ladders.

## Daily Practice
- Pre-shift inspection of all harnesses, lanyards, anchors — tag out any with deployed indicators, cuts, or corrosion.
- Train every worker on competent-person rescue planning; a suspended worker needs prompt rescue to avoid suspension trauma.
- Keep the deck clean of debris and offcuts to prevent slips.

title: Surface Preparation and Priming for Lasting Adhesion
content:
## Prep Is 80% of the Job
No coating outperforms its preparation. Adhesion failures (peeling, blistering) trace almost entirely to skipped prep. Follow the sequence: **clean, repair, sand, spot-prime, prime**.

## Cleaning
- Interior: degrease kitchens/baths with TSP substitute; rinse and dry.
- Exterior: pressure-wash at **1,500-2,500 PSI** with a cleaning solution to remove chalk, mildew, and dirt; treat mildew with a bleach solution. Allow **24-48 hrs** to fully dry before coating.

## Repair and Patch
- Fill nail holes and cracks with lightweight spackle (interior) or exterior-grade filler.
- Re-caulk gaps at trim with a paintable **siliconized acrylic latex** (e.g., elastomeric for siding gaps). Caulk does not bridge moving joints unless rated for movement.

## Sanding and Dulling
- Scuff glossy surfaces to **promote mechanical bond**; 150-220 grit for trim, 80-120 for heavy buildup.
- Feather-sand peeling paint edges so transitions don't telegraph.

## Choosing the Right Primer
- **Bare drywall / new construction**: PVA drywall primer or a high-build (Sherwin-Williams ProBlock, PPG SealGrip).
- **Bare wood (exterior)**: alkyd or acrylic wood primer; bleeding woods (cedar, redwood) need a **stain-blocking** primer.
- **Stains, smoke, water, tannin, knots**: **Zinsser B-I-N (shellac)** for the toughest stains and odor; **Zinsser 123** (water-based bonding) for general use; **Kilz** for water stains.
- **Glossy / slick / tile / laminate**: a bonding primer (123, STIX) plus scuff-sanding.
- **Bare metal**: rust-inhibitive metal primer.

## Spot-Priming vs. Full Priming
- Spot-prime patches and bare areas, then full-prime when substrate is porous/inconsistent or color is changing dramatically.
- Tint primer toward the topcoat color to improve hide and reduce topcoat count.

## Mil Thickness and Dry Times
- Apply primer at the spec WFT (typically **3-4 wet mils**) for ~1.0-1.5 dry mils.
- Respect recoat windows: shellac primers recoat in ~45 min; acrylics ~1 hr; alkyds often need overnight.

## QA Checklist
- Surface clean, dull, dry, and dust-free (tack-wipe before topcoat).
- No flashing of patched areas (prime to equalize porosity).
- Caulk skinned over before painting to avoid cracking.

title: Interior Repaint System: Cut-In, Roll, Sheen, and Coverage
content:
## System Overview
A durable interior repaint is a **system**: correct sheen, two coats at proper spread rate, and clean cut-in technique. Premium lines — Sherwin-Williams Duration/Emerald, Benjamin Moore Regal Select/Aura, Behr Premium Plus — are engineered for one-coat hide but should be applied in two for uniform sheen.

## Selecting Sheen by Room
- **Flat/Matte**: ceilings, low-traffic adult bedrooms; hides imperfections, hardest to scrub.
- **Eggshell**: living rooms, bedrooms, hallways — the default wall sheen; washable, low glare.
- **Satin**: kids' rooms, hallways, higher durability.
- **Semi-gloss**: trim, doors, kitchens, baths — moisture-resistant and scrubbable.
- **Gloss**: cabinets, high-wear trim, accent.

## Coverage Math
- Premium wall paint covers **~350-400 sq ft per gallon** per coat on a smooth, primed surface.
- Textured, porous, or color-change surfaces drop to ~250-300; always **buy for two coats** plus 10%.

## Cut-In Technique
- Use a quality **2-2.5" angled sash brush** (Purdy Clearcut, Wooster).
- Load, tip off excess, and cut a clean line at ceiling/trim with a **3-4" band** wide enough that the roller won't kiss the edge.
- Cut-in and roll **one wall at a time** to keep a **wet edge** and avoid hatbanding/picture-framing (flashing where brushed and rolled paint meet).

## Rolling
- Match nap to surface: **3/8"** for smooth walls, **1/2"** for light texture, **3/4"** for heavy/stucco.
- Roll in a **W or M pattern**, then lay off in long vertical strokes for uniform stipple.
- Keep the roller loaded; a dry roller causes lap marks and uneven mil build.

## Two-Coat Discipline
- Respect the **recoat window** (typically 2-4 hrs for waterborne acrylics).
- Maintain consistent film thickness; thin coats build evenly, heavy coats sag and flash.

## Order of Operations
1. Ceilings first (flat).
2. Walls second.
3. Trim/doors last (semi-gloss) so dust from sanding/rolling is settled.

## QA
- Inspect in raking light for holidays, roller skips, and flashing.
- Pull tape while the final coat is still slightly wet, or score the edge, to avoid peeling the film.

title: Exterior Paint System and Weather Windows
content:
## Build the Right System
Exterior durability comes from a coordinated system: clean substrate, stain-blocking/bonding primer where needed, and **two coats** of a 100% acrylic topcoat. Top systems: Sherwin-Williams Duration/Emerald Exterior, Benjamin Moore Aura/Regal Select Exterior, PPG Manor Hall, Behr Marquee.

## Substrate-Specific Notes
- **Wood siding/trim**: spot-prime bare wood; back-prime replacement boards; caulk after priming.
- **Stucco/masonry**: must cure (new stucco ~28 days) and be within pH spec; use a masonry/elastomeric where hairline cracking is present.
- **Fiber cement (Hardie)**: factory-primed boards still need field priming on cut edges; use 100% acrylic.
- **Previously chalky paint**: wash thoroughly; prime with a chalk-binding primer if chalk persists after rinsing.

## Weather Windows (the make-or-break)
- **Air and surface temp**: most acrylics apply at **35-50°F minimum** (check the low-temp line) up to ~90°F. Surface temp matters more than air temp.
- **Avoid direct sun / hot surfaces** above ~90°F — paint skins and flashes; chase the shade around the building.
- **Dew point**: surface must be **at least 5°F above dew point** and rising; never paint onto condensation.
- **Rain**: most acrylics need **4-6 hrs (ideally 24)** of dry time before rain; read the early-rain-resistance rating.
- **Humidity**: high RH extends dry/recoat times dramatically.

## Application
- Spray-and-backbrush/backroll for penetration into wood grain and texture — spraying alone leaves a film that bridges rather than bonds.
- Maintain a wet edge; work board-by-board on lap siding to hide stops at natural breaks.
- Two coats at the published spread rate (**~250-400 sq ft/gal** depending on texture).

## Sequencing
- Body first, then trim, then doors/shutters.
- Coordinate with sun rotation to keep surfaces shaded during and just after application.

## QA
- Verify mil build with a wet-film gauge on each coat.
- Confirm caulk lines intact and tooled.
- No painting late in the day if temps will drop below the low-temp threshold before cure.
code_references: manufacturer TDS application temps & dew-point rule

title: Airless Spray Application: Tip Sizes and Mil Thickness
content:
## Why Spray
Airless spraying lays a uniform, high-build film fast — ideal for siding, fences, cabinets, and large interiors. Top units: **Graco Magnum/Ultra/ProContractor, Wagner Control Pro/SprayTech, Titan**. Control comes from the right **tip**, **pressure**, and **technique**.

## Reading a Spray Tip
Airless tips are coded by three digits, e.g., **517**:
- First digit x 2 = **fan width** at 12" (5 -> ~10").
- Last two digits = **orifice size in thousandths** (17 -> 0.017").

## Tip Selection by Coating
- **Stains / lacquers (thin)**: 0.009-0.013".
- **Interior wall/ceiling latex**: **0.015-0.019"** (515-519).
- **Heavy exteriors / elastomerics**: **0.021-0.031"+**.
- **Cabinets/fine finish**: fine-finish tips (FFLP) 0.010-0.014" at lower pressure.
Match tip to the gun's max GPM and the material's viscosity; oversized tips outrun the pump.

## Pressure
- Set pressure **just high enough to break the fan cleanly** (no tails/fingers). Too high = overspray and fast tip wear; too low = tails and poor atomization.
- Replace worn tips: a tip wears wider/larger, increasing material use and ruining the pattern.

## Technique for Even Mil Build
- Hold the gun **~12" from and perpendicular to** the surface.
- Move at a **steady speed**, keep the wrist locked (arc = uneven film).
- **Trigger before and release after** each pass; **overlap each pass by 50%**.
- Cross-hatch (vertical then horizontal) on flat panels for uniformity.

## Mil Thickness
- Check the TDS target **wet mils**; verify with a wet-film gauge.
- Typical wall acrylic: ~4-6 wet mils per coat -> ~1.5-2 dry mils. Two coats build the system thickness the warranty assumes.
- **Backroll/backbrush** sprayed coats on porous/textured substrates for adhesion.

## Setup and Cleanup
- Strain paint; prime the pump; mask adjacent surfaces (overspray travels).
- Use the reversible tip to clear clogs (don't disassemble under pressure).
- Relieve pressure before servicing; flush thoroughly to protect packings.

## Safety
Airless injection injuries are surgical emergencies — never put a hand in front of the tip; engage the trigger lock and use the tip guard.

title: Diagnosing Paint Failures: Peeling, Blistering, Lap Marks, and Flashing
content:
## Read the Failure, Find the Cause
Every coating defect has a fingerprint. Identify the pattern, then trace to prep, product, environment, or technique.

## Peeling / Flaking
- **Symptom**: paint lifts from substrate or between coats.
- **Causes**: moisture behind the film, dirty/chalky/glossy surface, no primer, incompatible coatings, painting below temp.
- **Fix**: scrape to sound substrate, sand edges, correct the moisture source (gutters, flashing, vapor), prime properly (Zinsser 123/B-I-N), recoat.

## Blistering
- **Symptom**: bubbles in the film.
- **Causes**: painting in direct sun/hot surface (solvent flash), moisture vapor pushing through, or painting over a damp substrate.
- **Fix**: identify if blisters go to substrate (moisture) or only top coat (heat). Cure the cause, scrape, prime, repaint in proper conditions (surface <90°F, follow the shade).

## Lap Marks
- **Symptom**: visible streaks/bands of higher gloss or build.
- **Causes**: losing the **wet edge**, dry roller, painting in heat/wind that speeds drying.
- **Fix**: maintain a wet edge, keep the roller loaded, add an extender (e.g., Floetrol) in hot/dry conditions, complete each plane in one session.

## Flashing / Picture-Framing / Hatbanding
- **Symptom**: dull/glossy halo where brushed cut-in meets rolled field, or over patches.
- **Causes**: uneven porosity (unprimed patches), different application methods, inconsistent film build.
- **Fix**: spot-prime patches, prime to equalize porosity, cut-in and roll while wet (roll into the cut-in band), keep mil build consistent.

## Cracking / Alligatoring
- **Causes**: excessive film build, brittle/old coatings, hard topcoat over soft.
- **Fix**: remove failed film, prime, use flexible 100% acrylic.

## Burnishing / Sheen Variation
- **Causes**: scrubbing flat paint, touch-ups not feathered, mixing batches.
- **Fix**: use scrubbable sheen (eggshell/satin), box paint (intermix gallons), feather touch-ups.

## Mildew
- **Symptom**: black/green spotting in shade/moisture.
- **Fix**: wash with mildewcide, kill the moisture source, use a mildew-resistant exterior acrylic.

## Prevention Checklist
- Clean, dull, dry, primed substrate.
- Right product for substrate/exposure.
- Apply within temp/dew-point/RH window.
- Maintain wet edge and consistent mil build.
code_references: EPA RRP for failed pre-1978 paint

title: Painter Safety: VOCs, Respirators, and Ladder Use
content:
## Respiratory Protection
Solvents, isocyanates (2K urethanes), and spray mists pose inhalation hazards.
- **Brush/roll low-VOC latex**: ventilate; generally no respirator needed, but cross-ventilate enclosed spaces.
- **Spraying or solvent coatings**: wear a NIOSH-approved **half-face respirator with organic-vapor (OV) cartridges + P100 pre-filters**. Replace cartridges on schedule (odor breakthrough = too late).
- **Isocyanate/2K products**: supplied-air respirator may be required — read the SDS Section 8.
- Respirators require **fit testing and a medical clearance** under OSHA 1910.134 when use is mandatory.

## VOCs and Ventilation
- Choose **low-/zero-VOC** lines (Sherwin-Williams Harmony, BM Natura) for interiors and occupied spaces.
- Provide mechanical ventilation/exhaust when spraying indoors; control ignition sources — solvent vapors are flammable (OSHA 1910.107).
- Keep SDS on site for every product.

## Lead (Pre-1978)
- EPA **RRP Rule**: renovation disturbing painted surfaces in pre-1978 housing/child-occupied facilities requires a **Certified Renovator**, containment, HEPA cleanup, and dust-wipe verification. Never dry-sand or open-flame lead paint.

## Ladder Safety (OSHA 1926.1053)
- **4:1 ratio** for extension ladders; **3 ft** above the landing.
- Inspect before use; remove damaged ladders from service.
- Maintain **3 points of contact**; don't overreach (keep your belt buckle within the rails); never stand on the top two rungs.
- Set on firm, level ground; use stabilizers/standoffs; tie off the top.
- Keep metal ladders away from energized lines.

## Scaffolds and Lifts
- Fully plank, guardrail, and inspect scaffolds; tag-out incomplete scaffolds.
- Lifts/boom work: wear a harness tied to the basket anchor.

## Skin, Eye, and Housekeeping
- Nitrile gloves and safety glasses for solvents and pressure washing.
- Manage rags soaked in oil/alkyd — **spontaneous combustion risk**; store in a sealed metal can or lay flat to dry.
- Keep walkways clear of hoses, drop cloths, and buckets to prevent trips.

title: Floating LVP/Click-Lock Installation: Expansion Gap and Underlayment
content:
## System Overview
Floating luxury vinyl plank (LVP/SPC) clicks together and rests on the subfloor — it is **not** glued or nailed down. Leading products: **Coretec (LVP/SPC), Shaw Floorte, Mohawk SolidTech, Pergo Extreme**. SPC cores are rigid and dimensionally stable; WPC is softer/warmer.

## Acclimation and Subfloor
- Acclimate planks flat in the room **48 hrs** at normal living temperature (most SPC tolerates wider temp swings but still benefits).
- Subfloor must be **flat to 3/16" over 10 ft** (grind highs, fill lows with patch). Vacuum clean; remove debris that would telegraph.
- Test concrete moisture (see moisture-testing article); use the manufacturer-approved moisture barrier on slabs.

## Underlayment
- Many SPC planks have an **attached pad (IXPE/cork)** — do **not** add a second pad (excess deflection breaks the locking joints).
- For bare-back planks, install the recommended thin underlayment; on concrete add a **6-mil poly vapor barrier** lapped 8" and taped.

## Expansion Gap (critical)
- Leave a **1/4" to 3/8" expansion gap** at all walls and vertical obstructions. Floating floors move with temperature/humidity; pinching the field causes **peaking/buckling**.
- Use spacers; cover the gap with baseboard/quarter-round fastened to the **wall, not the floor**.

## Layout
- Measure the room; ensure the **final row is at least 1/3 plank** wide — rip the first row if needed.
- Stagger end joints **6-8" minimum** (random, no H-patterns or stair-stepping).
- Plan plank direction along the longest wall or toward the main light source.

## Installation
- Click long-side, then tap the end seam home with a **tapping block and white mallet** (a black mallet/rubber can mark planks).
- Maintain straight rows; check every few rows with a chalk line.
- Undercut door casings and slide planks beneath.

## Transitions and Large Areas
- Use T-molds/transitions at doorways and where runs exceed the manufacturer's **max continuous run** (often ~40-50 ft) without an expansion break.

## QA
- No gaps at end seams; joints flush (no lippage).
- Floor floats freely; cabinets/heavy islands should be set on the subfloor (don't trap the floor under them).

title: Solid Hardwood Nail-Down Installation and Acclimation
content:
## When to Nail Down
Solid 3/4" hardwood (and engineered over wood subfloor) is **nailed/stapled** to a wood subfloor. Leading mills: **Bruce, Shaw, Mohawk, Somerset**. Solid wood is **not** for below-grade or over concrete without a sleeper/plywood system.

## Acclimation (do not skip)
- Deliver and **acclimate** flooring in the installed space until the **wood moisture content** is within **2-4%** of the subfloor (planks <3" wide: within 4%; wider plank: within 2%).
- Building must be at normal living conditions (**60-80°F, 30-50% RH**), HVAC running. Use a pin/pinless moisture meter on both flooring and subfloor — don't acclimate by calendar, acclimate by meter reading.

## Subfloor Prep
- Plywood/OSB subfloor flat to **3/16" over 10 ft**; fasten squeaks; clean.
- Lay a vapor-retarder **asphalt-saturated felt (#15)** or red rosin paper to slow moisture and reduce squeaks.
- Mark joist locations for stability of starter rows.

## Layout
- Snap a working line **3/8" off the longest straight wall** for the expansion gap.
- Dry-lay to balance the room; rack out boards for color/grain mix from multiple cartons.

## Fastening Pattern
- **First 1-2 rows**: face-nail (and/or top-nail + blind-nail) near the wall where the floor nailer won't fit; pre-drill to avoid splitting; fill holes with matching putty.
- **Field**: blind-nail through the tongue at **45 degrees** with a flooring nailer/stapler (Bostitch, Powernail).
- **Fastener spacing**: every **6-8"** and **within 1-2" of each board end**; hit joists where possible for squeak control.
- **Cleats vs. staples**: cleats flex better with seasonal movement; match fastener length to thickness (2" for 3/4").

## Expansion Gap
- Maintain **3/4" (or thickness of flooring)** gap at all walls; covered by baseboard/shoe.

## Finishing
- Last rows: blind-nail until the nailer no longer fits, then face-nail and pull tight with a pull bar.
- For unfinished floors, sand (36 -> 60 -> 80/100 grit), then stain/finish.

## QA
- No squeaks (fastener engagement), tight seams, consistent gap.
- Document moisture readings — gaps/cupping later usually trace to acclimation shortcuts.

title: Tile Installation Over Schluter DITRA with Thinset
content:
## Why DITRA
Schluter **DITRA** is an uncoupling membrane that lets tile and subfloor move independently, preventing cracked tile and grout over wood subfloors and minor cracks. It also waterproofs and supports vapor management. The system is only as good as the **thinset under and over** it.

## Subfloor Requirements
- Over plywood/OSB: subfloor deflection must meet **L/360** (tile) and meet DITRA's joist-spacing tables.
- Flat to **1/8" in 10 ft**; clean and structurally sound.

## Setting DITRA (thinset #1 — bonding to subfloor)
- **Plywood/OSB**: use **unmodified thinset** (Schluter recommends unmodified between DITRA and wood so it can cure properly under the impervious membrane) — verify current manufacturer guidance.
- **Concrete**: modified or unmodified per spec.
- Trowel with a **1/4" x 3/16" V-notch** (or 11/64" for DITRA); comb in one direction.
- Embed the **fleece side down**, press with a float/screed across the full sheet to fully collapse ridges; butt sheets, don't overlap.

## Setting Tile (thinset #2 — into the DITRA cavities)
- Choose trowel notch by tile size:
  - **Mosaics / small**: 1/4" x 1/4" square notch.
  - **8-12" tile**: **1/4" x 3/8"** square notch.
  - **Large-format (15"+ or plank)**: **1/2" x 1/2"** or a LFT/euro-notch; **back-butter** to ensure >=80% (dry) / 95% (wet) coverage.
- Use a quality **modified thinset** for the tile (e.g., Mapei Ultraflex, Bostik) per the tile/spec; mix to a creamy, slump-free consistency and let slake.
- Comb thinset straight, set tile with a slight twist perpendicular to ridges, and **periodically pull a tile** to verify coverage.

## Movement and Layout
- Maintain **perimeter movement joints** and add field movement joints per TCNA EJ171 (~every 20-25 ft interior, less in wet/sunny areas).
- Use Schluter trim/edge profiles (**RONDEC, SCHIENE, JOLLY**) at edges and transitions; DILEX for movement joints.
- Use tile leveling clips on large format to fight **lippage** (keep under **1/32"** with narrow grout joints).

## Grout and Finish
- Wait for thinset cure before grouting; sponge clean and tool joints uniformly.
- Caulk (matching) all change-of-plane and movement joints — never grout them rigidly.

title: Subfloor Preparation and Concrete Moisture Testing
content:
## Moisture: The #1 Flooring Killer
Adhesive failures, cupping, mold, and delamination almost always trace to moisture in the slab or subfloor. Test **before** install — every manufacturer warranty requires it.

## Concrete Moisture Test Methods
- **In-situ Relative Humidity (ASTM F2170)** — the industry standard. Drill probes to **40% of slab depth** (20% if slab dries from both sides), insert sensors, equilibrate **24 hrs**, read RH.
  - Typical limits: **<=75-85% RH** depending on the flooring/adhesive (check the TDS; many resilient products cap at 80%).
- **Calcium Chloride / MVER (ASTM F1869)** — measures moisture vapor emission rate (lbs/1,000 sq ft/24 hr); common limit **3-5 lbs**. Less favored than RH but still specified.
- **Surface pH** (ASTM F710): many adhesives require **pH 7-9**; high pH (alkaline) degrades adhesives.
- A quick **plastic-sheet test (ASTM D4263)** screens for condensation but is not a substitute for quantitative testing.

## Wood Subfloor Moisture
- Use a pin/pinless meter; subfloor and wood flooring should be within the manufacturer's MC differential (typically **2-4%**).

## Flatness and Profile
- General flooring flatness: **3/16" in 10 ft** (LVP/laminate/hardwood); tile/large-format tighter (**1/8" in 10 ft**).
- Grind high spots; fill low spots with a **cementitious patch/self-leveler** (Mapei, Ardex) primed per spec.
- Crack-isolation membrane (Schluter DITRA, RedGard) over working cracks.

## Subfloor Soundness
- Wood subfloor: properly fastened, no deflection beyond **L/360** (L/480 for natural stone). Re-screw squeaks to joists.
- Remove old adhesive/cutback; some old cutback contains asbestos — test before grinding.

## Vapor Retarders and Barriers
- On-grade/below-grade slabs: install the manufacturer's moisture-control system or a **6-mil poly** under floating floors; for glue-down, use a **moisture-mitigation epoxy** when RH exceeds the limit.

## Documentation
- Record test method, location, depth, equilibration time, RH/MVER/pH, and date.
- Photograph; attach to the job file. No test = no warranty and a likely callback.

title: Diagnosing Floor Failures: Cupping, Gaps, Lippage, and Hollow Tiles
content:
## Match the Symptom to the Cause
Floor complaints are predictable once you know the mechanisms: moisture, movement, and bond.

## Cupping (edges higher than center)
- **Cause**: moisture imbalance — bottom of the board wetter than the top (slab moisture, crawlspace humidity, plumbing leak, no vapor barrier).
- **Diagnose**: meter the boards and subfloor; inspect crawlspace/slab; check HVAC/RH.
- **Fix**: correct the moisture source first, let the floor re-equilibrate (it often flattens), then re-sand if needed. Sanding cupped-but-wet floors causes **crowning** when they dry — fix moisture first.

## Crowning (center higher than edges)
- **Cause**: top wetter than bottom, or a cupped floor sanded flat then dried.
- **Fix**: dry to equilibrium, then sand flat.

## Gapping / Shrinkage
- **Cause**: low humidity (winter heating), flooring installed at high MC then dried, inadequate acclimation.
- **Fix**: stabilize indoor RH (humidify to 35-45%); minor seasonal gaps are normal and close in summer. Persistent gaps may need board replacement.

## Peaking / Buckling (floating floors)
- **Cause**: no/insufficient **expansion gap**, floor pinched by trim or cabinets, double-padding.
- **Fix**: relieve the perimeter to 1/4-3/8", free the floor from fasteners trapping it, re-engage joints.

## Lippage (height difference between adjacent tiles/planks)
- **Cause**: uneven subfloor, warped tiles, insufficient thinset coverage, no leveling system, joints too narrow for tile warpage.
- **Fix**: for tile, demo and reset the high tile with full coverage; prevent with flat substrate, **leveling clips**, and slightly wider grout joints on large format. Allowable lippage per TCNA depends on joint width.

## Hollow-Sounding Tiles
- **Cause**: voids under tile from poor thinset coverage (<80% dry/95% wet), not back-buttering large format, skinned-over thinset.
- **Risk**: cracks and debonding under load.
- **Fix**: sound the floor; replace tiles that are hollow at edges/corners or near traffic. Prevent with correct **trowel notch**, proper mixing/slaking, and pulling test tiles.

## Squeaks (wood)
- **Cause**: subfloor-to-joist movement, missed fasteners, no underlayment paper.
- **Fix**: screw subfloor to joists; for finished floors, use shims/adhesive from below.

## Prevention Summary
- Test moisture, acclimate by meter, flatten the substrate, full thinset coverage, correct expansion gaps.

title: Flooring Crew Safety: Knees, Dust, and Material Handling
content:
## The Trade's Signature Injuries
Flooring work concentrates stress on knees, lungs, hands, and backs. Most injuries are cumulative and preventable.

## Knee Protection
- Wear **gel or hard-cap kneepads** rated for the work; rotate to kneeling stools/creepers where possible.
- Prolonged kneeling causes **prepatellar bursitis** ("carpet layer's knee") and meniscus damage — alternate positions and stretch.
- Use a **knee kicker** correctly (strike with the lower leg, not the knee) to avoid joint trauma.

## Silica Dust (the serious hazard)
Cutting/grinding tile, concrete, and thinset releases **respirable crystalline silica** — a lung carcinogen.
- OSHA 1926.1153 PEL: **50 micrograms/m3** over 8 hrs.
- Use **Table 1 controls**: wet-cutting saws (water-fed) or tools with **HEPA dust extraction/shrouds**.
- Wear at minimum a **NIOSH N95**; for heavy grinding without engineering controls, a half-face P100.
- Never **dry-sweep** silica dust — HEPA vacuum or wet methods only.

## Adhesive, Solvent, and Old-Floor Hazards
- Many adhesives/sealers are flammable and emit VOCs — ventilate and kill ignition sources.
- **Old vinyl/cutback (pre-1980s)** may contain **asbestos** — test before disturbing; abatement may be required by law.
- Wear nitrile gloves with epoxies/urethanes; some cause sensitization.

## Material Handling and Ergonomics
- Tile, thinset, and self-leveler bags are heavy — **lift with the legs**, team-lift >50 lb, use carts/dollies.
- Stage materials close to the work to cut carrying distance.

## Tool and Cut Safety
- Tile/miter saws: use the guard, push sticks, eye and hearing protection; keep water reservoirs full on wet saws.
- Utility knives: cut away from the body, fresh blades (dull blades slip), retract when set down.
- Flooring nailers/staplers: keep hands clear, disconnect air before clearing jams.

## PPE Checklist
- Kneepads, safety glasses, hearing protection, N95/P100, nitrile gloves, steel/composite-toe boots.
- Keep the work area clean of offcuts and trip hazards; manage trailing cords/hoses.

title: Irrigation System Design: Zones, GPM/PSI, and Head Spacing
content:
## Start With the Water Supply
Every design begins with two numbers measured at the site:
- **Static pressure (PSI)**: read with a gauge at a hose bib (typical residential **45-80 PSI**).
- **Available flow (GPM)**: bucket test (gallons / seconds x 60) or meter/service-line size. Design to use **~75%** of available GPM to leave headroom and limit velocity (<5 ft/s in pipe).

## Zone the System
- Group heads by **plant type and sun exposure** (hydrozoning) and by **matched precipitation** — never mix rotors and sprays on one zone.
- Each zone's total head GPM must stay **under available flow**. Split into more zones rather than starving heads.
- Account for pressure loss: friction in pipe, elevation (**~0.43 PSI per foot** of rise), valves, and backflow.

## Heads and Spacing (head-to-head coverage)
Sprinklers are designed for **head-to-head** (100%) overlap — each head throws to the adjacent heads.
- **Spray heads** (Rain Bird 1804, Hunter PROS Pro-Spray): radius **8-15 ft**, higher precip (~1.5-2.0 in/hr). Space at the radius.
- **Rotors** (Hunter PGP/PGP-Ultra, Rain Bird 5000): radius **25-45 ft**, lower precip (~0.4-0.8 in/hr) for larger turf.
- **Operating pressure**: sprays ~**30 PSI**, rotors ~**40-45 PSI** at the nozzle. Use **pressure-regulated** bodies (PRS) to hold spec and stop misting.

## Nozzle Selection and Precip Matching
- Within a zone, use **matched precipitation rate (MPR)** nozzles so quarter, half, and full heads apply equal depth — otherwise you over/under-water arcs.
- Adjust arc and radius at each head after install.

## Pipe Sizing and Layout
- Size laterals to keep velocity <5 ft/s; size mainline larger.
- Lay out heads first, then connect with the shortest practical pipe runs; avoid long single laterals that drop pressure at the last head.

## Controller and Scheduling
- Hunter/Rain Bird smart controllers (Hunter Pro-HC/Hydrawise, Rain Bird ESP-TM2) with weather/ET adjust.
- Schedule by **inches of water** (turf ~1-1.5 in/week), using **cycle-and-soak** on slopes/clay to prevent runoff.

## QA
- Run each zone; check coverage, fix misting (over-pressure) and doughnuts (clogged/wrong nozzle).
- Perform a **catch-cup audit** to verify uniform precip and adjust run times.
materials_required: Rain Bird 1804 spray heads w/ MPR nozzles

title: Drip Irrigation for Beds, Shrubs, and Trees
content:
## Why Drip
Drip delivers water slowly at the root zone, cutting evaporation/runoff and hitting **>90% efficiency** vs. ~60-75% for spray. Ideal for beds, shrubs, trees, and vegetable rows. Leaders: **Netafim, Rain Bird (XFD/XFS), Hunter (Eco-Wrap/PLD), Toro (Blue Stripe)**.

## Zone Requirements (drip is low-flow, low-pressure)
- Drip operates at **20-30 PSI** — far lower than spray. Install a **pressure regulator** (typically 25 or 30 PSI) and a **filter (150-200 mesh)** at the zone to prevent emitter clogging.
- Keep drip on its **own zone** — never mix with sprays/rotors (different precip and pressure).

## Two Main Approaches
- **Inline emitter tubing (dripline)**: Netafim Techline, Rain Bird XFD — built-in pressure-compensating emitters at fixed spacing (**12", 18", 24"**) and flow (**0.4, 0.6, 0.9 GPH**). Best for beds and groundcover grids.
- **Point-source emitters**: 1/2" poly mainline with punched **0.5-2 GPH emitters** on 1/4" tubing to individual plants/trees. Best for spaced shrubs and trees.

## Layout and Spacing
- **Beds/groundcover**: parallel dripline rows **12-18" apart** with **12" emitter spacing** to wet a continuous band; tighter in sandy soil, wider in clay (water spreads laterally).
- **Shrubs**: 1-2 emitters per plant at the rootball edge.
- **Trees**: a **ring of emitters** at the dripline of the canopy, increasing count as the tree grows.
- Cap ends or loop the system to flush; install end-flush valves on long runs.

## Pressure-Compensating (PC) Emitters
- Use **PC** dripline on slopes and long runs so each emitter delivers the rated flow regardless of elevation/pressure differences.

## Installation
- Lay tubing on the soil; secure with **galvanized stakes** every 3-4 ft; cover with **mulch** (not soil that clogs emitters).
- Use barbed or compression fittings; flush the line before capping.

## Scheduling
- Drip runs **longer and less frequently** than spray — think in **gallons/runtime**, not inches. Example: 0.6 GPH emitters for 60 min = 0.6 gal per emitter.
- Use cycle-and-soak on slopes; deep, infrequent watering drives deep roots.

## QA
- Verify regulator/filter installed; flush; confirm every emitter drips; check for blowouts at fittings.
- Inspect filter regularly; clean to prevent clogging.

title: Irrigation Controllers and Backflow Prevention
content:
## Backflow: Protecting the Potable Supply
Irrigation systems are a **cross-connection** — fertilizer/chemicals injected via the lines or stagnant water can be siphoned back into drinking water. Code (plumbing code + local cross-connection ordinances) **requires an approved backflow preventer** on every irrigation connection.

## Backflow Device Types (match the hazard and local code)
- **Atmospheric Vacuum Breaker (AVB)** — cheapest, must be **6" above the highest head**, no valves downstream, not for continuous pressure.
- **Pressure Vacuum Breaker (PVB)** — common residential choice; installed **12" above the highest head/outlet**, testable, protects against back-siphonage only.
- **Double Check Valve Assembly (DCVA)** — back-siphonage and back-pressure, low-hazard, can be below grade in a vault.
- **Reduced Pressure Zone (RPZ / RP)** — highest protection (high-hazard, e.g., fertigation/chemical injection); must be above grade with air-gap drain; required where chemicals are injected.

## Installation and Testing Rules
- Devices like PVB/RPZ must be **above grade** and at the code-required height; RPZ cannot be submerged (it discharges).
- Most jurisdictions require **annual testing by a certified backflow tester** with results filed to the water authority (ASSE 1013 RPZ / 1015 DCVA / 1020 PVB standards).
- Provide freeze protection in cold climates (insulate or remove/winterize).

## Controllers and Required Features
- Modern controllers (**Hunter Pro-HC/X-Core, Rain Bird ESP-TM2/ESP-Me, Toro**) provide independent zone scheduling.
- **Rain sensors / soil-moisture sensors are required by code** in many states (e.g., FL Statute 373.62, and EPA WaterSense) to prevent watering during/after rain — a **rain shutoff device** is the common compliance item.
- **Smart/WiFi controllers** (Hunter Hydrawise, Rain Bird ST8) use weather/ET data and satisfy WaterSense.

## Master Valve and Flow Sensing
- A **master valve** + **flow sensor** (Hunter HFS, Rain Bird) shuts the system on a broken-pipe high-flow event — best practice and sometimes required commercially.

## Electrical
- Controller and valve wiring per **NEC**; use direct-burial UF wire, waterproof connectors (DBY/DBR) at every splice, and protect the transformer circuit.

## QA / Compliance Checklist
- Approved, correctly sized backflow device at correct height, tested and tagged.
- Rain/freeze sensor installed and functional.
- Permit pulled where required; as-built and test report on file.

title: Paver Patio Installation: Base Compaction, Sand, and Belgard Units
content:
## A Patio Is Only as Good as Its Base
Most paver failures (settling, heaving, rutting) are base failures. Leaders: **Belgard, Techo-Bloc, Unilock, Pavestone**. The system is **compacted aggregate base + bedding sand + pavers + edge restraint + joint sand**.

## Excavation
- Excavate to accommodate: base + 1" bedding sand + paver thickness.
- **Base depth**: **4-6" for pedestrian patios/walks**, **8-12" for driveways/vehicular**. Over-excavate poor/clay soils and add geotextile fabric.
- Establish **slope away from structures at 1-2% (1/4" per foot minimum)** for drainage.

## Base Course
- Use **dense-graded aggregate ("road base"/Class II / crushed 3/4"-minus with fines)** that compacts and locks.
- Place and compact in **lifts of 2-3" max** — compacting deep lifts leaves voids that settle later.
- Compact each lift with a **plate compactor** (vibratory plate; reversible for thick base) to ~95% Proctor; lightly moisten for compaction.
- Check grade and slope with a level/laser after each lift.

## Bedding Sand (screed layer)
- Spread **1" of coarse concrete/bedding sand** (ASTM C33), screeded uniform over 1" pipe screed rails. **Do not** compact the bedding sand before laying.
- Bedding sand is a setting bed, **not** a tool for fixing base grade — fix grade in the base.

## Laying Pavers
- Start from a straight edge/90-degree reference; maintain pattern (herringbone is strongest for vehicular).
- Leave consistent **1/8" joints**; set pavers down (don't slide, which plows sand).
- Cut borders with a splitter or wet saw; full pavers on the field, cuts at the edge.

## Edge Restraint
- Install **paver edge restraint** (plastic edging spiked with 10" landscape spikes, or concrete toe) around the entire perimeter — without it, pavers spread and joints open.

## Compaction and Joint Sand
- Sweep in **joint sand** (or **polymeric sand** for better weed/wash resistance), then **plate-compact the pavers** (with a protective pad) to seat them and vibrate sand into joints.
- Top off joints, recompact; for polymeric sand, mist per directions to activate.

## QA
- Verify slope (1-2%), no rocking pavers, full joints, restraint secured.
- Sweep clean; polymeric sand off paver faces before activation to avoid haze.

title: Grading and Drainage: 2% Slope, French Drains, and NDS Systems
content:
## Water Management Is Job One
Most landscape and foundation problems are water problems. Proper grading and drainage protect structures, hardscapes, and plantings. Top drainage products: **NDS (catch basins, channel drain, EZ-Drain), ADS (corrugated pipe).**

## Surface Grading
- **Positive slope away from foundations**: IRC R401.3 requires the ground to fall a minimum of **6" within the first 10 ft** (a **5% slope**) away from the building. Where lot lines limit this, use swales/drains.
- General lawn/hardscape drainage: maintain **~2% (1/4" per foot)** so water sheets off without ponding; up to ~2-3% for turf, less can pond.
- Avoid **negative slope** (water toward the house) and **birdbaths** (low spots) — the most common callbacks.

## Swales
- Shallow, vegetated channels that intercept and route runoff; slope the swale invert at **>=1%** toward a discharge point or drain.

## French Drains (subsurface)
- Trench **at least 1% slope** to daylight or a drywell.
- Line with **geotextile filter fabric**, add a **perforated pipe** (perforations **down**) bedded in **clean 3/4" washed gravel**, wrap the fabric (burrito) to keep fines out, then backfill.
- Pre-fabbed options: **NDS EZ-Drain** (pipe pre-wrapped in aggregate/fabric) speeds install.
- Use a **drywell/dry well** where there's no daylight outlet, sized to the contributing area and soil percolation.

## Catch Basins and Channel Drains
- **NDS catch basins** at low points/turf depressions collect surface water; connect to solid **SDR/corrugated pipe** sloped to daylight.
- **Channel/trench drains** (NDS Dura Slope/Spee-D) across driveways, patios, and garage aprons intercept sheet flow.
- Pop-up emitters at pipe ends discharge to lawn; daylight outlets should have a rodent screen.

## Downspouts
- Tie gutters into **solid (non-perforated) pipe** carrying water well away from the foundation (10+ ft) to daylight or a drywell — don't dump at the base of the wall.

## Soil and Compaction
- In clay soils, plan for slow percolation — favor surface conveyance and larger drywells.
- Avoid compacting planting areas; compact only structural/hardscape subgrades.

## QA
- Run a hose/flood test; confirm flow to discharge with no ponding after ~15 min.
- Verify slopes with a level/laser; document invert elevations.
code_references: IRC R401.3 — surface drainage (6" in 10 ft)

title: Sod Installation: Soil Prep, Laying Pattern, and Establishment
content:
## Instant Lawn, If You Prep Right
Sod gives an instant lawn but lives or dies on soil prep and watering. The goal is fast **root knitting** into the soil below.

## Soil Preparation
- Clear debris, weeds, and old turf; spray glyphosate or strip existing grass 1-2 weeks ahead if needed.
- **Test soil pH** (target ~6.0-7.0 for most turf) and amend per test (lime to raise, sulfur to lower).
- **Till to 4-6"**, incorporate **2-3" of compost** for structure and nutrient holding.
- Apply a **starter fertilizer high in phosphorus** (e.g., 10-20-10) and rake in.
- **Grade and level**: final grade **1" below** walks/driveways (to account for sod thickness) and slope **~2% away from structures**.
- Lightly firm with a roller so footprints don't sink, then rake to a fine, moist seedbed.

## Ordering and Timing
- Order sod for **same-day delivery and install** — sod heats and dies on the pallet within 24-48 hrs, faster in summer.
- Best installation: spring/fall for cool-season (fescue, bluegrass); late spring/summer for warm-season (Bermuda, Zoysia, St. Augustine).

## Laying Pattern
- Pre-moisten the soil so roots meet damp earth.
- Start along a **straight edge** (walk/driveway). Lay rows in a **running-bond (brick) pattern** — stagger end seams like brickwork.
- **Butt seams tight**, no gaps or overlaps; press edges together (gaps dry out and brown).
- On slopes, lay sod **perpendicular to the slope** and stake pieces to prevent sliding.
- Cut around edges/sprinkler heads with a sharp knife.

## Rolling and Initial Water
- Roll the new sod (lightly water-filled roller) to press roots into contact and remove air pockets.
- **Water immediately** and deeply — the soil under the sod should be wet to **1"+** within the first hour.

## Establishment Watering
- Days **1-7**: keep sod and soil **constantly moist**, watering 2-4x/day.
- Week **2**: reduce frequency, increase depth as roots take.
- Weeks **3-4**: taper toward normal deep, infrequent watering; **don't mow** until rooted (tug test resists lift) and grass reaches ~3"+, removing no more than 1/3 of the blade.

## QA
- No gaps/overlaps, tight seams, good soil contact (no air pockets), even grade.
- Coordinate irrigation coverage so no dry corners brown out.

title: Trenching, Utility Locates, and Excavation Safety
content:
## Call Before You Dig — Always
Striking a buried utility can be fatal and is illegal without a locate. Before any excavation:
- Call **811** (or local one-call) **at least 2-3 business days** before digging; mark the dig area first (white paint).
- Utilities mark lines by color: **red=electric, yellow=gas/oil, orange=comm/cable, blue=potable water, green=sewer, purple=reclaimed water, pink=survey**.
- Hand-dig ("pothole") within the **tolerance zone** (commonly **18-24" each side** of a marked line) — no machine excavation there.
- Private utilities (irrigation mains, landscape lighting, invisible fence, septic lines) are usually **not** located by 811 — locate them yourself.

## Trench Cave-In Protection (OSHA 1926 Subpart P)
Soil collapse is the leading excavation killer (a cubic yard of soil weighs ~2,700 lb).
- **Protective systems required for trenches 5 ft deep or more** (and shallower if a competent person sees hazard): **sloping/benching, shoring, or a trench box (shield)**.
- **20 ft+** depth requires a registered professional engineer's design.
- A **competent person** must classify soil (Type A/B/C) and inspect daily and after rain/changes.

## Access and Spoil
- Provide a **ladder/egress within 25 ft** of workers in trenches 4 ft+.
- Keep **spoil piles and equipment >=2 ft** back from the trench edge.
- Watch for **water accumulation** (don't work in a trench filling with water without controls) and **hazardous atmospheres** in deep/confined excavations (test air).

## Equipment and Trencher Safety
- Walk-behind/ride-on trenchers (Ditch Witch, Vermeer): keep bystanders clear of the chain/boom, never reach into a running chain, and follow lock-out before clearing.
- Keep equipment a safe distance from **overhead power lines** (min approach distances per voltage; assume energized).

## PPE and Practices
- Hi-vis vest, hard hat, steel-toe boots, eye protection, gloves.
- Locate, then trench in lifts; backfill and compact in lifts to avoid future settling.
- If you nick a gas/electric line, **stop, evacuate uphill/upwind, and call 911 and the utility** — do not attempt repair.

## QA / Compliance
- Valid, unexpired locate ticket on site.
- Protective system in place for depth; daily competent-person inspection logged.
- Egress and spoil setbacks verified.

title: Service Entrance & Meter Base Installation NEC 230
content:
## Service Entrance Conductors & Meter Base

The service entrance is the transition point where utility-owned conductors meet the customer-owned electrical system. **NEC Article 230** governs everything from the service drop/lateral to the service disconnect.

### Conductor Sizing

For a typical **200A residential service**, service entrance conductors are sized per **NEC 310.12** (dwelling services) which permits 83% of the standard ampacity:

- **200A service**: `2/0 AWG` copper or `4/0 AWG` aluminum (SE/SER or in conduit)
- **400A service**: parallel `3/0` copper or `250 kcmil` aluminum sets
- Grounded (neutral) conductor sized per **250.24(C)** and **Table 250.102(C)(1)**

### Meter Base & Mounting

- Use a UL-listed ringless or ring-type meter socket rated for the service amperage (e.g., **Milbank U4801** or **Eaton/Cutler-Hammer** lever-bypass socket for 200A)
- Mount the meter center at **48 in to 66 in** above finished grade (verify with local POCO standard)
- Maintain working clearance per **110.26**: 36 in deep, 30 in wide, 78 in high

### Service Disconnect & 2020 NEC 230.85

- **230.85** now requires an **emergency disconnect** for one- and two-family dwellings, located in a readily accessible **outdoor** location, marked "EMERGENCY DISCONNECT."
- Acceptable means: meter-main combo (e.g., **Square D QO200M200** with integral 200A main), service disconnect ahead of the panel, or a disconnect tagged per 230.85(E).
- **230.70** requires the disconnect at a readily accessible location nearest the point of entrance.
- **230.71** (2020) limits to **one** service disconnect per enclosure (the old "six-handle rule" was removed).

### Grounding & Bonding

- Bond the neutral to the enclosure at the service disconnect ONLY (main bonding jumper per **250.28**).
- Drive two ground rods (**250.53(A)(2)**) unless a single rod tests ≤25 ohms; supplement with concrete-encased electrode (Ufer) per **250.52(A)(3)**.
- Grounding electrode conductor per **Table 250.66**: `#4 Cu` for 200A.

### Weatherhead & Drip Loops

- Service mast must withstand drop loading; use `2 in` rigid for spans needing support.
- Provide drip loops; conductors enter weatherhead from below to prevent water ingress per **230.54(F)**.

### Common Inspection Failures

- Missing emergency disconnect labeling
- Neutral bonded at both meter and panel (double bond)
- Insufficient burial depth on laterals (24 in for direct-burial per **300.5**)

Always coordinate the meter set and cut-in with the serving utility before energizing.

title: Sub-Panel & Feeder Sizing NEC 215/408
content:
## Sub-Panels and Feeders

A sub-panel (downstream distribution panel) extends capacity to a garage, addition, or detached structure. Correct feeder sizing and the four-wire separation rule are the two most-failed items at inspection.

### Feeder Conductor Sizing (NEC 215)

Feeder ampacity must equal or exceed the calculated load per **215.2** and **Article 220**. Common sub-panel feeders:

- **60A sub-panel**: `6 AWG` Cu (75°C column, 310.16)
- **100A sub-panel**: `3 AWG` Cu or `1 AWG` Al
- **125A sub-panel**: `1 AWG` Cu or `2/0` Al
- Apply **215.2(A)(1)** minimum and add 25% for continuous loads.

### The Critical 4-Wire Rule

In a sub-panel you MUST:

- Run **separate** equipment grounding conductor (EGC) and grounded neutral
- **Isolate the neutral bus** from the enclosure (remove the main bonding jumper / bonding screw)
- Land grounds on a bonded ground bar kit (e.g., **Square D PK7GTA**)
- This prevents parallel neutral current on the EGC and metal raceways per **250.142(B)**

### Detached Structures (250.32)

- Since 2008 NEC, a feeder to a detached building requires an EGC; you may **no longer** re-ground the neutral at the second building.
- Install a grounding electrode system (ground rod/Ufer) at the detached structure per **250.32(A)**.

### Overcurrent Protection (240.4 / 408)

- Feeder breaker in the main panel protects the feeder conductors.
- Sub-panel bus rating (e.g., 100A or 125A) must be ≥ the feeder breaker.
- **408.36**: panelboard must be protected by an OCPD ≤ its rating.
- Label per **408.4**: every circuit's purpose must be legibly identified; **408.4(B)** requires the supply source on the panel.

### Working Clearance & Mounting (110.26 / 240.24)

- Maintain 36 in depth, 30 in width working space.
- Breaker handles must not exceed 6 ft 7 in to the top operating handle.
- Do not install panels in clothes closets or bathrooms (**240.24(D)/(E)**).

### Example Calculation

Detached garage: lighting 600 VA, two 20A receptacle circuits, one 30A welder. Use **Article 220 Part III** general method or the **220.84** optional method. A 60A feeder on `6 AWG` Cu typically suffices; verify voltage drop on long runs (>100 ft) and upsize to `4 AWG` to keep VD under 3%.

### Common Failures

- Bonding screw left in sub-panel (neutral-ground bond)
- Grounds and neutrals sharing one bar
- No EGC pulled to detached structure

title: Standby Generator with Transfer Switch & Interlock
content:
## Backup Power: Transfer Switches & Interlocks

Never back-feed a generator without isolating the utility. **NEC 702** (optional standby) and **445** govern these installations. Three legal connection methods exist.

### Method 1: Automatic Transfer Switch (ATS)

For whole-home standby units like the **Generac Guardian 24kW** or **Kohler 20RCA**:

- ATS (e.g., **Generac RXSW200A3** 200A service-rated) monitors utility and starts the generator on outage.
- Service-entrance-rated ATS replaces or sits ahead of the main panel.
- Sized to the generator output: a 24kW LP unit delivers ~100A at 240V.
- Provide a load-shed module or **smart management modules (SMM)** for HVAC/EV loads.

### Method 2: Manual Transfer Switch

For portable generators (e.g., **Honeywell/Reliance 31410CRK** 10-circuit):

- Pre-wired to selected critical circuits.
- Generator connects via an L14-30 inlet box.

### Method 3: Mechanical Interlock Kit

- Listed interlock (e.g., **Square D QOM2 interlock**, **Eaton** kit) physically prevents the main and generator breaker from being on simultaneously.
- Must be a **listed** kit matched to the panel; field-fabricated interlocks are NOT permitted (**404.2 / listing**).
- Generator inlet wired to a back-fed breaker secured with a hold-down per **408.36(D)** / **408.40**.

### Critical Code Requirements

- **702.4**: standby system capacity must handle the connected load.
- **250.20 / 250.30 + 445.20**: bonding of the generator neutral depends on whether the transfer switch is a **switched-neutral (SDS)** or **solid-neutral (non-SDS)** type. With a 3-pole switch (neutral NOT switched), the generator neutral must be **unbonded** to avoid parallel neutral paths and ensure proper GFCI/breaker operation.
- Portable generators with bonded neutrals on a non-switched setup require a **floating-neutral** conversion.
- **GFCI receptacles** on portable units per OSHA for jobsite use.

### Sizing & Fuel

- LP/NG derate generator output ~10-15% vs. gasoline.
- Run a load calc: AC compressor LRA inrush often dictates unit size; soft-start kits reduce required kW.

### Installation Steps

- Set generator on composite pad, 18 in from structure, 5 ft from windows/openings per manufacturer.
- Run fuel line and trip the sediment trap.
- Pull feeder and control wiring (typically `#14-22` control + power feeder) to ATS.
- Program exercise cycle and test under load with a clamp meter.

### Common Mistakes

- Double-bonded neutral causing nuisance GFCI trips
- No breaker hold-down on back-fed interlock breaker
- Undersized inlet conductors for continuous generator output

title: Whole-Home Surge Protection NEC 230.67
content:
## Type 1 & Type 2 Surge Protective Devices

Since the **2020 NEC, 230.67** mandates a **surge protective device (SPD)** on services supplying dwelling units. The 2023 NEC extends similar requirements to other occupancies and replacement panels.

### SPD Types (NEC 285 / UL 1449)

- **Type 1**: connected on the **line side** of the service disconnect; no external overcurrent device required. Examples: **Siemens FS140**, **Eaton CHSPT2ULTRA** (Type 1 & 2 rated).
- **Type 2**: connected on the **load side** of the service disconnect (in or beside the panel). Examples: **Square D HEPD80**, **Leviton 51120-1**.
- **Type 3**: point-of-use (plug strips), at least 30 ft of conductor from the panel; **not** a substitute for 230.67.

### NEC 230.67 Requirements

- SPD must be **Type 1 or Type 2**.
- Must be installed at the service equipment (or feeder for a detached structure per 230.67(C)).
- Where service equipment is replaced, the SPD must be provided (2023).

### Specs That Matter

- **Voltage Protection Rating (VPR)**: lower is better; quality units clamp at ~**700-900V** L-N (UL 1449 4th edition).
- **Surge Current Rating (kA)**: residential whole-home units 40-80 kA per phase.
- **SCCR**: must meet or exceed the available fault current at the panel.
- **Nominal Discharge Current (In)**: 10 kA or 20 kA ratings preferred.

### Installation Best Practices

- **Keep leads SHORT and STRAIGHT.** Every inch of lead adds ~1.5-2 kV of let-through under fast transients. Trim to <6 in where possible.
- Land on a 2-pole breaker (Type 2) sized per manufacturer (typically 30A-50A) or directly on the bus for breaker-style integrated SPDs.
- Twist the conductors and avoid sharp 90° bends.
- Connect the ground/neutral lead to the bonded bus at the service.

### Layered Protection

A proper strategy cascades:

- **Service-level Type 2** (HEPD80) catches the big transients.
- **Type 3 point-of-use** protects sensitive electronics (AV, networking).
- Coordinate so the service SPD has the higher energy rating.

### Status & Maintenance

- Most units have a green LED/indicator; a tripped MOV shows red or no light. SPDs are sacrificial and degrade with cumulative surges.
- Document install date; recommend inspection after major lightning events.

### Common Failures

- Long, looped SPD leads defeating performance
- Wrong type for line-side placement
- Missing SPD on panel replacements (2023 NEC)

title: Solar PV Interconnection NEC 690/705
content:
## Grid-Tied Solar PV: Interconnection Rules

Utility-interactive PV systems are governed by **NEC Article 690** (solar) and **705** (interconnected power production). The point of connection determines your design.

### The 120% Busbar Rule (705.12(B)(3)(2))

When back-feeding a load center, the sum of the main breaker plus the PV/inverter breaker cannot exceed **120% of the busbar rating**:

- Example: 200A busbar × 120% = 240A allowed. With a 200A main, the PV breaker may be ≤ 40A.
- The PV back-fed breaker must be at the **opposite end** from the main supply (705.12 sum rule / load-side connection).
- Alternatives: **line-side tap** (705.11), **supply-side connection**, or a **derated main** breaker.

### Inverters & Rapid Shutdown (690.12)

- **String inverters**: **SolarEdge HD-Wave SE7600H** with P-series power optimizers provide module-level rapid shutdown.
- **Microinverters**: **Enphase IQ8** series — each module has its own inverter; meets rapid shutdown inherently.
- **690.12** requires conductors inside the array boundary to drop to ≤80V within 30 seconds of initiation; module-level electronics satisfy this.
- Provide a **rapid shutdown initiator** and the standardized **placard** at the service per 690.56(C).

### Conductor & OCPD Sizing

- PV source/output circuit conductors sized at **156%** of Isc (690.8: 125% × 125%).
- Inverter output circuit at 125% of continuous output current.
- DC arc-fault protection per **690.11**; DC disconnects per **690.13/690.15**.

### Grounding & Bonding

- Equipment grounding per **690.43**; use listed WEEB clips or lugs for module frames.
- Many transformerless inverters are functionally grounded — follow **690.41(B)** ground-fault protection.

### Labeling (690.13, 705.10, 690.56)

- "PHOTOVOLTAIC POWER SOURCE" on DC conduits.
- Directory at the service showing all power sources (705.10).
- Rapid shutdown placard with the building diagram.

### Energy Storage Integration

- Batteries (e.g., **Tesla Powerwall 3**, **Enphase IQ Battery 5P**) fall under **Article 706**.
- Microgrid interconnect devices (MID) for backup; PV/battery hybrid often uses a **705.12** smart panel or **gateway**.

### Common Plan-Review Failures

- Busbar 120% violation with full-size main and large PV breaker
- Missing rapid shutdown placard/initiator
- PV breaker not at opposite end of bus
- No AC disconnect within sight of the meter (POCO requirement)

title: Pool & Spa Equipotential Bonding NEC 680
content:
## Pool, Spa & Hot Tub Bonding — NEC Article 680

Water + electricity is the most heavily regulated area of the NEC. **Article 680** exists to prevent electrocution and the dangerous **voltage gradients** that cause drowning panic. Equipotential bonding is the heart of it.

### Equipotential Bonding Grid (680.26)

All metal within the pool environment is tied together with a **#8 AWG solid copper** bonding conductor so everything sits at the same potential:

- **Conductive pool shell / structural rebar** (680.26(B)(1)) — bond rebar with listed clamps before the gunite pour.
- **Perimeter surfaces** within 3 ft of the inside pool wall (680.26(B)(2)) — the unencapsulated rebar or a #8 ring 18-24 in from the wall, 4-6 in deep.
- **Metal fittings, ladders, handrails, diving board anchors**.
- **Pump motors** — bonded with #8; many require a bonding lug.
- **Metal equipment** (heaters, niches).
- **Water bonding**: an approved bonding fitting providing ≥9 sq in of conductive surface in contact with pool water (680.26(C)).

This grid is **NOT** the same as grounding — it does not need to return to the panel, but bonded metal that is also grounded ties the system together.

### GFCI Protection (680.5 / 680.21 / 680.22)

- **All** pool pump motor branch circuits require GFCI (680.21(C)).
- Receptacles within **6 ft to 20 ft** of pool wall require GFCI; one required convenience receptacle 6-20 ft away (680.22(A)).
- Pool/spa lighting (low-voltage and line-voltage) GFCI per 680.23.
- Spas/hot tubs: GFCI on the supply (680.44).

### Underwater Luminaires (680.23)

- No-niche/wet-niche fixtures fed with listed cord; forming shell bonded.
- **12V** fixtures preferred (e.g., **Pentair** / **Hayward ColorLogic**); transformer must be listed for pool use with grounded shield.

### Clearances (680.8 / 680.9)

- Overhead conductors: maintain clearances over pools (e.g., service drop ≥ 22.5 ft over water for ≤750V).
- No outlets within 6 ft horizontal unless GFCI-permitted.

### Heaters & Equipment Disconnect (680.12)

- A maintenance disconnect within **sight** and ≥5 ft from the pool/spa.

### Common Inspection Failures

- Missing perimeter (deck) bonding ring
- No water bond fitting
- Pump not bonded with #8 solid
- Non-GFCI receptacle near pool
- Bonding conductor smaller than #8 or stranded where solid required

title: Recessed LED Can Lighting & IC-Rated Housings
content:
## Recessed Downlights: IC-Rated, Airtight & LED

Recessed lighting selection hinges on insulation contact, air sealing, and the move from incandescent cans to integrated LED.

### IC vs. Non-IC (NEC 410.116)

- **IC-rated** housings may be in **direct contact with thermal insulation** — required wherever batt or blown insulation surrounds the can.
- **Non-IC** housings require **3 in clearance** from insulation (410.116(A)(2)) and ½ in from combustible materials except at the point of support.
- Installing a non-IC can buried in insulation is a fire hazard and a code violation.

### Airtight (AT) & Energy Code

- **IC-AT** housings limit air leakage (≤2.0 CFM at 75 Pa) — required by **IECC** and many local energy codes for the building envelope.
- Gasketed trims further reduce stack-effect losses in vaulted/attic ceilings.

### New-Construction vs. Remodel Cans

- **New-construction** (e.g., **Halo H750ICAT**) mount to joists with bar hangers before drywall.
- **Remodel/retrofit** cans use spring clips to grab the drywall from a cut hole.
- **Canless / wafer LEDs** (e.g., **Halo HLB6**, **Lithonia WF6**) use a small junction box and a thin disc — ideal for shallow plenums and tight ceilings; UL-listed for IC and airtight.

### Wiring & Connections

- Most LED canless units include an integral **junction box** with quick-connect — feed with `14/2` or `12/2 NM-B`.
- Provide proper conductor temperature rating; LED drivers run cooler than incandescent but follow the listing.
- Honor **wet/damp location** ratings for showers and exteriors (use shower-rated trims).

### Spacing & Layout

- Rule of thumb: spacing ≈ ceiling height ÷ 2 (8 ft ceiling → ~4 ft apart).
- Keep cans 18-24 in off walls for wall-wash; tighter for accent.
- Match **color temperature** (2700K-3500K residential) and **CRI ≥ 90**; many units are selectable CCT (2700/3000/3500/4000/5000K).

### Dimming

- Confirm the LED is **dimmer-compatible**; pair with a listed LED dimmer (e.g., **Lutron Diva DVCL-153P**) and check the manufacturer compatibility chart to avoid flicker/drop-out.
- For deep, flicker-free dimming use **forward/reverse phase** dimmers matched to the driver.

### Common Mistakes

- Non-IC cans buried in insulation
- Mismatched dimmer causing flicker
- Missing damp/wet rating in baths
- Overloading a 15A circuit — LED draw is low, but count drivers and other loads
materials_required: IC-AT recessed housings or canless LEDs

title: Smart Lighting & Dimming: Lutron Caseta & RA2 Select
content:
## Whole-Home Smart Lighting with Lutron

Lutron's residential platforms scale from a few switches to a complete system. Choosing the right tier and wiring topology prevents callbacks.

### Platform Tiers

- **Caseta** — DIY/pro entry tier. **Smart Bridge (L-BDG2-WH)** or **Bridge Pro** controls up to 75 devices. Uses **Clear Connect RF** (no neutral required on many dimmers).
- **RA2 Select** — mid-tier; **RR-SEL-H2 main repeater** supports up to 100 devices over a wider RF range; pro-programmed.
- **RadioRA 3** — current pro flagship, **Sunnata** keypads/dimmers, processor-based, up to 200 devices.
- **HomeWorks QS/QSX** — luxury whole-home, wired + RF, theatrical scenes.

### Neutral vs. No-Neutral Dimmers

- Caseta **PD-6WCL** dimmers work **without a neutral** (trickle through the load) — great for retrofits in older boxes lacking a neutral.
- High-wattage or certain LED loads may need a **neutral** model or a **bypass (LUT-MLC)** when fewer than the minimum number of bulbs are connected.
- Always verify the **minimum/maximum load** rating and the LED compatibility list.

### 3-Way & Multi-Location

- Use a Lutron **Pico remote** as the companion instead of a physical 3-way traveler — the Pico communicates by RF to the main dimmer.
- This eliminates traveler wiring and works on existing 2-wire runs.
- Mount Picos in wall-mount kits (**PICO-WBX-ADAPT**) for a hardwired look.

### Load Types & Dimming Curves

- Match dimmer to load: **CL** dimmers for dimmable CFL/LED; ELV/MLV for low-voltage transformers.
- Set the **low-end trim** to eliminate flicker/dead travel at the bottom.
- For 0-10V architectural fixtures use **Lutron Diva 0-10V (DVTV)** or RA control modules.

### Integration

- Bridge integrates with **Alexa, Google, Apple HomeKit, Sonos, Ecobee**.
- RA2 Select / RadioRA 3 integrate with **Control4, Crestron, Savant** via published drivers.

### Programming Best Practices

- Build **scenes** (Entertain, Goodnight, Away) and **timeclock** events with astronomic sunrise/sunset offsets.
- Use occupancy/vacancy sensors (**Lutron Maestro**) on garages, baths, closets.
- Label devices clearly in the app for the homeowner.

### Troubleshooting

- Flicker → wrong dimmer type or missing bypass; check LED compatibility chart.
- RF dropouts → add a repeater; keep devices within range, avoid metal enclosures.
- Won't pair → factory reset (tap/hold pattern) and re-add to the bridge.

title: Motor Circuits & VFD Basics NEC 430
content:
## Motors and Variable Frequency Drives

Motor circuits don't follow the normal 125% conductor rule — they use **NEC Article 430** and the motor FLC tables, not the nameplate amps, for most sizing.

### Conductor Sizing (430.22)

- Single motor branch conductors = **125% of the motor Full-Load Current (FLC)** from **Table 430.248/250** (NOT the nameplate).
- Example: 5 HP, 230V, 1Φ → Table FLC 28A → conductor ≥ 35A → `8 AWG` Cu.

### Overload Protection (430.32)

- Sized **115%-125%** of nameplate FLA (Service Factor ≥1.15 → 125%; SF 1.0 → 115%).
- Provided by the overload relay/heaters in the starter or the drive's electronic overload.

### Branch-Circuit Short-Circuit & Ground-Fault Protection (430.52)

- This is the breaker/fuse, sized as a **percentage of FLC**, much higher than the conductor rating because it must allow inrush:
 - Inverse-time breaker: up to **250%** of FLC
 - Time-delay (dual-element) fuse: up to **175%**
- Use Table 430.52 maximums; the OCPD protects against faults, the overload protects against running overcurrent.

### Disconnecting Means (430.102)

- A disconnect within sight of the motor and the controller, rated ≥115% of FLC.

### VFD Considerations

- A **VFD** (e.g., **ABB ACS580**, **Eaton PowerXL DG1**, **Allen-Bradley PowerFlex 525**) converts fixed AC to variable frequency/voltage for soft start and speed control.
- **Input conductor sizing**: use the drive's rated input current per 430.122 (125% of rated input for power conversion equipment).
- **Output to motor**: use VFD-rated cable (e.g., **Belden VFD cable**) with a continuous shield/symmetrical ground to control reflected-wave and bearing currents.
- **dV/dt and reflected wave**: long leads (>50-100 ft) cause voltage doubling at the motor; add a **dV/dt or load reactor** to protect winding insulation.
- Use an **inverter-duty motor** (NEMA MG-1 Part 31) for VFD service.
- Provide a **line reactor** for harmonic mitigation and drive protection.

### Grounding & EMI

- Bond the VFD per **250**; use 360° shield termination on output cable.
- Keep drive output away from signal/low-voltage cabling to avoid noise.

### Common Issues

- Sizing the breaker to the conductor (nuisance trips on inrush)
- Using THHN instead of VFD cable on the output (insulation failure)
- No load reactor on long motor leads
- Standard motor on VFD failing from bearing fluting (add shaft grounding ring)

title: Arc-Flash Hazards & NFPA 70E PPE Categories
content:
## Arc-Flash Safety & NFPA 70E

An arc flash can reach **35,000°F** and produce a pressure blast that throws workers across a room. **NFPA 70E** is the standard for electrical safety in the workplace; OSHA enforces it under the General Duty Clause and 1910 Subpart S.

### The Hierarchy: De-Energize First

- **NFPA 70E 110.x / 130.2**: the only truly safe condition is an **electrically safe work condition (ESWC)** — de-energize, LOTO, test dead, and ground if needed.
- Energized work requires an **Energized Electrical Work Permit** and is allowed only when de-energizing introduces a greater hazard or is infeasible.

### Approach Boundaries (130.4 / 130.5)

- **Limited Approach Boundary** — shock protection boundary for qualified/unqualified persons.
- **Restricted Approach Boundary** — only qualified persons with shock PPE.
- **Arc Flash Boundary** — distance at which incident energy = **1.2 cal/cm²** (onset of second-degree burn).

### Incident Energy & PPE Categories (Table 130.7(C)(15))

PPE is selected by **incident energy analysis** (preferred) or the **PPE category method**:

- **Category 1**: ≥4 cal/cm² — arc-rated shirt/pants or coverall, face shield, hard hat, safety glasses, hearing protection, leather gloves.
- **Category 2**: ≥8 cal/cm² — AR clothing 8 cal, arc-rated flash hood/balaclava.
- **Category 3**: ≥25 cal/cm² — AR flash suit jacket and pants, AR flash hood.
- **Category 4**: ≥40 cal/cm² — full 40 cal arc flash suit and hood.
- Above **40 cal/cm²** is generally considered too dangerous for energized work — de-energize.

### Voltage-Rated Gloves

- Rubber insulating gloves (e.g., **Salisbury Class 0** rated 1000V) with leather protectors; inspect and air-test before each use, retest per ASTM every 6 months.

### Arc Flash Labeling (130.5(H))

Equipment must carry a label showing:

- Nominal system voltage
- Arc flash boundary
- Available incident energy (cal/cm²) and the working distance, OR the required PPE category

### Practical Field Rules

- Use insulated tools (**Klein 1000V** rated) within the restricted boundary.
- Stand to the side when operating breakers; use remote racking where possible.
- Verify your meter (test-known-test) per the absence-of-voltage procedure.
- Re-evaluate when equipment, available fault current, or protective settings change (study refresh every 5 years per 130.5).

### Common Violations

- Working hot without a permit or analysis
- Cotton/synthetic clothing under AR layers (synthetics melt)
- Outdated or missing arc flash labels

title: Fiber Optic Cabling: Singlemode vs Multimode & Fusion Splicing
content:
## Fiber Optics: Fiber Types, Connectors & Fusion Splicing

Fiber carries data as light, immune to EMI and capable of distances copper can't touch. Choosing the right glass and terminating it cleanly is the craft.

### Singlemode vs. Multimode

- **Singlemode (OS2)** — 9µm core, yellow jacket. Lasers at 1310/1550nm. Distances of **10-40+ km**. Used for campus backbones, ISP, long runs. Lowest attenuation (~0.4 dB/km at 1310).
- **Multimode (OM3/OM4/OM5)** — 50µm core, aqua (OM3/OM4) or lime green (OM5). VCSEL/850nm. **OM4** reaches **400m at 10G**, ~150m at 40/100G. Cheaper optics for data-center/building backbones.
- Match transceivers to fiber: never mix OS2 with multimode optics.

### Connectors

- **LC** — small-form-factor duplex, dominant for SFP/SFP+.
- **SC** — push-pull, common on ONTs and older gear.
- **ST** — bayonet, legacy.
- **MPO/MTP** — multi-fiber (12/24f) for 40/100G parallel optics.
- **APC vs UPC**: green **APC** (8° angled) for singlemode/RF video, lower back-reflection; blue **UPC** for general. Never mate APC to UPC.

### Fusion Splicing

A fusion splicer (e.g., **Fujikura 70S+**, **Sumitomo Q102**) welds two fibers with an electric arc for ~0.02-0.1 dB loss:

- **Strip** the 250µm coating with a Miller stripper to bare 125µm glass.
- **Clean** with 99% isopropyl and lint-free wipes — contamination is the #1 cause of high-loss splices.
- **Cleave** with a precision cleaver (e.g., **CT-50**) for a flat 90° endface; cleave angle <0.5°.
- Load into the splicer; it aligns cores (core-alignment splicers) and arcs.
- Protect with a **heat-shrink splice sleeve** and store slack in the tray/cassette.

### Termination Alternatives

- **Pre-polished mechanical (fast) connectors** for quick field termination.
- **Pigtail + fusion splice** is the gold standard for low loss in a panel.

### Testing & Loss Budget

- **Visual Fault Locator (VFL)** red laser checks continuity/macrobends.
- **OLTS / light source + power meter** for insertion loss (Tier 1).
- **OTDR** (e.g., **EXFO MaxTester**) traces events, locates breaks, characterizes splices (Tier 2).
- Budget: 0.75 dB per mated connector pair, 0.3 dB per splice, fiber km attenuation — verify the link meets the application loss budget.

### Safety & Best Practices

- Never look into a live fiber; **invisible IR laser** can damage the retina.
- Dispose of fiber scraps in a sharps container.
- Maintain bend radius ≥10× cable OD; respect minimum 30mm for most patch cords.

### Common Failures

- Dirty endfaces (always inspect with a 200x scope)
- APC/UPC mismatch
- Exceeding bend radius causing high loss

title: Coax RG6 Distribution & MoCA Networking
content:
## Coaxial Cabling & MoCA

Despite fiber and Cat6, coax remains essential for CATV, satellite, OTA antennas, and high-speed networking over existing cable via MoCA.

### Cable Selection

- **RG6** — 18 AWG center, the residential standard for CATV/SAT/broadband. Use **quad-shield RG6** (60% braid + foil, dual) in high-RF or bundled runs.
- **RG6 with solid copper center** for satellite (carries DC for the LNB); CCS (copper-clad steel) is fine for CATV/data but not where DC power passes.
- **RG11** for long runs (>150 ft) to cut attenuation.
- Sweep-tested to **3 GHz** for DOCSIS 3.1/MoCA 2.5.

### Connectors & Termination

- **Compression F-connectors** (e.g., **PPC EX6XL**, **Thomas & Betts Snap-N-Seal**) — far superior to crimp/twist-on for moisture and return loss.
- Strip with a coax stripper to the proper exposure, seat the connector, and compress with a tool (e.g., **Klein VDV002-820**).
- Weatherproof outdoor fittings with boots/dielectric grease.
