### Splitters & Signal Levels

- Every 2-way splitter loses ~3.5 dB; a 4-way ~7 dB. Budget signal: aim for **0 dBmV ±10** at the modem.
- Use a **drop amplifier** if levels are low, but never amplify a too-noisy upstream.
- **MoCA requires a 1-2.3 GHz-rated splitter**; cheap 5-1000 MHz splitters block MoCA.

### MoCA Networking (Multimedia over Coax)

- **MoCA 2.5** delivers up to **2.5 Gbps** actual ~1 Gbps+ over existing RG6 — ideal for backhaul to a remote AP or hard-to-wire room.
- Adapters: **goCoax WF-803M**, **Hitron**, **ScreenBeam ECB6250**.
- Install a **MoCA PoE (Point-of-Entry) filter** at the demarc/ground block. This reflects MoCA signal back into the home (improves throughput) and prevents your LAN from leaking onto the neighbor's line — a security must.
- MoCA uses 1125-1675 MHz; it coexists with CATV/internet on the same coax.

### Grounding (NEC 820)

- Bond the coax shield/ground block to the building grounding electrode system per **NEC 820.100** with #14 or larger, ≤20 ft to the GES.
- Ground block as close as practicable to the cable entrance.

### Troubleshooting

- Pixelation/dropouts → check connector compression, water ingress, signal level with a meter.
- MoCA not linking → wrong splitter (must pass >1 GHz), missing PoE filter, or split between adapters degrading signal.

### Common Mistakes

- Twist-on connectors causing ingress and return-loss issues
- 1 GHz splitter blocking MoCA
- Missing PoE filter (security + performance)
- Unbonded ground block (NEC 820 violation)

title: Access Control & Card Reader Systems
content:
## Access Control: Readers, Controllers & Door Hardware

Electronic access control replaces keys with credentials and audit trails. A clean install coordinates the controller, reader, lock, and egress devices.

### System Architecture

- **Controller/panel** (e.g., **HID VertX/Mercury**, **Avigilon ACM**, **Brivo**, **Kantech**) is the brain; cloud platforms (**Brivo, Verkada, Openpath/Avigilon Alta**) push management to a portal.
- Each door has: a **reader**, an **electric lock**, a **request-to-exit (REX)** device, and a **door position switch (DPS)**.

### Readers & Credentials

- **HID Signo / iCLASS SE** readers support **13.56 MHz Seos/iCLASS** smart credentials and mobile (NFC/BLE).
- Avoid legacy **125 kHz prox** for new work — it's easily cloned.
- Reader-to-controller wiring: traditionally **Wiegand** (data0/data1) but the industry standard is now **OSDP (Open Supervised Device Protocol, TIA SIA OSDP v2.2)** over **RS-485** — supervised, encrypted (Secure Channel), and bidirectional. Use **22 AWG shielded** multi-conductor.

### Locking Hardware

- **Electric strike** — fail-secure typical on non-egress doors.
- **Maglock (1200 lb)** — fail-safe; requires REX + emergency egress (push-to-exit, motion REX) and tie to fire alarm to **release on alarm** per **NFPA 101 / IBC 1010**.
- **Electrified mortise/exit device** for code-compliant single-motion egress.

### Egress & Life Safety (Critical)

- Free egress must always be maintained — never require knowledge or a key to exit.
- Maglocks must release on **fire alarm, loss of power, and a clearly marked exit push button** (IBC 1010.4.1).
- Coordinate with the fire alarm via relay/addressable module.

### Power

- Use a supervised **access control power supply** (e.g., **Altronix eFlow/Trove**) with battery backup; size for lock inrush.
- PoE options: **HID, Openpath** door controllers powered by **PoE+** simplify wiring.

### Cabling Pull List (per door)

- Reader: 22/6 shielded (or Cat6 for IP/PoE readers)
- Lock: 18/2
- DPS + REX: 22/4
- Bundle as a **composite access cable** to each door.

### Programming & Best Practices

- Set up **schedules, access levels, anti-passback**, and **threat levels/lockdown**.
- Enable **OSDP Secure Channel** encryption; change default reader keys.
- Test fail-safe/fail-secure behavior and fire release before handoff.

### Common Mistakes

- Maglock with no fire-alarm release (life-safety violation)
- Unshielded reader cable causing read errors/EMI
- Using clonable 125 kHz prox
- Undersized power supply browning out locks

title: Structured Wiring Media Enclosure Layout (Leviton)
content:
## Structured Media Enclosures: The Home's Network Hub

The structured media center (SMC) is where all the low-voltage home-runs converge. A clean, planned enclosure is the difference between a serviceable system and a rat's nest.

### Enclosure Selection

- **Leviton 42-series** (14", 28", 42" tall) recessed enclosures, or **On-Q/Legrand** plastic/metal cans.
- Size to the home: a 28" can suits a typical house; large homes need a 42" or a wall-mount rack instead.
- **Metal enclosures** are required where you put a network switch/AP and need grounding and heat dissipation; vented covers for active gear.

### Power

- Install a **duplex receptacle inside or adjacent** to the can (Leviton offers a flush AC module). Active gear (switch, ONT, router, PoE injectors) needs power — this is the #1 oversight.
- Provide a dedicated 15-20A circuit if loading several devices.

### Module Layout

Plan top-to-bottom by service:

- **Demarc/ONT** and ISP gear at top.
- **Network**: patch panel + small switch (e.g., **Leviton 110 patch panel** or a **Ubiquiti USW-Lite-8-PoE** if it fits).
- **Voice**: telephone bridge module (legacy/RJ31X for alarm).
- **Coax**: amplified or passive **video splitter module** (e.g., Leviton 1x8 bi-directional amp).
- Leave a **service loop** (12-18 in) on every cable for re-termination.

### Cooling & Heat

- Active gear generates heat in a closed can — use **vented covers** or a small fan kit; avoid stacking a hot PoE switch in a sealed plastic box.
- For homes with a big switch + NVR, move to a **wall-mount rack** instead of an SMC.

### Cable Management

- Dress and comb cables; service loops coiled neatly.
- Maintain Cat6 **bend radius (4× OD)** and don't cinch zip ties tight (kinks ruin NEXT performance) — use **Velcro**.
- Keep coax/fiber separated and respect their bend radii.

### Grounding

- Bond metal enclosures and the coax/intersystem bonding to the building GES per **NEC 820.100 / 770.100 / 250.94 (intersystem bonding termination)**.

### Labeling

- Label every port to its room/jack per **TIA-606** (see admin standard). Keep a printed map inside the cover.

### Common Mistakes

- No power inside the can (active gear stranded)
- Plastic sealed can cooking a PoE switch
- No service loops — can't re-terminate
- Crushed Cat6 from tight zip ties
- Unbonded metal enclosure

title: WiFi AP Placement & Heat-Mapping with UniFi
content:
## Wireless Access Point Placement & RF Heat-Mapping

Great Wi-Fi is engineered, not guessed. Placement, channel planning, and a validation survey separate pro installs from consumer mesh.

### Survey & Design

- Do a **predictive survey** from the floor plan (e.g., **Ekahau, UniFi Design Center**) and a **post-install validation** survey (e.g., **Ekahau Sidekick, NetSpot, UniFi WiFiman**) to heat-map real coverage.
- Target **-67 dBm or better** at the edge of each coverage cell for reliable roaming/voice.
- Plan **15-20% cell overlap** for seamless roaming; too much overlap causes co-channel interference.

### AP Selection (Ubiquiti UniFi)

- **U6/U7 Pro/Enterprise** ceiling APs for general coverage; **U6 In-Wall** for hospitality/per-room.
- **U6 Mesh / Swiss-Army** for outdoor/patio.
- Wi-Fi 6/6E adds the **6 GHz** band — huge clean spectrum but shorter range; plan denser APs.

### Placement Rules

- **Ceiling-mount, center of coverage area**, antennas radiating down/out.
- Avoid mounting above ductwork, in soffits, or behind metal/foil insulation, mirrors, fish tanks, and concrete cores.
- One AP rarely covers two floors well — plan per-floor.
- Keep APs away from microwaves and high-power devices.

### Channel & Power Planning

- **2.4 GHz**: only use channels **1, 6, 11** (non-overlapping); keep TX power **low** to limit the oversized 2.4 cell.
- **5 GHz**: use **40/80 MHz** widths (not 160 in dense areas — fewer non-overlapping channels) and enable **DFS** channels for more capacity.
- **6 GHz**: wide channels available; use for capacity zones.
- Disable low data rates (1/2/5.5/11 Mbps) to force clients to roam and reduce airtime waste.

### Wiring & Power

- Home-run **Cat6/6A** to each AP from a **PoE+/PoE++** switch (UniFi U7 Enterprise can need PoE++/802.3bt).
- Keep runs ≤ **90m** permanent link.

### Roaming & SSID

- Single SSID across all APs with **802.11k/v/r** fast roaming enabled for seamless handoff.
- Separate **IoT/Guest** SSIDs on their own VLANs.

### Validation

- Walk the site with a heat-map app; confirm signal, SNR, and throughput in every room.
- Check **channel utilization** and retry rates, not just signal bars.

### Common Mistakes

- Too few APs at max power (interference, sticky clients)
- APs in closets/behind TVs
- 2.4 GHz at 40 MHz or wrong channels
- One SSID per AP (no seamless roam)
- 160 MHz width in a dense multi-AP environment

title: Managed Switches & VLAN Fundamentals
content:
## Managed Switches, VLANs & Network Segmentation

A managed switch turns a flat network into a segmented, secure, prioritized system. VLANs are the core tool.

### Why VLANs

VLANs logically separate one physical switch into multiple broadcast domains:

- **Security**: isolate IoT/cameras/guest from trusted devices.
- **Performance**: contain broadcast traffic.
- **Management**: apply policy/QoS per segment.

Typical residential/commercial VLAN plan:

- VLAN 1/10 — **Management** (switches, APs, controller)
- VLAN 20 — **Trusted LAN** (PCs, NAS)
- VLAN 30 — **IoT** (smart home, no internet-to-LAN)
- VLAN 40 — **Cameras/NVR** (often no internet)
- VLAN 50 — **Guest** (internet only, client isolation)

### 802.1Q Tagging

- **Access (untagged) port**: belongs to one VLAN; for end devices.
- **Trunk (tagged) port**: carries multiple VLANs between switches/router; tag with **802.1Q** VLAN IDs.
- **Native/PVID**: untagged VLAN on a trunk — keep consistent to avoid VLAN hopping.

### Inter-VLAN Routing & Firewall

- Routing between VLANs happens at the **router/L3 switch/gateway** (e.g., **UniFi UDM/UXG, pfSense**).
- Apply **firewall rules** to block IoT→LAN while allowing LAN→IoT (stateful return), and block camera VLAN from internet.

### PoE Budgeting

- On PoE switches (e.g., **Ubiquiti USW-Pro-Max-24-PoE**, **Netgear/Cisco**), sum device draw vs. the switch **PoE budget** (watts). PoE (15.4W), PoE+ (30W), PoE++/bt (60-90W).
- A 24-port switch may have a 400W budget — don't overload with PTZ cameras/APs.

### QoS & Other Features

- **QoS/DSCP** prioritize voice/video.
- **STP/RSTP** prevent loops — leave enabled.
- **LAG/LACP** aggregate uplinks for bandwidth/redundancy.
- **IGMP snooping** for multicast (streaming/AV-over-IP).
- **Storm control** and **port isolation** for guest segments.

### Best Practices

- Document VLAN/IP scheme and port maps.
- Use a dedicated management VLAN; never leave default VLAN 1 for production.
- Disable unused ports; enable **DHCP snooping** and **802.1X** in enterprise.
- Firmware updates on a maintenance window.

### Troubleshooting

- No connectivity on a VLAN → check PVID/tagging, trunk allowed-VLAN list, and gateway/DHCP scope.
- IoT can't reach internet → missing firewall allow or wrong VLAN DHCP.
- Loop/broadcast storm → STP disabled or double-patched ports.

### Common Mistakes

- Mismatched native VLAN on trunks
- Forgetting to tag a VLAN on the uplink
- Overloaded PoE budget
- Leaving everything on VLAN 1

title: Cable Labeling & Administration ANSI/TIA-606
content:
## Cabling Labeling & Documentation: ANSI/TIA-606-C

A structured cabling system isn't complete until it's labeled and documented. **ANSI/TIA-606-C** is the administration standard that makes the plant maintainable for the next tech.

### Why It Matters

- Reduces MACs (moves/adds/changes) time and error.
- Required for warranty certification on many manufacturer systems (e.g., **CommScope/Panduit/Leviton** 25-year warranties).
- Provides a permanent record tying every jack to its termination.

### Identifier Classes

TIA-606 defines four administration classes by infrastructure size (Class 1 single room up to Class 4 multi-site). For a typical building (Class 2), label:

- **Telecommunications spaces (TR/ER)**
- **Horizontal links** (every cable/jack/port)
- **Backbone cables**
- **Grounding/bonding (TMGB/TGB)**
- **Firestopping locations**

### Identifier Format

A common horizontal link ID encodes location → rack → panel → port:

- Example: **`1A-A01`** = Telecom Room 1A, patch panel A, port 01.
- Or building/floor scheme: **`B1-2-TR2-PP3-024`**.
- The **same identifier appears at BOTH ends** — the wall jack and the patch panel port must match.

### Label Requirements

- **Machine-printed**, not handwritten (legibility/permanence).
- **Self-laminating** wrap labels for cables (e.g., **Brady, Panduit**) resist abrasion.
- Use a thermal-transfer printer (**Brady M611/BMP41**, **Dymo Rhino**, **Panduit**) — inkjet/laser fades.
- Labels must be UV/moisture resistant for outdoor/plenum.

### What Gets Labeled

- Both ends of every cable
- Patch panels (port and panel ID)
- Faceplates/outlets (icon + ID)
- Racks and rack units
- Cross-connect/blocks
- Conduits/sleeves and pathways
- Grounding busbars (TMGB/TGB)

### Records & Documentation

- Maintain a **cable schedule / spreadsheet or DCIM** linking ID → location → cable type → test results.
- Include **as-built drawings**, floor plans with drop locations, and **certification test reports** (Fluke DSX) per link.
- Color-coding by service per **606-C** (e.g., blue = horizontal data, green = network connections, etc.) when adopted by the owner.

### Best Practices

- Label as you terminate — never "come back later."
- Keep the cable schedule in the media enclosure/TR and digitally.
- Verify the printed map matches reality at closeout.

### Common Failures

- Handwritten or missing labels
- Jack and panel IDs don't match
- No as-built or test documentation (warranty denied)
- Faded inkjet labels

title: CCTV NVR Storage Sizing & Retention
content:
## Sizing NVR Storage for Video Surveillance

The most common surveillance design error is undersized storage. Retention is driven by camera count, resolution, frame rate, codec, and motion vs. continuous recording.

### The Bandwidth-to-Storage Chain

Each camera produces a **bitrate (Mbps)**. Storage = total bitrate × time:

- **Storage (GB) = bitrate (Mbps) ÷ 8 × 3600 × hours × days × cameras ÷ 1000**
- Rule of thumb: **1 Mbps ≈ 10.8 GB/day** of continuous recording.

### Typical Bitrates (H.265)

- **2MP/1080p**: 2-4 Mbps
- **4MP**: 4-8 Mbps
- **8MP/4K**: 8-16 Mbps
- **H.265/HEVC** roughly halves H.264 size; **smart codecs** (Hikvision H.265+, Dahua Smart H.265, **Axis Zipstream**) cut another 30-50% on low-motion scenes.

### Worked Example

- 8 cameras × 4MP at 6 Mbps continuous = 48 Mbps total
- 48 ÷ 8 = 6 MB/s × 86,400 s/day = ~518 GB/day
- 30 days ≈ **15.5 TB** → spec **2× 10TB** drives (allow RAID/overhead).

### Recording Modes

- **Continuous** — maximum storage, never misses anything.
- **Motion/event** — 40-70% savings but risks missing pre-roll; always set **pre/post-record buffers** (5-10 s).
- **Smart events** (line cross, intrusion, AI person/vehicle) reduce false triggers and storage.

### Drives & RAID

- Use **surveillance-rated drives**: **WD Purple, Seagate SkyHawk** — rated for 24/7 write and many camera streams (ATA streaming).
- **RAID**: RAID-1/5/6 for redundancy on critical sites; remember RAID is not a backup.
- Account for **OS/overhead** — never fill drives 100%.

### Platform Examples

- **Ubiquiti UniFi Protect** (UNVR holds up to 7× HDDs), **Hikvision/Dahua NVRs**, **Avigilon, Milestone XProtect, Blue Iris** (PC-based).
- Verify the NVR's **total incoming bandwidth/throughput** and **max channel** limits — not just disk capacity.

### Best Practices

- Confirm the **retention requirement** (often 30-90 days; some jurisdictions/insurers mandate specific periods).
- Set per-camera substreams for live view to save bandwidth.
- Provide UPS for the NVR and network.
- Build in **20-30% headroom**.

### Common Mistakes

- Sizing to camera count, ignoring bitrate
- Consumer drives failing under 24/7 write
- No pre-record buffer (missed the start of events)
- Forgetting NVR throughput ceiling

title: Cellular DAS & In-Building Signal Boosters
content:
## Cellular DAS & Signal Boosters

When cell signal dies indoors (low-E glass, concrete, metal roofs), a **Distributed Antenna System (DAS)** or **signal booster (BDA)** restores coverage. Choosing the right class and following FCC/carrier rules is mandatory.

### Passive vs. Active DAS / Booster Types

- **Consumer/Industrial Booster (BDA)** — bidirectional amplifier. A **donor (outdoor) antenna** captures the carrier signal, the amp boosts it, and **indoor antennas** rebroadcast. Examples: **weBoost/Wilson Pro 70 Plus, SureCall Fusion5X, Cel-Fi GO/QUATRA**.
- **Passive DAS** — booster + coax + splitters feeding multiple dome antennas (small/medium buildings).
- **Active DAS** — fiber/Cat6 to remote radio units; large venues, carrier-grade.

### FCC & Carrier Rules (Critical)

- **FCC Part 20** consumer boosters must be **FCC-certified** and you must **register** the device with the carrier (free).
- Boosters self-oscillate if donor and server antennas are too close — maintain **vertical/horizontal isolation** (often 50-75 ft separation or shielding). Modern units (Cel-Fi) auto-adjust gain.
- **Class A/B** industrial boosters and **carrier consent** are required for larger installs; **public safety DAS (ERRCS)** is a separate, code-mandated system.

### Public Safety / ERRCS (IFC 510 / NFPA 1225)

- First-responder radio coverage (700/800 MHz) is required in many new buildings by **IFC Section 510** and **NFPA 1225 (formerly 72 Ch.24)**.
- Requires **survivable pathway** (2-hour rated cable), monitored **NEMA 4 enclosure**, battery backup (12-24h), annunciator at the FACP, and AHJ/FCC/FirstNet coordination.
- This is NOT a consumer booster job — it's a licensed, permitted system.

### Design Steps

- **Site survey**: measure outdoor signal (dBm/RSRP) at the donor location with a cellular analyzer; identify strongest carrier/band.
- **Donor antenna**: directional **Yagi/LPDA** aimed at the tower; mount high on the roof.
- **Cable**: low-loss **LMR-400 / 50-ohm** coax (cellular is 50Ω, not 75Ω); minimize length to cut loss.
- **Indoor antennas**: dome (omni) for open areas, panel (directional) for hallways; place per a coverage plan.
- **Grounding/lightning**: surge protector on the donor line, bond per **NEC 810/820**.

### Testing

- Verify uplink/downlink improvement at the edges; check for oscillation (amp shutting down).
- Document RSRP/SINR before and after.

### Common Mistakes

- Using 75Ω coax (RG6) instead of 50Ω
- Insufficient donor/indoor antenna isolation → oscillation shutdown
- Treating ERRCS as a consumer booster (code/permit violation)
- Unregistered booster (FCC violation)

title: Smart-Home Hubs: Control4, Crestron & Savant
content:
## Whole-Home Automation Hubs & Controllers

The automation controller is the brain tying lighting, AV, HVAC, shades, security, and access into unified scenes. Choosing and architecting the platform sets the project's ceiling.

### Platform Comparison

- **Control4** — dealer-installed, excellent price/performance and the broadest device driver library. Controllers: **CORE 1, CORE 3, CORE 5**. **Composer Pro** programming. Strong for residential AV + lighting + integration. OS3 UI.
- **Crestron** — the high-end/commercial flagship. **Crestron Home (CP4-R/PC4-R)** for residential simplified setup; full **VC-4 / SIMPL/C# / Crestron Toolbox** for unlimited custom programming. Conference rooms, large estates, theatrical control.
- **Savant** — Apple-centric UX, strong AV-over-IP and energy/power (Savant Power) integration. **Savant Pros / Smart Host**.
- **Lower tiers**: **Home Assistant, Hubitat, Josh.ai (voice)** for budget or DIY-adjacent.

### Architecture & Networking

- The controller lives on the **wired network**; put it on the management/trusted VLAN.
- Reliable **PoE switch, UPS-backed network, and a quality router** are prerequisites — automation reliability is only as good as the LAN.
- Use **IP control** wherever possible; fall back to **RS-232 (serial)** and **IR** for legacy gear (pull control wire during rough-in).

### Integration Protocols

- **Lighting**: Lutron RA2/RA3/HomeWorks, Control4 dimmers, DALI for commercial.
- **Shades**: Lutron Sivoia/QS, Somfy.
- **HVAC**: thermostat drivers (Ecobee, Honeywell), or BACnet in commercial.
- **AV**: HDBaseT/AV-over-IP matrix (NetGear AV Line, SDVoE), IP drivers for AVRs/displays.
- **Voice**: Alexa/Google/Josh.ai bridges.
- **Security/Access**: alarm + camera + door integration.

### Programming Best Practices

- Build **scenes** (Movie, Goodnight, Welcome, Vacation) and **conditional logic/macros**.
- Use **astronomic time clock** (sunrise/sunset) and occupancy triggers.
- Keep a **naming convention** and documented driver list for the next programmer.
- Provide an intuitive client UI; don't over-automate (homeowner override always available).

### Reliability & Service

- Provide **remote management** (Control4 4Sight/BakPak, Crestron XiO Cloud, Domotz) for off-site support.
- UPS the controller and network core.
- Document the full system for service and warranty.

### Common Mistakes

- Underbuilt network behind a premium controller
- No serial/IR control wire pulled for legacy devices
- Over-automation frustrating the client
- No remote-management/monitoring for service

title: Cable Certification & Testing with Fluke DSX
content:
## Copper Cable Certification: Fluke DSX-8000

There's a difference between a cable that "links" and one that's **certified** to a standard. A Fluke DSX certifier runs the full battery of TIA-568 transmission tests and produces the report your warranty depends on.

### Verification vs. Qualification vs. Certification

- **Verification** — basic continuity/wiremap (cheap testers). Confirms pairs are correct.
- **Qualification** — confirms a link can support a service (e.g., 1G/10G) (e.g., Fluke CIQ).
- **Certification** — full standards-compliant test vs. **TIA-568.2-D** Cat5e/6/6A limits with PASS/FAIL margins (Fluke **DSX-8000/DSX-5000**, **Versiv**). Required for manufacturer warranties.

### Permanent Link vs. Channel

- **Permanent Link** — the fixed cabling (patch panel to wall jack), excludes patch cords; uses PL adapters. This is the standard certification test.
- **Channel** — includes patch cords end-to-end (up to 100m total). Use for as-used validation.

### Key Parameters Tested

- **Wiremap** — pin-to-pin, opens, shorts, split pairs, miswires.
- **Insertion Loss (Attenuation)** — signal loss over length/frequency.
- **NEXT / PSNEXT** — Near-End Crosstalk between pairs.
- **ACR-F / ELFEXT (PSACRF)** — far-end crosstalk.
- **Return Loss** — reflections from impedance mismatch (kinks, bad terminations).
- **Propagation Delay & Delay Skew** — timing between pairs.
- **Length** — must be ≤ 90m permanent link / 100m channel.
- Cat6A tested to **500 MHz**, Cat6 to **250 MHz**, Cat5e to **100 MHz**.

### Reading Failures

- **NEXT fail** — excessive untwist at termination; re-terminate keeping twists to within ½ in of the punchdown.
- **Return loss fail** — kinked cable, over-tightened ties, or impedance mismatch (CCA cable, mixed Cat).
- **Insertion loss fail** — cable too long, wrong category, or high temperature.
- **Length/delay fail** — run exceeds 90m or wrong NVP set.
- **Wiremap fail** — split pair (looks continuous but fails crosstalk) or crossed pins.

### Best Practices

- Set the correct **test limit** (e.g., TIA Cat6A Perm Link) and **cable NVP**.
- Calibrate/field-cal the tester and use the matching adapter (PL vs channel).
- Keep firmware/limits updated; use **LinkWare** to manage and export PDF reports.
- Test 100% of links and archive results for the closeout package and warranty.

### Common Mistakes

- Wrong test limit selected (false pass/fail)
- Dirty/worn test adapters skewing results
- CCA or mixed-category cable causing return-loss fails
- Excessive untwist failing NEXT

title: Conference Room AV: Codecs, Mics & Displays
content:
## Conference Room & Huddle Space AV

A modern meeting room blends video conferencing, audio capture, displays, and control. The goal: anyone walks in, joins a call, and it just works.

### Platform & Codec

- Decide the **UC platform**: **Zoom Rooms, Microsoft Teams Rooms (MTR), Google Meet**, or a traditional **codec** (**Cisco Room Kit, Poly G7500, Logitech Rally**).
- **Room compute**: a Teams/Zoom appliance or mini-PC drives the experience; native room systems certified for the platform avoid quirks.

### Displays

- Single 4K display for huddle rooms; **dual displays** (far-end + content) for medium/large rooms.
- Commercial-grade panels (**Samsung/LG/Sony Pro**) rated for long duty cycles, or LED video walls for large boardrooms.
- Mount at proper height; provide **HDMI + USB-C** guest input at the table.

### Cameras

- **Auto-framing / speaker-tracking** cameras (Logitech Rally, Poly Studio, Huddly, Cisco) keep participants centered.
- For large rooms, multi-camera with **director/AI switching**.
- Mount at eye line under/over the display for natural framing.

### Audio — The Make-or-Break

- Audio is where rooms fail. Use proper **DSP** with **acoustic echo cancellation (AEC)** and noise reduction (**Biamp Tesira, QSC Q-SYS, Shure IntelliMix**).
- Microphones: **ceiling array mics** (**Shure MXA920, Sennheiser TeamConnect Ceiling 2**) with beamforming for clean, cable-free table; or table/boundary mics for small rooms.
- Speakers: distributed ceiling speakers for even coverage; avoid a single soundbar in large rooms.
- Set **gain structure** and run AEC tuning; treat the room acoustically (panels) to cut reverb.

### Connectivity & Signal

- **AV-over-IP** (**SDVoE, NETGEAR AV Line, Crestron NVX**, Q-SYS) or HDBaseT matrix to route sources to displays.
- Single **USB-C / Cat6** table connection for BYOD with **USB extension** (USB 3.0 over Cat/fiber) to the rack.
- Dedicated **AV VLAN** with **IGMP/QoS** for AV-over-IP multicast.

### Control

- **Touch panel** (Crestron/Q-SYS/Logitech Tap) for one-touch join, source, volume, and room mode.
- Occupancy-based power on/off and scheduling panels outside the door.

### Power & Rack

- Equipment in a ventilated rack or credenza; provide adequate circuits and UPS for the codec/network.

### Testing

- Place test calls; verify **far-end audio (no echo), mic pickup at all seats, camera framing, content share, and BYOD**.

### Common Mistakes

- Skimping on DSP/AEC (echo, dropouts)
- Single mic for a large table
- No AV VLAN/IGMP for AV-over-IP
- Wrong display height / camera angle
- No BYOD or guest input at the table

title: Shielded Cat6A Grounding & Bonding Best Practices
content:
## Shielded Twisted Pair (F/UTP, S/FTP) Grounding

Shielded copper (Cat6A/Cat7) is specified in high-EMI environments (factories, data centers, hospitals, near power) and for 10GBASE-T at full length. But a shield only protects if it's bonded correctly — a floating or double-grounded shield can be worse than UTP.

### When to Use Shielded

- High **EMI/RFI** (motors, VFDs, fluorescent ballasts, radio transmitters).
- **Alien crosstalk (ANEXT)** mitigation for 10GBASE-T in dense bundles — F/UTP greatly reduces ANEXT vs. UTP.
- Where physical separation from power per TIA-569/NEC can't be maintained.

### Shield Constructions

- **F/UTP** — overall foil, UTP pairs. Common Cat6A shielded.
- **S/FTP** — braid screen overall + foil on each pair. Maximum protection.
- Requires **shielded keystone jacks, shielded patch panels, and shielded patch cords** end-to-end — a single UTP component breaks the screen.

### The Golden Rule: Single-Point Ground

- Ground the shield at **ONE end only** (the TR/patch panel end) to drain induced current to ground.
- **Grounding both ends** can create a **ground loop** if the two grounds are at different potentials — circulating current induces noise and can damage equipment.
- Modern guidance (TIA) sometimes permits both-end bonding **only** when the building bonding network is robust and equipotential; default to single-point in mixed environments.

### Bonding Path (TIA-607 / J-STD-607 & NEC 250)

- Shielded patch panel bonds to the **rack/cabinet**, which bonds to the **TGB (Telecommunications Grounding Busbar)** via a **#6 AWG** bonding conductor.
- TGB connects to the **TMGB (Main busbar)**, which bonds to the building **grounding electrode system** per **NEC 250.94 (intersystem bonding)** and **TIA-607-D**.
- Use listed **bonding jumpers**, paint-piercing washers on racks, and keep the path low-impedance.

### Termination Practice

- Maintain the shield **360° continuous** to the jack — don't cut/strip back the foil at the connector.
- Don't nick conductors; keep untwist minimal for NEXT.
- Verify shield continuity with a certifier that tests the screen.

### Testing & Verification

- Certify with **Fluke DSX** including **shield/screen continuity**.
- Measure **resistance to ground** of the grounding busbar (target low ohms).

### Safety & Code

- Proper bonding is a **shock/fault-current safety** measure, not just performance — a shield carrying fault potential must have a path to ground.
- Follow **NEC 800.100 / 770.100** for communications bonding and **250** for the GES.

### Common Mistakes

- Shield grounded at both ends → ground loop noise
- Floating shield (grounded nowhere) → antenna effect, worse than UTP
- Mixing UTP jacks/cords into a shielded channel
- Rack not bonded to TGB

title: Sump Pump & Sewage Ejector Installation
content:
## Sump Pumps vs. Sewage Ejectors

A **sump pump** moves clear groundwater out of a perimeter-drain basin; a **sewage ejector** lifts gray/black water and solids from below-grade fixtures up to the building drain. They are not interchangeable. Ejectors must pass 2" solids per IPC 712.3.2 and require a sealed, vented basin.

### Sump Pump Basin

- Set an 18" x 22" or 24" deep polyethylene basin (Zoeller, Liberty) on `3/4" washed stone` so the inlet ties to the footing drain tile.
- A `Zoeller M53` 1/3 HP submersible moves ~43 GPM at 5 ft head. Use a vertical or tethered float; verify pump-down and turn-on levels with at least 6" of differential to limit short-cycling.
- Discharge in `1-1/2" Sch 40 PVC` with a check valve (`Zoeller 30-0181` spring-loaded) within 12" of the pump. Add a `3/16" weep hole` below the check valve to prevent air-lock.

### Sewage Ejector

- Use a 30-gal sealed basin. A `Zoeller M267` 1/2 HP ejector passes 2" solids and delivers ~128 GPM at low head.
- Discharge `2" minimum` (IPC Table 712.4.2). Vent the basin per IPC 712.3.5 — never cap a sewage basin airtight without a vent to the DWV system.
- Install a `gas-tight` cover with grommeted penetrations for discharge, vent, and power.

### Electrical & Backup

- Dedicated 15/20A GFCI circuit. Never on an extension cord.
- Add a battery backup (`Basement Watchdog`) or water-powered backup for sumps in flood-prone areas.

### Testing

- Fill the basin with a hose and verify cut-in/cut-out, check-valve hold, and quiet shutoff.
- Confirm discharge daylights at least 10 ft from the foundation and not into the sanitary sewer where prohibited.

### Common Problems & Service

- **Short-cycling:** float differential too small, waterlogged, or a stuck check valve recirculating water back into the basin. Widen the on/off gap or clear the weep hole.
- **Pump runs but no water moves:** air-locked impeller — confirm the 3/16" weep hole is open and free of debris.
- **Frequent ejector calls:** verify the basin lid is gas-tight and the vent is open; a plugged vent causes slow fill and odor.
- Test float operation quarterly and clean the inlet screen. Keep a spare pump on hand for flood-season failures — a basement floods fast when a sole pump dies during a storm.

**Pro tip:** Label the discharge and install a true union check valve so the pump can be pulled without cutting pipe. Photograph the float settings before service so you can restore them exactly.

title: Water Softener & Whole-House Filtration
content:
## Treating Hard & Contaminated Water

Hardness above `7 gpg` (grains per gallon) scales fixtures and water heaters. A salt-based ion-exchange softener swaps Ca/Mg for sodium across a resin bed and regenerates on a brine cycle.

### Sizing

- Grain capacity = people x 75 gal/day x hardness (gpg). A family of 4 at 15 gpg ≈ 4,500 grains/day; spec a `32,000-grain` unit (1 cu ft resin) regenerating roughly every 7 days.
- Add 5 gpg of compensating hardness for every 1 ppm of dissolved iron.

### Installation

- Install on the `cold main` downstream of the pressure regulator and any well pressure tank, but ahead of the water heater.
- Plumb a `bypass valve` so the house has water during service. Use `3/4" or 1" PEX/copper` to match the main.
- Provide an air gap drain for brine/backwash per IPC 802.1.1 — never hard-pipe the discharge into the drain.
- Run a hose-bibb or unsoftened cold leg to exterior spigots and the kitchen drinking tap to avoid sodium loading.

### Whole-House Filtration

- Sediment pre-filter: `5-micron` spun poly cartridge ahead of the softener protects the resin and valve.
- Carbon block (catalytic GAC) removes chlorine/chloramine and taste; size for `>= 1.0 GPM` per fixture-unit demand to avoid pressure drop.
- For point-of-use, add a reverse-osmosis unit (`50 GPD` membrane) under the sink with its own air-gap faucet.

### Startup & Programming

- Set hardness, regeneration time (2 a.m.), and salt type. Use `solar or pellet salt`, not rock salt, in cabinet brine tanks.
- Sanitize the resin bed on first startup, then flush until clear.
- Verify softened output with a titration test (`< 1 gpg`).

### Maintenance & Troubleshooting

- **Salt bridging:** a hardened salt dome leaves an air gap above the brine so the unit stops regenerating effectively; break the bridge with a broom handle and keep the tank no more than two-thirds full.
- **Resin fouling:** iron-fouled resin loses capacity — use a resin cleaner (Iron-Out) periodically and pre-treat high-iron water with an air-injection iron filter ahead of the softener.
- **Hard water after regen:** check the bypass is closed, the bypass valve isn't leaking internally, and program settings match measured hardness.
- Change sediment and carbon cartridges on schedule (typically every 3-6 months) and sanitize RO membranes annually.

**Safety:** Do not soften water for low-sodium dietary needs without a potassium-chloride alternative or a separate hard-water drinking tap. Provide the required air gap on the brine drain so a sewer backup can never siphon into the potable system.

title: Frost-Free Hose Bibb & Freeze Protection
content:
## Preventing Freeze Damage to Supply Piping

Frozen water expands ~9%, splitting copper and bursting fittings. The fix is a combination of correct hardware, slope, and insulation.

### Frost-Free (Frost-Proof) Sill Cocks

- A frost-free hose bibb (`Woodford Model 17`, `Mansfield 400`) has a long stem that seats the valve washer 8-14" inside the heated wall, so no water sits in the exterior portion.
- **Critical:** the bibb must pitch `1/4" downward` toward the exterior so the barrel self-drains. Install level or backward and it will hold water and freeze even though it is "frost-free."
- Always disconnect hoses in winter — a connected hose traps water and defeats the drain-down, the #1 cause of split frost-free bibbs.

### Vacuum Breaker

- Code requires a hose-connection vacuum breaker (`ASSE 1011`) on every sill cock to prevent backsiphonage of contaminated water (fertilizer, pool chemicals) into the potable system. Most frost-free units include an integral, replaceable breaker cap.

### Freeze Protection of Runs

- Keep supply lines on the warm side of insulation; never run water pipe in an exterior wall cavity outboard of insulation.
- Use self-regulating `heat-trace cable` (Easy Heat, Raychem) on vulnerable runs, taped per the maker's spacing, with `pipe insulation` over it.
- Seal rim-joist and sill penetrations with foam to stop wind-chill on pipes.

### Cold-Climate Shutoffs

- For seasonal cabins, install a `stop-and-waste` valve or boiler drain at the low point to blow lines down with compressed air (`< 50 psi`).

### Troubleshooting a Leaking Frost-Free Bibb

- **Drips from the spout after shutoff:** worn stem washer or seat — rebuild with the maker's repair kit (Woodford 30000 series) rather than replacing the whole bibb.
- **Water gushes from the vacuum breaker cap when the hose is on:** the integral breaker has failed — replace the `vacuum breaker repair cap`, a $10 part.
- **Wall leak only when valve is open:** a split barrel from a past freeze; the crack is hidden inside the wall and the unit must be replaced and the cause (level install, connected hose) corrected.
- Verify pitch with a level on the barrel before sheetrock goes up — a frost-free bibb installed dead level will still freeze.

**Safety:** A vacuum breaker is a cross-connection control device, not optional. Cap any bibb missing one, and never remove the breaker to stop a winter drip — replace the internal valve seat instead.

title: Garbage Disposal & Dishwasher Hookup
content:
## Wiring & Plumbing the Sink Disposal/Dishwasher Group

### Disposal Mounting

- Most disposals (`InSinkErator Evolution`, `Badger 5`) use a 3-bolt EZ-mount ring. Bed the sink flange in plumber's putty or the supplied foam gasket, set the fiber/backup gasket and mounting ring, then twist-lock the disposal.
- A 1/2 HP unit suits most homes; spec `3/4-1 HP` for heavy use or septic with bio-charge cartridges.

### Dishwasher Knockout — The #1 Mistake

- A new disposal ships with the `dishwasher inlet knockout plug` still in place. Punch it out with a screwdriver and **remove the plastic slug from inside the disposal** before connecting the dishwasher drain hose, or the dishwasher will not drain and may flood.

### High Loop / Air Gap

- Code requires backflow protection for the dishwasher drain. Use an `air gap` fitting on the countertop (required in many UPC jurisdictions) or, where allowed, a `high loop` secured to the underside of the counter above the flood rim. This prevents waste water siphoning back into the dishwasher.

### Drain Assembly

- Tie the disposal discharge into the trap with a `1-1/2" tubular` trap arm. Use a continuous waste tee for a double bowl. Maintain trap-to-vent distances per IPC 909.
- Never connect a disposal upstream of a trap shared with a second compartment without proper tee orientation, or you'll get gurgling and slow drainage.

### Electrical

- Hardwire or cord-connect to a `switched, GFCI-protected` receptacle. Use the supplied strain relief; confirm the bare/green ground lands on the disposal grounding screw.

### Test

- Run water, switch on, and check the gasket and discharge clamp for leaks. Run a dishwasher cycle and verify the drain hose carries water and the high loop/air gap stays dry.

### Troubleshooting

- **Disposal hums but won't spin:** jammed flywheel — cut power, free it with the supplied hex wrench in the bottom socket, then press the red `reset` button.
- **Dead, no hum:** tripped overload (reset button) or tripped circuit; verify switch and outlet with a meter.
- **Leaks at the sink flange:** putty/gasket not seated — re-bed the flange. **Leaks at the dishwasher nipple:** loose hose clamp or the knockout slug left inside.
- **Dishwasher won't drain:** knockout plug not removed (the classic), or a kinked drain hose.

**Tip:** Always run cold water while grinding; hot water melts grease and coats the chamber. Never put fibrous waste (celery, potato peels) or grease down a disposal on a septic or low-slope drain.

title: Shower/Tub Valve Rough — Pressure-Balance vs. Thermostatic
content:
## Selecting & Setting the Shower Valve

### Anti-Scald Requirement

IPC 424.3 / ASSE 1016 require shower and tub-shower valves to be **pressure-balancing, thermostatic, or combination** to limit outlet temperature to `120 deg F` and prevent thermal shock when another fixture is used.

### Pressure-Balance (PB)

- A spool/piston reacts to pressure swings, holding a near-constant hot/cold ratio. Single handle controls volume and temp together.
- Examples: `Delta Monitor 17 Series`, `Moen Posi-Temp`. Set the rotational-limit stop during trim so max temp is `<= 120 deg F`.
- Good value; temperature can drift slightly as inlet temps change seasonally.

### Thermostatic (TMV)

- A wax/bimetal element actively holds a setpoint regardless of pressure or supply-temp changes. Often paired with separate volume controls and `Delta 17T` / `Moen ExactTemp`.
- Best for multi-head/body-spray systems and when precise, repeatable temperature matters.

### Roughing In

- Set valve height per the spec sheet (commonly `valve 28-48"`, showerhead drop at `72-78"`, tub spout `4"` above tub rim). Use the maker's plaster/mud guard to set finished-wall depth — too deep and the trim won't reach.
- Plumb `hot to left, cold to right`. Cap the showerhead riser and use a drop-ear 90 anchored to backing.
- For PB/TMV with integral stops, you can isolate the valve for trim without shutting the house down.
- Pressure-test (air or water) before closing the wall; document the test per local AHJ.

### Body Sprays / Multiple Outlets

- Total flow can exceed a single valve's capacity; use a high-flow thermostatic valve and a volume/diverter rated for combined GPM, and verify the water heater can supply it.

### Trim-Out & Common Errors

- At trim, remove the plaster guard, install the cartridge (or confirm orientation), and set the rotational limit stop with a thermometer in the stream — adjust until max output reads `<= 120 deg F` at design supply temp.
- **Valve set too deep:** the trim sleeve/escutcheon won't reach the wall and you'll cut tile to fix it; always dry-fit the trim against the mock finished-wall thickness during rough.
- **Reversed hot/cold:** handle indexes backward; pull and rotate the cartridge or re-pipe.
- **No isolation stops engaged:** some cartridges (Moen 1222, Delta RP46074) have integral stops — use them to service the valve without draining the house.

**Pro tip:** Always install with the cartridge accessible and set the limit stop on every PB valve — an unset stop is a scald hazard and a code fail. Keep the spec sheet with the job file so the right repair cartridge can be ordered later.

title: Toilet Install — Flange, Wax Ring & ADA Height
content:
## Setting a Water Closet Correctly

### Flange Height — The Make-or-Break Detail

- The closet flange should sit `flush to 1/4" above` the finished floor, with the flange on TOP of the finished floor. A flange set below finished floor is the leading cause of recurring leaks and rocking.
- If the flange is too low after new tile, use a `flange spacer/extender kit` (stacked rings + new gasket) rather than doubling wax rings.
- Closet bolts (`5/16"`) drop into the flange slots at 3 and 9 o'clock; secure with the supplied retainer washers so they stand vertical.

### Wax vs. Waxless

- Standard `wax ring` (with or without horn) seats once — do not reuse. For uneven setups or repeat removals, a `waxless seal` (Fluidmaster PerfectSeal / Sani Seal foam gasket) reseats and is more forgiving.

### ADA / Comfort Height

- ADA-compliant water closets seat `17-19"` from finished floor to seat top (ANSI A117.1 / ADA 604.4). "Comfort height" bowls (`TOTO Drake`, `Kohler Cimarron`) meet this and ease aging-in-place; standard height is ~15".
- For accessible stalls, the centerline must be `16-18"` off the side wall and clearances per ADA 604.

### Setting the Bowl

- Set the bowl straight down onto the wax/seal without rocking; press with body weight to compress.
- Hand-tighten nuts alternately — **snug, not torqued**. Overtightening cracks china. Shim any rock and caulk the base (leave a gap at the rear so a future leak is visible).

### Supply & Test

- Connect a braided `3/8" x 7/8"` closet supply to a quarter-turn stop. Fill, set fill valve to the marked waterline, and check for tank-to-bowl and base leaks through several flushes.

### Troubleshooting a Newly Set Toilet

- **Rocks side to side:** shim with composite toilet shims and re-caulk; never overtighten bolts to stop rock — that cracks the china.
- **Leaks at the base on flush:** wax seal failed (flange too low, bowl shifted during set, or reused ring). Pull, replace with a waxless seal and a flange spacer if needed.
- **Phantom flushing / runs:** flapper or fill valve seal — adjust the chain or replace the flapper (Fluidmaster 400A fill valve is a common drop-in).
- **Weak/incomplete flush:** clogged rim jets or wrong water level — clean jets and set the fill valve to the tank's marked line.

**Tip:** Caulk the base per IPC 405.5 for sanitation; the rear gap exposes hidden leaks early. On uneven tile, dry-set the bowl and shim before committing to the wax seal.

title: Sewer Line & Cleanouts — PVC, Cast-Iron Transition & Fernco
content:
## Building Sewer Materials, Slope & Cleanout Code

### Pipe & Slope

- Building sewer in `PVC SDR-35` or `Sch 40 DWV` (Charlotte Pipe). Minimum slope per IPC Table 704.1: `1/4" per ft` for 2-1/2" and smaller, `1/8" per ft` for 3"-6". More than `1/2" per ft` lets water outrun solids and causes clogs.
- Bed and haunch in compacted sand/pea gravel; never bridge pipe over a rock.

### Cleanouts (IPC 708)

- Required: at the building drain/sewer junction, at each `change of direction > 45 deg`, every `100 ft` of horizontal run, at the base of stacks where required, and an `upper-terminal/two-way` cleanout near the property line.
- Cleanout size matches pipe up to 4". Provide `18" clearance` (12" for <= 2") in front of the opening for rodding access.
- Bring cleanouts to grade with a riser and `countersunk plug`; do not bury them.

### Cast-Iron to PVC Transition

- Use a `shielded transition coupling` (Fernco Proflex / Mission) with a full stainless shear band — these are listed for above- and below-ground per ASTM C1277/C1540 and resist shear and sag. 
- Plain unshielded `Fernco flexible couplings` are for repair/limited applications; check the AHJ before using them on a load-bearing buried main, where many jurisdictions require a banded coupling.
- For caulked hub cast iron, a `compression donut` or proper no-hub band with the correct torque (`60 in-lb`) is required.

### Backwater & Connection

- Where a fixture is below the next upstream manhole rim, a `backwater valve` is required by IPC 715.
- Tie into the public main with the utility-approved saddle/wye; never use a sanitary tee laid horizontally (use a wye + 1/8 bend).

### Fittings & Directional Rules

- For horizontal-to-horizontal and horizontal-to-vertical changes on the drainage side, use long-sweep fittings: `wyes, combos, and long-radius bends`. Short-turn 90s and horizontal sanitary tees on their back trap solids and are prohibited on flow lines per IPC 706.
- Maintain `developed-length` limits and ensure each cleanout opens in the direction of flow so a cable can travel downstream.
- Support buried PVC continuously on firm bedding; aerial/exposed runs need hangers every `4 ft` per IPC 308 with no sags that create bellies.

### Transition Best Practice

- When joining new PVC to an old cast-iron hub, cut the cast back to sound metal, deburr, and use a full-shielded banded coupling torqued to spec. Mark the transition location on the as-built for future service.

**Code note:** Pressure/air-test or fill-test the building sewer per IPC 312 and call for inspection before backfill. Photograph the open trench, slope, and bedding for the inspection record.

title: Hot-Water Recirculation Pump Installation
content:
## Eliminating the Wait for Hot Water

Recirculation moves cooled water in the supply lines back toward the heater so hot water is at the fixture quickly, saving water and time.

### Two System Types

**Dedicated return loop (best):** A separate `3/4" return line` runs from the farthest fixture back to the water heater drain or a tee on the cold inlet. A bronze circulator (`Grundfos UP15-10`, `Taco 006`) mounts on the return and runs on a timer/aquastat.

**Comfort/retrofit (no return line):** A pump at the heater plus a `thermostatic bypass valve` under the farthest fixture uses the cold line as the return. Easier retrofit, but it warms the cold line slightly. Examples: `Grundfos Comfort System`, `Watts Premier`.

### Installation

- Mount the circulator on the return with flow in the correct direction (cast arrow). Use `bronze/stainless` pump bodies on potable water — iron circulators are for closed heating loops only.
- Isolate with `ball valves` and unions so the pump can be serviced. Add a `swing check` to prevent thermosiphon backflow.
- Power from a switched receptacle; many pumps include a built-in 24-hr timer and `aquastat` that cycles the pump only when loop temp drops below ~95 deg F.

### Tankless Considerations

- Standard tankless units won't fire on tiny recirc flow. Use a `recirc-capable` model with internal pump and buffer (`Rinnai RUR`, `Navien NPE-A`) or an external buffer tank, or the heater short-cycles and wears out.

### Energy & Comfort

- Run on a timer matched to occupancy (mornings/evenings) or an on-demand button to cut standby loss.
- Insulate all hot and recirc piping with `3/4" wall` foam to maximize savings.

### Troubleshooting Recirc Systems

- **Still slow to get hot water:** pump not running (check timer/aquastat and power), check valve installed backward, or air-bound loop — bleed air at the high point.
- **Cold line runs warm:** expected with comfort/bypass systems; if excessive, the bypass thermostatic valve is stuck open — replace it.
- **Pump noisy/cavitating:** air in the loop or insufficient system pressure; purge and verify the expansion/PRV setup.
- **Tankless won't maintain temp on recirc:** confirm a recirc-capable model and that buffer/internal-pump settings are enabled; a standard tankless can't sense the low flow.

### Efficiency Tuning

- Pair the pump with a `motion-sensor or smart-plug schedule` so it only runs during occupied hours, and insulate the full loop to hold the savings.

**Tip:** A check valve is mandatory — without it, gravity thermosiphon will heat the cold side and waste energy 24/7.

title: Well Systems & Pressure Tanks
content:
## Private Well Pump & Pressure-Tank Setup

### Pump Types

- **Submersible** (deep wells, >25 ft): a multi-stage pump (`Grundfos SQ`, `Goulds`) hangs below the water table on poly/Sch 80 drop pipe. 
- **Jet pump** (shallow, <25 ft): surface-mounted, uses suction. Shallow-well single pipe vs deep-well two-pipe convertible.

### Pressure Tank & Air Charge

- Use a `bladder/diaphragm tank` (Well-X-Trol, Amtrol). The tank stores water under air pressure so the pump isn't cycling on every faucet open.
- **Critical:** with the tank empty/depressurized, set the air pre-charge `2 psi below cut-in`. For a 40/60 switch, pre-charge to `38 psi`. Wrong pre-charge causes waterlogging and rapid pump short-cycling that burns out the motor.
- Size for adequate `drawdown` so the pump runs >= 1 minute per cycle; a typical home uses a 20-44 gal tank.

### Pressure Switch & Controls

- A `Square D FSG2` pressure switch (40/60 or 30/50) starts/stops the pump. Some include a low-pressure cutoff to protect against a dry/dropped well.
- Submersibles need a `control box` (for 3-wire) or built-in start components (2-wire). Protect with a `pressure relief valve` set below pipe/tank rating.

### Sanitary & Code

- Provide a sanitary, vermin-proof well cap and pitless adapter; never a buried open well casing.
- A `check valve` at/near the pump holds prime and keeps the column from draining back.
- Shock-chlorinate the well after any service, then flush before use.

### Treatment Sequence

- Typical order: well -> pressure tank -> sediment filter -> iron/sulfur treatment -> softener -> carbon -> house. Acidic well water (`pH < 6.5`) needs a calcite neutralizer to stop copper-pipe pinhole leaks.

### Troubleshooting Well Systems

- **Rapid pump cycling (machine-gunning):** waterlogged tank — the bladder failed or the pre-charge is wrong. Drain, check pre-charge to 2 psi below cut-in; if it won't hold air, the bladder is ruptured and the tank needs replacement.
- **Low pressure / pump runs constantly:** worn pump, leak in the drop pipe, clogged screen, or a dropping water table. Check amp draw against nameplate.
- **No water, motor hums then trips:** locked rotor or failed start components/control box on a submersible.
- **Sand/grit at fixtures:** failing well screen or pump set too low in the casing.

### Pump Protection

- A `low-pressure cutoff` or pump-saver relay prevents dry-running burnout if the well draws down. Never let a submersible run dry — it relies on pumped water for motor cooling.

**Tip:** Check the air pre-charge yearly with a tire gauge on the Schrader valve, system depressurized.

title: Home-Run PEX Manifold (Uponor ProPEX)
content:
## Designing a Home-Run Manifold System

In a home-run (parallel) layout each fixture gets its own dedicated line from a central manifold — like a breaker panel for water. This gives balanced pressure, fewer in-wall fittings, and individual shutoffs.

### Manifold Selection

- Use an engineered manifold (`Uponor ProPEX Branch/Valved Manifold`, copper or MepLok) with separate hot and cold blocks and labeled, valved ports.
- Locate centrally near the water heater to minimize run lengths and water waste.

### Pipe Sizing

- Run `1/2" PEX-a` to most fixtures; `3/8"` only for low-demand (lavatory) where run length is short. Tubs/showers and the manifold trunk warrant `3/4"`.
- PEX-a (Uponor) is repaired/expanded with the cold-expansion `ProPEX` ring — the tubing memory shrinks back over the fitting for a strong, full-bore connection. No O-rings, fewer failure points than crimp.

### Installation Best Practices

- Maintain bend radius >= `6x OD`; use a `bend support` for tighter turns, never kink (a kinked section must be cut out, not heat-straightened in supply piping per most makers).
- Sleeve PEX through framing and at slab penetrations; keep `12" from gas vents/flues` and away from recessed-can heat.
- Protect tubing within 1-1/4" of stud edges with `nail plates` (IPC 305.5).
- Pressure-test at `100 psi` air or `1.5x working pressure` water before closing walls.

### Pressure Balancing & Future Service

- Label every manifold port (e.g., "Hot - Master Shower"). A leaking fixture line can be isolated at the manifold without shutting the house down — a major selling point.
- Leave the manifold in an accessible chase/panel per IPC 606.1.

### Trunk-and-Branch vs. Home-Run

- Home-run uses more tubing but eliminates buried tees and balances pressure when multiple fixtures run. A `mini-manifold` (sub-manifold) approach groups nearby fixtures off a local manifold to cut tubing footage while keeping most of the benefits.
- Size the manifold trunk and water-heater feed for total simultaneous demand using fixture units (IPC Table 604.3 / Appendix E) so the system doesn't starve during peak draw.

### Troubleshooting ProPEX Joints

- **Weeping joint:** ring not fully seated or expander not fully inserted before the fitting — cut out and redo; ProPEX joints are not adjustable once set.
- **Cold-weather looseness:** in sub-freezing temps the tubing memory recovers slowly; follow Uponor's cold-weather dwell times before pressurizing.

**Pro tip:** Expand the ProPEX ring with the correct head, fully seat the fitting, and let it set per the cold-weather dwell chart — rushing in cold temps causes a loose joint. Keep manifold labeling consistent so future service is fast.

title: Drain Cleaning & Jetting
content:
## Diagnosing & Clearing Drain Stoppages

### Identify the Stoppage Type

- **Single fixture slow/clogged:** local to the trap/branch — soap, hair, grease. Cable or hand-auger the fixture arm.
- **Multiple fixtures, lowest backs up first:** main-line blockage. Toilet gurgles when the washer drains, or floor drain overflows = main is the culprit.
- **Gurgling/slow venting with no clog:** suspect a `blocked vent` (bird nest, ice cap) creating siphon/air-lock, not a drain clog.

### Cabling (Snaking)

- Sink/branch: `1/4"-3/8"` cable in a hand or drill auger. Mainline: `5/8"-3/4"` cable on a sectional/drum machine (`RIDGID K-400/K-7500`) with the right cutter head.
- Run the cable through a cleanout, not the toilet, when possible. Let the machine feed slowly; forcing a knotted cable can damage old pipe or rupture a coupling.

### Hydro-Jetting

- For grease, sludge, and root mat, a `jetter` (1,500-4,000 psi, 4-18 GPM) scours the full pipe diameter where a cable only punches a hole.
- Match nozzle to job: penetrator for the clog, then a `rotary/flusher` nozzle pulled slowly back to wash debris downstream.
- **Caution:** Do not jet `Orangeburg`, badly corroded cast iron, or compromised clay — high pressure can blow out the pipe. Camera-inspect first.

### Camera & Locate

- After clearing, run a `push camera` (RIDGID SeeSnake) to find root intrusion, bellies, offset joints, or breaks, and `locate/sonde` the depth for any needed dig.

### Root & Recurring Clogs

- Roots returning every few months indicate a cracked joint; recommend spot repair or lining.
- Recurring kitchen clogs point to grease — recommend a high-loop, strainer use, and avoid pouring fats.

### Jetting Setup Details

- Match GPM and pressure to pipe size: a `1.5-4 GPM` cart jetter clears 1.5-3" kitchen/lav lines; a `trailer jetter (4,000 psi, 12-18 GPM)` is for 4-8" mainlines and root mats.
- Always pull the nozzle slowly back toward the cleanout so debris washes downstream, not packed tighter ahead of the nozzle.
- Keep a `relief/anti-recoil` setup and never start the jetter with the nozzle out of the pipe — the whip is dangerous.

### Documentation & Upsell

- Record camera footage with on-screen footage counter and locate marks; deliver it to the customer. Recurring roots or a confirmed belly justify a recommendation for `spot repair`, `pipe bursting`, or `CIPP lining` rather than repeat snaking.

**Safety:** Wear face/eye protection and gauntlet gloves; mainline cables and jetter whip can cause serious injury. Never leave a running machine unattended, and keep loose clothing clear of the rotating cable drum.

title: Cold-Climate Heat Pump & Defrost (Mitsubishi Hyper-Heat)
content:
## Heating Below Zero with Air-Source Heat Pumps

Cold-climate (ccASHP) inverter heat pumps now deliver useful capacity well below freezing, displacing fossil heat in northern climates.

### Hyper-Heat Performance

- `Mitsubishi H2i / Hyper-Heat` units maintain `100% rated capacity at 5 deg F` and run down to `-13 deg F` with a flash-injection compressor and enhanced vapor injection.
- Compare to standard heat pumps that lose ~50% capacity at 17 deg F. Always size from the NEEP ccASHP database capacity at your `99% design temp`, not the nameplate.

### Defrost Cycle

- In heating, the outdoor coil is the evaporator and frosts up. The unit periodically reverses to defrost: a `reversing valve` flips to cooling mode, the outdoor coil warms and sheds ice, and the indoor fan stops to avoid blowing cold air.
- Demand-defrost (temperature/pressure sensed) is far more efficient than fixed-timer defrost. Brief steam/melt and a puddle under the unit during defrost are **normal**, not a refrigerant leak.
- Mount the unit on a `wall bracket or stand` 12-18" above grade/snow line with a `condensate pan heater` so meltwater doesn't refreeze and heave the unit.

### Backup / Balance Point

- Determine the `thermal balance point` where heat-pump output equals the home's loss; size auxiliary (electric strip, gas, or hydronic) for below that.
- Wire lockout so backup doesn't run when the heat pump alone can satisfy load, preventing energy waste.

### Line Set & Charge

- Pull vacuum to `< 500 microns`, weigh in charge per line length, and verify against subcooling/superheat targets in cold ambient.
- Insulate the suction line fully; in heating it carries hot gas, in cooling cold gas — gaps cause loss and condensation.

### Troubleshooting Cold-Climate Operation

- **Excessive ice build-up / poor heat:** demand-defrost sensor fault, low charge, or the unit drowning in drifted snow — clear the coil and verify the defrost thermistor and reversing valve operation.
- **Cold air from indoor unit during defrost:** normal; the indoor fan stops or slows. If it blows cold during a heat call (not defrost), check `O/B` reversing-valve wiring and the thermostat heat-pump configuration.
- **Capacity falls off a cliff at design temp:** unit undersized from nameplate instead of NEEP cold-climate data — re-evaluate the balance point and backup sizing.

### Commissioning

- Record outdoor ambient, indoor/outdoor temps, suction/discharge pressures, and verify the line-set length charge adjustment. Confirm the base-pan heater draws current in deep cold.

**Tip:** Keep the outdoor unit clear of snow drift and ensure the base pan drain heater is energized in deep cold. Mount on a stand tall enough to clear local maximum snow depth.

title: Rooftop Package Unit (RTU) Commercial Install
content:
## Setting & Commissioning a Commercial RTU

Packaged rooftop units (`Carrier 48/50 WeatherMaker`, `Trane Precedent`, `Lennox Energence`) combine compressor, coils, blower, and gas heat in one curb-mounted cabinet.

### Curb & Rigging

- Set a `factory roof curb` level and flashed into the membrane; the curb gasket seals the unit-to-curb joint. Out-of-level curbs cause condensate pan overflow and door leaks.
- Rig with a crane and a spreader bar rated for the unit weight (a 7.5-ton RTU can exceed 1,500 lb). Verify roof structural capacity with the SE for both unit weight and live/snow load.

### Duct & Airflow

- Match supply/return openings to the curb; transition with `internally lined` ductwork to control noise.
- Set blower for design `400 CFM/ton` (cooling) and verify external static pressure is within the fan curve. High static trips limit switches and starves cooling.

### Gas, Electrical & Economizer

- Pipe gas with a `drip leg/sediment trap`, union, and exterior shutoff per NFPA 54; size for the unit's MBH input.
- Provide a fused disconnect within sight; verify `MCA/MOCP` on the nameplate sizes the wire and breaker.
- Most commercial RTUs include an `economizer` for free cooling — set the changeover/enthalpy control and confirm dampers stroke fully.

### Condensate & Startup

- Trap the condensate drain per the draw-through pan (negative pressure) requirement, prime the trap, and route to an approved point.
- Startup: check rotation (3-phase), `superheat/subcooling`, gas manifold pressure, temperature rise across heat exchanger, and economizer operation. Record all readings.

### Curb Adapters (Replacements)

- When swapping brands, use a `curb adapter` to mate new unit footprint to existing curb; verify duct alignment.

### Safety & Access

- Provide `roof access, a service walkway, and required clearances` around the unit per IMC 306 so techs can service it safely. Fall-protection tie-off points are required near roof edges.
- Verify the unit's `MCA/MOCP` against the installed wire and breaker; 3-phase units must be checked for correct `rotation` (scroll compressors and blowers are direction-sensitive — reversed rotation damages a scroll fast).
- Confirm the gas line has an exterior shutoff, drip leg, and that the flue/combustion air meets NFPA 54.

### Maintenance Setup

- Leave the economizer changeover and damper linkage accessible; stuck-closed economizers are a top cause of high summer bills and no free cooling.
- Set belt tension (belt-drive units) and confirm filter access.

**Tip:** Document amp draw, charge, static, and temp rise at commissioning for the O&M file and warranty. Curb-mounted condensate must drain freely — verify the trap is primed and the pan slopes correctly before leaving.

title: Air Handler & Evaporator Coil Replacement
content:
## Replacing the Indoor Coil / Air Handler

### Match the Coil to the Condenser

- The evaporator coil must be the **AHRI-matched** model for the outdoor unit and metering device, or capacity and efficiency drop and warranty is void. Look up the AHRI certificate by outdoor + indoor + (if applicable) furnace combination.
- Confirm `cased vs uncased`, airflow direction (upflow/downflow/horizontal), and `TXV/piston` match the refrigerant (R-410A vs R-454B/A2L).

### Removal & Prep

- Recover refrigerant to an approved cylinder per EPA 608 — venting is a federal violation. Never cut into a charged system.
- Cut the line set with a tubing cutter (no torch on a charged/oily line). Cap and label.

### Setting the Coil / Air Handler

- Seal the coil case to the plenum with `mastic and foil tape`; a leaky cabinet bypasses air around the coil and kills capacity.
- Slope the unit toward the drain pan and provide a **secondary/emergency drain pan** with a float switch when over a finished space (IMC 307.2.3).
- For air handlers, set on a vibration pad; verify filter rack and access doors seal.

### Refrigerant Connections

- Braze with `dry nitrogen purge` at 2-3 psi flowing to prevent internal oxidation/scale that fouls the TXV.
- Pressure-test with nitrogen to the lower of nameplate/component rating, then evacuate to `< 500 microns` and hold with the pump valved off.
- Weigh in charge for line length; verify `superheat/subcooling`.

### Airflow & Startup

- Set blower to design CFM/ton; measure total external static with a manometer.
- Verify `temperature split` (typ. 16-22 deg F) and check the new coil and connections for leaks with an electronic detector.

### Common Replacement Pitfalls

- **Cabinet/plenum air bypass:** an unsealed coil case lets return air sneak around the coil, dropping capacity and causing high temp split with poor cooling. Seal every seam.
- **Mismatched metering device:** installing a piston coil on a system designed for a TXV (or vice versa) throws the charge off — match per the AHRI certificate.
- **No secondary protection:** a coil over finished living space needs an aux pan + float switch (IMC 307.2.3) or the next clog floods the ceiling.
- **Skipping the nitrogen purge:** brazing without flowing nitrogen leaves cupric-oxide scale that plugs the TXV screen weeks later.

### Final Verification

- After charging, log subcooling/superheat, total external static, supply/return temps, and amp draw. Leak-check all field joints with an electronic detector or bubbles before insulating.

**Tip:** Replace the filter drier whenever the system is opened; a saturated drier passes moisture and acid downstream. Always pull a deep vacuum and confirm decay with the pump valved off, not just a momentary reading.

title: Condensate Drain, Pump & Float Switch
content:
## Diagnosing & Preventing Condensate Overflow

Water damage from a plugged condensate line is one of the most common (and preventable) HVAC callbacks.

### Drain Configuration

- A cooling coil produces gallons of condensate per day. The primary drain leaves the pan, runs through a `P-trap`, and drains by gravity at `1/8" per ft` minimum.
- **Trap depth matters:** draw-through coils (negative pressure, most furnaces/air handlers) need a trap deep enough that the blower can't suck the trap dry or pull air, which stalls drainage. Use a clear trap or maker's `condensate trap` sized to the static.

### Secondary Protection

- Where overflow would damage a building, IMC 307.2.3 requires one of: a secondary drain line, an auxiliary drain pan with its own drain, a `pan float switch`, or an in-line `condensate switch`. Best practice is BOTH a secondary pan and a float switch.
- Wire the `float/safety switch` (`RectorSeal Safe-T-Switch SS2`) in series with the 24V `Y/thermostat` circuit so a high level shuts off cooling before it overflows.

### Condensate Pumps

- When gravity drainage isn't possible, use a `condensate pump` (Little Giant VCMA-20) with its own integral safety float wired to shut the system down on high level.
- Provide a check/vent loop per the maker to stop back-drain and air-lock.

### Common Failures

- **No cooling, blower runs, water in pan:** float switch tripped on a clogged drain. Clear the line (wet/dry vac at the termination, then flush) and reset.
- **Slimy biofilm/algae clog:** install drain-pan tablets and an accessible cleanout tee; flush each spring.
- **Water from supply registers:** undersized/no trap pulling air, or duct sweating from a leaky uninsulated plenum.

### Maintenance

- Add a `cleanout tee` near the pan, pour pan treatment, and vacuum the line annually.

### Sizing & Material

- Primary drain `3/4" minimum` (IMC 307.2.2) sloped at least `1/8" per ft` to an approved point — never to a crawlspace, walkway, or where it can freeze. PVC or CPVC; secure with hangers so it doesn't sag and trap debris.
- For pumps, route discharge in `3/8"-1/2" vinyl/PVC` up and over to gravity drain; add a `vent loop and check valve` per the maker to stop back-siphon and air-lock.

### Wiring the Safety Circuit

- The float switch is normally-closed in the 24V circuit. For straight cooling, break `Y`; on a heat pump or to stop the air handler entirely, break `R` or use the dedicated `S` terminals per the equipment so a high level shuts the system before it overflows.
- Test by lifting the float manually and confirming the system shuts down.

**Tip:** A clear trap and a labeled cleanout turn a flood callback into a 5-minute service. Pour pan treatment tablets each spring to keep biofilm from regrowing.

title: IAQ — MERV Filtration, UV & ERV/HRV Fresh Air
content:
## Improving Indoor Air Quality the Right Way

### Filtration & MERV

- `MERV` rates particle capture: MERV 8 (basic dust), MERV 11 (allergens), MERV 13 (fine particulate/smoke, ASHRAE recommended for IAQ). HEPA is MERV 17+, used in dedicated bypass units.
- **Trade-off:** higher MERV = higher static pressure. A 1" MERV 13 in a system designed for MERV 8 can starve airflow, freeze the coil, and overheat the blower. Upsize to a `4" media cabinet` (Aprilaire 213) to get MERV 13 at low pressure drop.
- Verify added filter pressure drop against the blower's available static; measure with a manometer before and after.

### UV / UVC

- A `coil UVC lamp` (Fresh-Aire UV) keeps the evaporator coil and drain pan free of biofilm/mold, preserving capacity and reducing odors.
- Air-stream UV for microbial inactivation requires adequate dwell/intensity. Bulbs degrade — replace annually; UVC damages eyes/skin and degrades nearby wiring insulation, so shield and interlock with the access door.

### Fresh Air — ERV vs HRV

- Tight homes need mechanical ventilation per `ASHRAE 62.2`. An `ERV` (energy recovery) transfers heat AND moisture between exhaust and intake — best in humid/mixed climates to avoid importing humidity. An `HRV` transfers heat only — preferred in cold, dry climates.
- Balance supply/exhaust airflow and verify with a flow hood. Provide a condensate drain and a winter `defrost/recirc` cycle on HRVs.

### Humidity Control

- Whole-house `bypass/steam humidifier` (Aprilaire 700) for winter dryness; `dehumidifier` or enhanced-dehumidification mode for summer. Target `30-50% RH` to limit mold and dust mites.

### Sizing Fresh Air & Balancing

- ASHRAE 62.2 ventilation rate is roughly `0.03 CFM per sq ft + 7.5 CFM per occupant`. Size the ERV/HRV to deliver continuous (or controlled-intermittent) airflow meeting that rate, and commission it with a flow hood at both the supply and exhaust grilles.
- Balance supply to exhaust within ~10% so the house isn't driven into excessive positive or negative pressure, which can backdraft combustion appliances or pull in humid/soil gas.
- Duct the ERV/HRV intake away from the dryer vent, plumbing vents, and the AC condenser; provide a condensate drain and a winter defrost cycle on HRVs.

### Verification

- Measure filter pressure drop before/after a MERV upgrade and confirm blower amps and total static stay within rating. Verify UV lamp output and replace bulbs annually.

**Best practice:** Don't bolt a high-MERV filter onto an undersized return — fix the filter area first, then raise efficiency. IAQ improvements must respect the airflow design, or you trade clean air for a frozen coil.

title: Hydronic / Boiler & Radiant Heat
content:
## Designing Hot-Water Heating Systems

### Boiler Selection

- `Mod-con (modulating-condensing)` boilers (`Navien NHB`, `Lochinvar`) hit `>= 95% AFUE` by condensing flue gas — only when return water is below ~130 deg F, so they pair best with low-temp radiant.
- Cast-iron/non-condensing boilers run higher temps for baseboard/radiators; protect them from sustained low-return condensation with a `boiler-protection/mixing valve`.
- Size from a Manual J, not the old boiler's nameplate — oversized boilers short-cycle and waste fuel.

### Near-Boiler Piping

- Use `primary/secondary` piping with `closely-spaced tees` (<= 4 pipe diameters apart) to hydraulically separate boiler flow from system flow. This protects the heat exchanger's minimum flow while zones vary.
- Install a `circulator` (Taco/Grundfos) sized to the system head, an `air separator` at the point of lowest solubility, an `expansion tank` charged to fill pressure (~12 psi residential), and a `30 psi relief valve` piped to within 6" of the floor.

### Radiant Floor

- Lay `1/2" PEX-a with oxygen barrier` (Uponor) at `9" on center`, max loop `~300 ft` for 1/2" to keep head/flow reasonable. Tie to a `manifold` with balancing valves and circuit setters.
- Slab: tie to wire/insulation over `R-10` sub-slab foam. Joist-bay: aluminum transfer plates with reflective insulation below.
- Pressure-test loops at `~50-60 psi` and leave under pressure during the pour to spot a leak immediately.

### Controls

- Use `outdoor reset` so supply temp tracks outdoor temp — lower water temp = higher efficiency and steadier comfort.
- Zone with thermostatic valves or zone circulators/valves and a control panel.

### Commissioning

- Purge air loop-by-loop, set system pressure, verify circulator flow direction, and balance each radiant circuit to design `delta-T` (~10-20 deg F).

### Combustion & Venting

- Mod-con boilers are `sealed-combustion, direct-vent` through PVC/CPVC/polypropylene per the listing — maintain the maker's max vent length and combustion-air sizing. Slope condensate-producing flue back to the boiler and `neutralize the acidic condensate` (pH ~3) before it hits cast-iron or metal drains.
- Atmospheric/cast-iron boilers need proper chimney draft and combustion air per NFPA 54; verify with a combustion analyzer at startup.

### Troubleshooting

- **Short-cycling:** oversized boiler, no outdoor reset, or too small a system volume — add a buffer tank or enable reset/anti-cycle.
- **Air noise / no heat in a zone:** trapped air — purge that loop at its isolation valves.
- **Low pressure / relief weeping:** waterlogged expansion tank or failed fill valve — recharge or replace the tank; never plug a weeping relief valve.

**Tip:** Always use O2-barrier PEX on ferrous systems; non-barrier tubing corrodes iron pumps and boilers. Add a magnetic dirt separator to protect the circulators and heat exchanger long-term.

title: Combustion Analysis & CO Testing
content:
## Verifying Safe Combustion on Gas Appliances

A combustion analysis is the only way to confirm an appliance is burning safely and efficiently — eyeballing the flame is not enough.

### The Analyzer

- Use a calibrated electronic analyzer (`Bacharach`, `Testo 320/330`, `Fieldpiece`) that reads `O2, CO, stack temp, CO2, excess air, and efficiency`. Zero it in fresh air before sampling.
- Sample in the flue downstream of the draft hood/diverter (or in the breech for sealed combustion) per the manufacturer.

### Target Readings (Natural Gas)

- `CO (air-free): < 100 ppm` for atmospheric; well-tuned units run `< 50 ppm`. Rising CO = incomplete combustion (dirty/cracked HX, misadjusted burner, poor air).
- `O2: ~7-9%` / excess air ~50-100% on atmospheric burners.
- Set/verify `manifold gas pressure` (typ. 3.5" WC NG, 11" WC LP) and clock the meter to confirm input MBH.
- Verify `temperature rise` across the heat exchanger is within the nameplate range — high rise = low airflow, low rise = overfiring/oversized.

### CO Safety Checks

- Test ambient CO at the appliance and in living space with the system running and exhaust fans/dryer on (`worst-case depressurization test`). Backdrafting a water heater pulls flue gas into the home.
- A `cracked heat exchanger` shows as CO rising when the blower starts and flame distortion — condemn and red-tag the unit; do not return it to service.
- Confirm proper `venting, draft, and combustion-air openings` per NFPA 54 / IFGC 304.

### Documentation & CO Alarms

- Record all readings on the service ticket. Recommend `low-level CO monitors` (not just UL 2034 alarms that only trip at high, prolonged levels).

### Worst-Case Depressurization Test

- With all exhaust fans, clothes dryer, and HVAC blower running and the house closed up, the building goes most negative. Verify atmospheric appliances (water heater, atmospheric furnace) still `draft properly` and don't spill flue gas at the draft hood. A match or smoke pencil at the diverter confirms draw; spillage means inadequate combustion air or an over-aggressive exhaust setup.

### Tuning Sequence

- Confirm clean burners and heat exchanger, set `manifold gas pressure` to spec, verify input by clocking the meter, then read CO/O2 in the flue. Adjust only what the maker allows; many modern units are factory-set and only need verification.
- Re-check after any airflow change (filter, duct), since low airflow raises temperature rise and can elevate CO.

**Safety:** Any CO reading climbing into the hundreds of ppm air-free, evidence of spillage, or a suspected cracked HX = shut off gas, ventilate, and red-tag. Never adjust a burner without an analyzer in the flue, and always test ambient CO before and after service.

title: Duct Sealing & Manual D Design
content:
## Sizing & Sealing the Duct System

A perfectly sized AC fails if the ducts leak or are undersized. Manual D translates the Manual J load and equipment CFM into actual duct dimensions.

### Manual D Basics

- Start with equipment `CFM` (design `400 CFM/ton` cooling) and the blower's `available static pressure` (ESP) minus coil, filter, registers, and balancing losses.
- Calculate `Available Static Pressure` and divide by `Total Effective Length` (TEL = measured run + fitting equivalent lengths) to get the `friction rate` (in. wc per 100 ft). Use that on a ductulator/software to size each trunk and branch.
- Target velocities: supply trunks `~700-900 fpm`, branches `~600 fpm`, returns lower to limit noise. Oversized return area reduces static and noise.

### Why Static Pressure Matters

- Most residential equipment is rated at `0.5" wc` total ESP. Restrictive duct/filter combos commonly measure `0.8-1.0"+`, cutting airflow, freezing coils, and overheating furnaces. Always measure ESP with a manometer at commissioning.

### Duct Sealing (Code)

- `IECC/IMC` require sealed ducts. Seal all joints, seams, and connections with `mastic` (UL 181A/B) or mastic-and-mesh — **never cloth duct tape**, which fails. Foil tape is acceptable only where listed.
- Mechanically fasten and seal the air handler/coil cabinet and plenum takeoffs; seal boot-to-drywall penetrations.
