- Leakage limits: many codes require total leakage `<= 4 CFM25 per 100 sq ft` (rough-in) verified by a `duct blaster` test, with the result documented for the permit.

### Insulation

- Ducts in unconditioned space: `R-8` (attic) / `R-6` per climate zone (IECC Table). Seal before insulating.

### Verification

- Pressure-test (duct blaster), measure ESP and room-by-room CFM with a flow hood, and balance to the Manual D design.

### Return-Side Design

- Returns are chronically undersized in older homes. Provide adequate `return free area` (sized at the friction rate, typically lower velocity than supply) and add `transfer grilles or jumper ducts` to closed-off bedrooms so door-closed pressure imbalance doesn't choke airflow.
- A high room-to-room pressure (`> 3 Pa` with doors closed) drives infiltration and comfort complaints — a Manual D fix, not a thermostat fix.

### Sealing Workflow

- Seal in this order: air-handler/coil cabinet, plenum takeoffs, trunk seams, branch connections, then register boots to drywall. Brush mastic into every joint, embed mesh on gaps over 1/8", and let it cure before insulating.
- Re-test with the duct blaster after sealing to confirm the leakage target and document the CFM25 result.

**Code note:** Keep the Manual J/S/D and duct-leakage test result with the permit package — many AHJs require all four. Measured external static pressure at commissioning should be recorded against the equipment's rated ESP.

title: Smart Thermostat & C-Wire (Ecobee/Nest)
content:
## Installing Wi-Fi Thermostats with Proper Power

### The C-Wire Problem

- Smart thermostats (`Ecobee`, `Google Nest`) need continuous 24V power. The `C (common)` wire completes the 24V transformer circuit back to the board. Without it, the stat "power steals" through the heat/cool wires, causing chatter, dropouts, or false calls.
- Check the existing bundle: a common `R, W, Y, G` (4-wire) setup has **no C**. Solutions:
  - Run a new wire (best) — pull `18/8 thermostat cable` if accessible.
  - Repurpose an unused conductor (e.g., the often-spare blue wire) and land it on `C` at both the stat and the air handler/furnace board.
  - Use the included `Power Extender Kit` (Ecobee PEK) or a `Fast-Stat`/add-a-wire adapter at the equipment to derive a common over existing wires.

### Terminal Mapping

- `R/Rc/Rh` = 24V power (jumper Rc-Rh for single-transformer systems). `W/W2` = heat stages. `Y/Y2` = cool stages. `G` = fan. `C` = common. `O/B` = heat-pump reversing valve (`O` energizes on cooling for most; `B` energizes on heating — set per equipment).
- **Heat pump:** wire `O/B` correctly and configure aux/emergency heat (`W/AUX, E`) or the system will heat when calling cool.

### Setup

- Cut 24V power before wiring. Photograph the old wiring first.
- In the app, select system type (conventional vs heat pump), staging, and `O/B` orientation. Set `cycles-per-hour` and minimum compressor `off-delay` (5 min) to protect the compressor.
- Add remote `room sensors` (Ecobee SmartSensor) for occupancy-based comfort.

### Verify

- Test each mode: heat, cool, fan, and (heat pump) aux/emergency. Confirm correct staging and that the reversing valve energizes in the right mode.

### Troubleshooting Power & Comms

- **Stat reboots / Wi-Fi drops / fan ghost-runs:** classic power-stealing symptoms on a no-C install — add a true C wire or PEK.
- **No power at all:** blown low-voltage fuse on the control board (often from a shorted thermostat wire) — find the short, replace the `3A automotive fuse`.
- **Heat pump heats on cool call:** `O/B` set wrong in the app — flip the reversing-valve orientation to match the equipment.
- **Aux heat won't engage:** `W/AUX` and `E` not wired or staging misconfigured.

### Compressor Protection & Comfort

- Enable the `minimum compressor off-time (5 min)` and reasonable cycles-per-hour to prevent short-cycling. Use room sensors to average or follow occupancy, and set schedules/eco modes to capture energy savings.

**Tip:** Never leave a thermostat power-stealing on a system without a true C — it's the top cause of intermittent "no heat/no cool" smart-stat callbacks. Always photograph the original wiring and label conductors before removing the old stat.

title: TXV vs. Piston Metering Diagnosis
content:
## Understanding & Diagnosing Refrigerant Metering Devices

The metering device drops high-pressure liquid into the low-pressure evaporator. Two common types behave very differently on the gauges.

### Fixed Orifice (Piston)

- A fixed bore meters by pressure differential. Cheap and simple but doesn't compensate for load — superheat swings widely with conditions.
- Used on many entry-level `Goodman/builder` systems. Diagnose by charging to a `superheat target` from the maker's charging chart (based on indoor wet-bulb and outdoor dry-bulb).

### Thermostatic Expansion Valve (TXV/TEV)

- A `sensing bulb` on the suction line and equalizer line modulate the valve to maintain a **constant superheat** across varying load. Standard on `>= 14 SEER` and all R-454B/A2L systems.
- Charge a TXV system by `subcooling` (not superheat), since the TXV controls superheat itself. Target subcooling is on the nameplate (commonly `8-12 deg F`).

### Diagnosing TXV Faults

- **Starving (overfeeding too little):** high superheat, low suction pressure, low subcooling at the coil, poor cooling, possible coil frost. Causes: lost bulb charge, ice/wax restriction, plugged inlet screen, bulb not insulated/clamped, low charge.
- **Flooding (overfeeding):** low superheat, high suction, risk of liquid floodback to compressor. Causes: bulb loose/warm-side, valve stuck open, overcharge.
- **Bulb mounting matters:** clamp the bulb at `4 or 8 o'clock` on a horizontal suction line, insulated — top mounting reads false superheat and a bottom on large lines reads oil.

### Hunting

- Rapid superheat swings = TXV "hunting," often from an oversized valve, low load, or a flooded bulb. Verify correct tonnage valve and proper bulb contact.

### Field Check

- Warm the bulb (in hand) and the valve should drive open (suction rises); chill it and it should throttle closed. No response = dead element, replace the valve.

### Replacing a TXV

- Recover the charge (EPA 608), cut out the old valve, and braze in the matched-tonnage valve with a `dry nitrogen purge` to keep scale out of the new seat. Replace the liquid-line `filter drier` at the same time — debris from the old failure will plug the new valve otherwise.
- Clamp and insulate the new sensing bulb at 4 or 8 o'clock on a clean horizontal section of suction line; poor bulb contact is the #1 cause of a "new valve still hunts" callback.
- Evacuate to `< 500 microns`, weigh in charge, then fine-tune to nameplate subcooling.

### Quick Field Reference

- Low superheat + high suction = flooding/overfeed. High superheat + low suction = starving/restriction. Always cross-check both readings before condemning the valve versus the charge.

**Tip:** Always confirm metering type before charging — charging a TXV by superheat or a piston by subcooling guarantees a wrong charge and a comeback.

title: Refrigerant Recovery & EPA 608 Compliance
content:
## Legal, Safe Refrigerant Handling

Under the Clean Air Act, venting refrigerant is illegal and recovery before opening any system is mandatory. EPA Section 608 certification is required to purchase and handle refrigerant.

### Certification Types

- `Type I` (small appliances), `Type II` (high-pressure: split systems, RTUs), `Type III` (low-pressure chillers), `Universal` (all). Carry your card; documentation is required for refrigerant purchase.

### Recovery Procedure

- Use a dedicated `recovery machine` (`Appion G5Twin`, `Yellow Jacket RecoverX`) and a `DOT-rated recovery cylinder` (gray body, yellow top) that is **not filled past 80%** by weight — overfilling risks hydrostatic rupture.
- Connect through a `filter on the recovery inlet`, recover to the EPA-required vacuum (e.g., `0 psig or required inches Hg` for the appliance size/type), then close, weigh, and label the cylinder.
- Keep recovered, recycled, and virgin refrigerant in separate, labeled cylinders. Mixed refrigerants must be sent for reclaim/destruction, not reused.

### Leak Repair Thresholds

- 608 sets `leak rate triggers` requiring repair on appliances with `>= 50 lb` charge (comfort cooling 10%/yr). Document leak inspections and repairs.

### A2L / Newer Refrigerants

- `R-454B / R-32` are mildly flammable (A2L). Use A2L-rated recovery equipment, ensure ventilation, eliminate ignition sources, and follow ASHRAE 15 charge limits and leak-detection requirements.

### Safety Hazards

- **Frostbite:** liquid refrigerant flashes to ~-15 to -40 deg F. Wear gloves and `safety glasses`.
- **Asphyxiation:** refrigerant displaces oxygen in low/confined spaces — ventilate.
- **Never** recover into a disposable (DOT-39) cylinder or heat a cylinder with an open flame. Don't mix refrigerants in one cylinder.

### Documentation

- Log recovered amounts, cylinder IDs, and disposition. Send full cylinders to a certified reclaimer.

### Speeding Recovery & Cylinder Care

- Recover faster with `large-bore hoses, a core-removal tool` on the service ports, and a `push-pull` method on larger charges. Keep the recovery cylinder cool (an ice bath lowers its pressure and speeds vapor recovery); a hot cylinder stalls the machine.
- Tare and track cylinder weight — stop at `80% fill` by weight, accounting for refrigerant density. Periodically `evacuate the recovery machine` after use so trapped refrigerant/oil doesn't degrade the next job.

### Records & Reclaim

- Maintain a log of recovered quantities, cylinder serial numbers, and disposition. Send full cylinders to an `EPA-certified reclaimer`; cross-contaminated refrigerant cannot legally be reused and must be reclaimed or destroyed.
- Verify your `608 card type` covers the appliance before purchasing refrigerant.

**Safety:** Recover fully before brazing — residual refrigerant + torch heat produces toxic phosgene/hydrofluoric byproducts. With A2L refrigerants, eliminate ignition sources and ventilate the work area before opening or recovering.

title: Framing Window & Door Rough Openings
content:
## Rough Opening Fundamentals

A rough opening (RO) is the framed hole that receives the window or door unit plus its installation clearances. Get the RO wrong and you either crush the jambs or leave gaps no flashing can close.

### Sizing the RO

- **Windows:** Add **1/2"** to manufacturer net frame size in BOTH width and height. Andersen 400-series and most vinyl units spec this. A 36x60 net frame = **36-1/2" x 60-1/2" RO**.
- **Doors:** Pre-hung interior = door width + **2"** width, +**2-1/2"** height off subfloor. A 2'-8" (32") door = **34" x 82-1/2" RO**.
- **Exterior pre-hung:** Add **3/4"** beyond unit dimension for shim/sill flashing.

Always confirm the exact RO on the cut sheet. Manufacturers vary.

### Assembly Components

```
King stud  -> full-height, plate to plate
Jack stud  -> (trimmer) supports header, RO width
Header     -> spans opening, carries load
Cripples   -> short studs above header / below sill
Rough sill -> bottom of window RO
```

### Step-by-Step

- **Layout:** Mark RO width on the bottom plate. Add jack + king stud thickness (**1-1/2"** each) outboard of each side.
- **Set king studs** plumb, nail to plates with (3) 16d (`0.131" x 3-1/4"`) Paslode framing nails each end.
- **Cut jacks** to header-bearing height = RO height + **1-1/2"** (sill plate) measured off subfloor. For doors, jacks land on subfloor; for windows they land on the bottom plate.
- **Build header** (see header span tables) and set on jacks. Nail header to king studs through the face.
- **Install rough sill** at RO height; double it on openings over 4'. Toenail cripples at 16" OC below.
- **Add upper cripples** above the header at matching wall layout so sheathing/drywall has backing at 16" OC.

### Code & Tolerance

Per **IRC R602.7**, headers must bear on jack studs unless an approved framing anchor is used. Keep RO **plumb within 1/8" over the height** and **level within 1/8"** across the sill — installers will thank you. Out-of-square openings telegraph into reveal gaps and binding sashes.

### Pro Tips

- Run the rough sill flat (face up) so flashing sits on a solid surface; back-pitch the sill or add a sloped sill pan (DuPont FlexWrap or a metal pan).
- For wide mulled units, verify header sizing against the combined unit width, not a single opening.
- Snap your header height once across the whole wall so all openings align for trim.
- Leave a **3/8"–1/2"** shim gap on each side — never frame tight.

title: Stair Stringer Layout & Cutting
content:
## Stair Geometry First

Stairs are unforgiving — a 1/4" error compounds across 14 treads. Start with total rise (finished floor to finished floor) measured in three spots; use the worst case.

### The Core Math (IRC R311.7)

- **Max riser:** `7-3/4"`
- **Min tread depth:** `10"` (nosing to nosing)
- **Max riser variation** between tallest and shortest: `3/8"`
- **Min headroom:** `6'-8"`

Divide total rise by 7.5 to estimate riser count, round to a whole number, then divide total rise by that count for exact riser height.

```
Total rise 109" / 7.5 = 14.5 -> use 15 risers
109 / 15 = 7.267" per riser (exact)
Treads = risers - 1 = 14 treads @ 10" run = 140" total run
```

### Laying Out the Stringer

- Use a framing square with **stair gauges (hexagon nuts)** clamped at riser (7-1/4") on the tongue and run (10") on the blade.
- Step the square down a 2x12 (`2x12 SYP #1` or LVL stringer), marking each riser/tread.
- Mark **15** rises and **14** runs.

### Dropping the Stringer

The first riser must account for finished tread thickness so the bottom and top risers end up equal. **Drop the stringer** by one tread thickness (e.g., 1" for a 1" tread) at the bottom. Cut the bottom horizontal line shorter by that amount.

### Cutting

- Cut with a circular saw to the inside of the line; **finish corners with a handsaw or jigsaw** — do NOT overcut, it weakens the stringer.
- Keep at least **3-1/2" of solid throat** below the deepest notch (IRC requires effective depth ≥ 3-1/2").
- For a 36"-wide stair, use **(3) stringers** (two outside + one center) for 2x or LVL treads; **(4)** if treads are thin.

### Attachment

- Top: hang with Simpson **LSC** adjustable stringer connectors or a ledger + joist hangers.
- Bottom: anchor to a kicker plate bolted to the slab with Simpson **Titen HD** screws.
- Glue and screw treads with GRK or construction screws + PL Premium to kill squeaks.

### Verify Before You Build

Dry-fit one stringer, set a level across the tread cuts — every tread must read level and every riser plumb. Confirm the top and bottom risers match within **3/8"** after finished surfaces. Re-check headroom along the stair run; a low beam or duct can fail inspection.

title: Installing Engineered LVL, Parallam & Glulam Beams
content:
## Engineered Beams vs. Sawn Lumber

Engineered wood products (EWP) deliver longer clear spans and dimensional stability that #2 sawn lumber can't match. Know your product:

- **Microllam LVL (Weyerhaeuser Trus Joist):** laminated veneer lumber, `1-3/4"` plies, very straight, great for headers and multi-ply beams.
- **Parallam PSL:** parallel strand lumber, available in larger solid sections (up to `7"` wide), highest capacity, takes point loads well.
- **Glulam:** glued-laminated, often cambered — **install camber UP (crown up)**, marked on the beam.

### Multi-Ply Fastening (Critical)

Follow the manufacturer's fastening table — this is where field crews fail. For a 2-ply 1-3/4" LVL (3-1/2" total) loaded from the top:

```
(2) rows 16d nails @ 12" OC, OR
(3) rows 10d @ 12" OC, OR
Simpson SDW22500 / SDS25 screws per Trus Joist guide
```

- **3-ply and 4-ply** members usually require **bolts (1/2" through-bolts)** or SDS screws from BOTH faces, because nails can't develop full transfer.
- **Side-loaded beams** (joists hanging off the face) need the fasteners sized so load passes through ALL plies — get the Weyerhaeuser fastening detail, never guess.

### Bearing

- Minimum bearing length is typically **3-1/2"** at ends, **3-1/2"** intermediate — confirm on the job-specific layout from the EWP supplier.
- Provide **full bearing**: studs/posts stacked plumb beneath, blocking solid to the foundation or beam below. A floating point load is the #1 cause of failure.
- Use a **bearing stiffener / squash blocks** where loads pass through floor systems.

### Handling & Storage

- Keep LVL/PSL **dry and out of standing water**; store on stickers, banded, off the ground. Wet EWP swells and delaminates.
- **Never notch or drill** an engineered beam outside the manufacturer's hole chart — these members have almost no allowance. A 1" hole in the wrong spot can fail the beam.

### Set & Connect

- Crane or carry into place, support on posts before releasing.
- Tie to columns with Simpson **CCQ/ECCQ** column caps or **HU/HUC** hangers for joists landing on it.
- Provide lateral bracing at bearing points (IRC R502.7) to prevent rotation.

Always file the manufacturer's stamped layout with the permit set — inspectors want the engineered design, not a span-table guess.

title: Deck Framing & Ledger Attachment per IRC R507
content:
## The Ledger Is Everything

Most catastrophic deck collapses trace to ledger failure. **IRC R507** (the prescriptive deck code) exists because of these failures. Nails alone are NOT permitted to attach a ledger to the band joist.

### Ledger Fastening (IRC R507.9.1.3)

Use **1/2" lag screws or through-bolts**, OR an approved screw like the FastenMaster **LedgerLOK**. Spacing per Table R507.9.1.3 depends on joist span:

```
Joist span <= 6'   -> fasteners @ 30" OC
Joist span 6'-8'   -> @ 23" OC
Joist span 8'-10'  -> @ 18" OC
Joist span 10'-12' -> @ 16" OC
Joist span 12'-14' -> @ 13" OC
```

- Stagger top and bottom rows; keep fasteners **2" from top/bottom edges and 5" min from ends**.
- **Lag into the rim through stacked 1/2" sheathing max.** Hollow rims (engineered I-joist band without blocking) need solid blocking behind the ledger.
- **NEVER attach a ledger to brick veneer or to a cantilevered floor.**

### Lateral Load Connection (IRC R507.9.2)

Required to resist pull-off. Use Simpson **DTT2Z** tension ties — minimum **(2)** for the deck, or **(4)** per the alternate method — connecting deck joists to the interior floor framing with the prescribed hold-down devices.

### Flashing

Flash the ledger: Z-flashing over the ledger, behind the WRB, with the bottom leg lapping the ledger face. Use **PVC or stainless** flashing; aluminum corrodes against ACQ pressure-treated lumber.

### Joists, Beams, Posts

- Joist hangers must be **galvanized/ZMAX or stainless** (Simpson **LUS** series) rated for treated lumber. Fill EVERY hanger hole with the proper Simpson **SD** or N10 nails — joist hangers are NOT for deck/drywall screws.
- Post-to-beam: Simpson **BCS** or **AC** caps. Post-to-footing: **ABU/PBS** standoff bases keeping wood **1"** off concrete.
- Footings sized per soil and tributary area; below frost depth (IRC R403.1.4).

### Guards & Connections

Guardrails ≥ **36"** high (IRC R312), able to resist a **200 lb** concentrated load. Tension-tie the rail posts with Simpson **DTT2Z** — do not just lag a 4x4 to the rim.

Document all fasteners on the deck permit; inspectors specifically check ledger and lateral-load hardware.

### Joist Spans & Spacing

Size joists from IRC Table R507.6 for the species and spacing: a `2x8 SYP @ 16" OC` spans roughly **11'-10"**; a `2x10 @ 16"` about **14'-0"**. Cantilevers are limited to **1/4 of the back-span**. Beam spans come from Table R507.5 — a built-up `(3) 2x10` beam carrying a 10' joist span runs about **7'-8"** between posts. Drop beams over post tops with caps, or use Simpson **LUS** face-mount hangers for flush beams. Double the outer joist (rim) and provide blocking at beam bearing to resist rotation.

title: Shear Walls & Hold-Downs with Simpson Strong-Wall & HDU
content:
## Resisting Lateral Loads

Shear walls transfer wind and seismic forces from the roof/floor diaphragm down to the foundation. They rely on three elements working together: sheathing nailing, chord/post overturning restraint (hold-downs), and a continuous load path.

### Sheathing & Nailing

Per the engineered design or IRC R602.10:

- **7/16" OSB or 15/32" plywood**, nailed `8d (0.131" x 2-1/2")` at **6" edges / 12" field** for standard walls.
- High-load shear walls go to **4" or 3" OC edge nailing** — watch for **double studs/3x members** at panel edges so you don't split the framing.
- Block all panel edges; stagger panel joints.

### Hold-Downs (Overturning)

When a shear wall wants to rotate, the end posts uplift. Hold-downs anchor the post to the foundation or to the post below.

- **Simpson HDU** series (HDU2, HDU5, HDU8, HDU11) — pre-deflected, screw-on hold-downs using **SDS25** screws to the post and an anchor bolt/SSTB or PAB to concrete.
- HDU5-SDS2.5 example: (14) SDS screws, **5/8" anchor bolt**, ~`4,565 lb` allowable.
- Install hold-downs **in pairs** at each end of the shear wall, on the SAME end posts the engineer specified.

### Strong-Wall Prefab Panels

Where a narrow wall can't develop enough shear (e.g., a garage front "portal"), use Simpson **Strong-Wall** (Wood Strong-Wall WSW or Steel Strong-Wall SSW). They install in widths as narrow as **12"–24"** and come with engineered anchorage templates. Set the anchor bolts to the template BEFORE the slab pour.

### Anchor Bolts (Sill)

- General sill: **1/2" anchor bolts @ 6' OC**, max 12" from plate ends, min 7" embed (IRC R403.1.6).
- Shear walls usually demand tighter spacing + **plate washers (3"x3"x0.229")** — never standard cut washers.

### Continuous Load Path

The whole point: roof-to-wall-to-floor-to-foundation must be connected. Stack hold-downs floor to floor (HDU + threaded rod), use Simpson straps (**CS/CMST**) across rim joists, and keep posts stacked. A broken path = an unbraced building.

Never substitute hold-down models or anchor sizes — the engineer's calc is specific. File the Strong-Wall anchorage detail with the inspector.

### Bracing Methods (IRC R602.10.4)

For conventional (non-engineered) homes, IRC offers prescriptive braced wall methods: **WSP** (wood structural panel), **CS-WSP** (continuous sheathing), **PFH** (portal frame with hold-downs) and **PFG** (portal frame at garage). The garage portal **PFG** uses a header strapped to the sheathed narrow piers with Simpson **CS16** coil strap and hold-downs at the base. Braced wall panels must be **at least 48" wide** (less for continuously-sheathed and portal methods) and located per the braced wall line spacing limits. When the layout can't satisfy prescriptive bracing, that's when the engineered Strong-Wall earns its cost.

### Installation Order

Set anchor bolts/templates before the slab, frame and sheathe the wall, nail the schedule, then install hold-downs and torque the anchor nuts to the catalog value. Re-check after the structure dries.

title: Fire Blocking & Draft Stopping per IRC R302.11
content:
## Stopping the Chimney Effect

Fire blocking cuts off concealed vertical and horizontal air channels so a fire can't race through wall and floor cavities. **IRC R302.11** mandates it; inspectors check it hard, and missing fire blocking is a common rough-frame failure.

### Where Fire Blocking Is Required (R302.11)

- **In concealed stud walls/partitions** — vertically at the ceiling and floor levels, and **horizontally at 10' intervals** along the wall.
- At interconnections between **concealed vertical and horizontal spaces** (soffits, drop ceilings, cove ceilings).
- In the **concealed space of stair stringers** at top and bottom.
- At **openings around vents, pipes, ducts, cables, wires** at ceiling/floor level — annular gaps must be sealed.
- At the top and bottom of **chimney chases**.

### Approved Materials (R302.11.1)

- **2" nominal lumber** (a 2x flat block).
- **Two thicknesses of 1" nominal** lumber with broken joints.
- **23/32" wood structural panel** with joints backed by the same.
- **1/2" gypsum board**.
- **1/4" cement-based millboard**.
- **Mineral wool / fiberglass** batt securely retained in the space.
- **Approved fire-block foam** (e.g., a listed orange firestop foam) and listed sealants around penetrations — NOT standard window-and-door foam.

### Draft Stopping (R302.12) — Different Animal

Draft stopping divides **large concealed floor/ceiling and attic spaces** so any area doesn't exceed **1,000 sq ft** (floor assemblies with usable space above and below). Materials: **1/2" gypsum, 3/8" wood structural panel**, or other approved. This applies mainly when there's a suspended ceiling or open-web truss floor with a finished ceiling below.

### Field Practice

- Block **horizontal runs in tall walls** (over 10' studs, e.g., great rooms, stairwells) — easy to forget.
- At a dropped soffit over cabinets, block where the soffit meets the wall cavity.
- Around a chimney/flue, maintain required clearance AND fire-block the chase with noncombustible material.
- Seal **plumbing/electrical penetrations** through top/bottom plates with fire-block foam or caulk.

Walk the frame before drywall with the code in hand: every cavity that connects two spaces needs a stop. It costs minutes now and saves a re-inspection.

### Common Field Locations Checklist

- **Soffits/dropped ceilings** over kitchen cabinets where the soffit cavity meets the wall stud bays.
- **Tub/shower walls** — the wet wall behind a tub often has an open chase to the floor below; block it.
- **Furred-out walls** and chases for plumbing stacks at every floor line.
- **Stair stringers** top and bottom, and the open triangular space under the run.
- **Around chimneys/flues** — noncombustible fire blocking only, maintaining clearance to combustibles.
- **Top/bottom of any 2-story open cavity** (balloon-framed walls, tall stairwell walls).

### Fire-Rated Wall Note

Fire blocking is NOT the same as a **fire-resistance-rated assembly** (e.g., 1-hour wall between a garage and dwelling, IRC R302.6, which requires `1/2"` gypsum on the garage side, `5/8" Type X` under habitable space). Don't confuse the two — a wall can need both concealed-space fire blocking and a rated membrane.

title: Steel Light-Gauge Stud Framing for Commercial Walls
content:
## Cold-Formed Steel Basics

Light-gauge (cold-formed steel, CFS) framing is standard in commercial interior partitions and load-bearing mid-rise. It won't rot, burn, or warp, but it demands different tools and tolerances than wood.

### Material Spec

Studs are identified by **web depth, flange, and mil thickness**:

```
362S162-33  -> 3-5/8" web, 1-5/8" flange, 33 mil (20 ga)
Common gauges:
  18 mil (25 ga) -> non-structural partitions
  30 mil (20 ga drywall)
  33/43/54/68/97 mil -> structural (20-12 ga)
```

Track (the top/bottom channel) is sized to receive the stud (e.g., 362T125-33).

### Layout & Track

- Snap lines for both faces of the wall. Lay bottom track to the line.
- **Anchor track to concrete** with Hilti/Simpson powder-actuated pins or Tapcons @ **24" OC** (16" in seismic/structural).
- Anchor top track to the deck/structure. For non-structural partitions to a deck that deflects, use a **slip/deflection track (top track with deep legs)** so vertical movement doesn't load the studs.

### Setting Studs

- Space studs **16" or 24" OC**. Seat into track, plumb, and fasten.
- **Structural studs:** screw to track with **#10 self-drilling (Tek)** screws each flange, or weld per spec.
- **Non-structural:** crimp or single screw; many shops friction-fit and screw only at openings.
- Keep the **knockouts aligned** for running conduit/plumbing; install bridging/bracing through them (cold-rolled channel + clip angles) at **48" OC vertically**.

### Openings

- Build headers from **box or back-to-back studs**; jamb studs are doubled or boxed. Use king/jamb stud assemblies and clip angles (Simpson **SCB/MSCA**).
- Add **flat-strap X-bracing** or sheathing for shear in load-bearing walls.

### Fastening to Steel

- Use **self-drilling screws** matched to steel thickness; for thick gauges pre-drill or use stronger drill-point screws.
- For attaching wood (e.g., blocking) to steel, **#8–#10 fine-thread** screws.

### Tools & Safety

- Cut with **aviation snips, a chop saw with a metal blade, or a plasma cutter** — burrs are razor sharp; wear cut gloves and eye protection.
- Avoid abrasive cut-off wheels indoors where the spark/dust isn't controlled.
- Galvanic note: keep dissimilar metals isolated to avoid corrosion.

Verify plumb within **1/8" in 10'** and keep studs from the track web by **3/8"** at slip tracks so the structure can move freely.

title: Subfloor Installation: Glue + Screw with Advantech & Zip System
content:
## A Squeak-Free, Stiff Floor

The subfloor is the platform for everything above it. A glued-and-screwed engineered panel deck eliminates squeaks and bounce when done right.

### Panel Selection

- **Huber Advantech** — high-density OSB, exceptional moisture resistance and stiffness, the contractor favorite. **23/32" (3/4")** for 16" OC joists, **7/8" or 1-1/8"** for 19.2"–24" OC.
- **Zip System** subfloor/roof panels have an integrated water-resistive layer.
- Match panel span rating to joist spacing — check the APA stamp (e.g., **48/24** or **24 OC**).

### Layout

- Run panels **perpendicular to the joists**, long edge across.
- **Stagger end joints** so they don't line up (offset by at least one joist bay).
- Tongue-and-groove edges go together; leave the **manufacturer's expansion gap**: typically **1/8" at panel ends and edges** (Advantech edges are designed to butt T&G tight but still gap ends). Follow Huber's instructions.

### Glue (Non-Negotiable for No Squeaks)

- Apply a **continuous 1/4" bead** of subfloor adhesive (**PL Premium**, Loctite PL, or Advantech's own subfloor adhesive) on EVERY joist top before laying the panel.
- For T&G joints, run a bead in the groove.
- **Work in sections you can fasten before the glue skins** (open time ~20-30 min, less in heat).

### Fastening

- **Screws beat nails** for squeak prevention. Use **#8 or #10 subfloor screws** (GRK, SPAX, or collated deck/subfloor screws).
- Spacing: **6" OC on panel edges, 12" OC in the field**. Some specs call 8"/8".
- If nailing, use **ring-shank 8d** — but screws are the standard for warranty-grade work.
- Don't overdrive past the panel surface.

### Moisture Management

- Advantech tolerates weather exposure during construction, but **don't let water pond** — sweep/squeegee standing water from low spots.
- Acclimate and dry the deck before installing finished hardwood; check moisture content with a meter.

### Common Mistakes

- Gluing the whole floor then running out of time before screwing — glue skins and does nothing. Glue and fasten bay by bay.
- Forgetting glue at panel butt joints over a joist.
- Driving fasteners into the joist edge (miss) — snap a chalk line over each joist as a fastening guide.

The result should be dead-flat, silent, and ready for tile backer or hardwood without re-leveling.
code_references: APA E30 Engineered Wood Construction Guide

title: Notching & Boring Limits per IRC R602.6
content:
## Don't Gut Your Studs

Plumbers and electricians will hack a wall to pieces if you let them. **IRC R602.6** governs how much you can notch and bore studs and plates without compromising structure.

### Stud Notching (R602.6)

For a nominal **2x4 (3-1/2" deep) stud**:

- **Bearing wall:** notch depth **<= 25%** of stud depth = **0.875" (7/8")** max.
- **Non-bearing wall:** notch **<= 40%** = **1.4"** max.

For a **2x6 (5-1/2")** bearing wall: 25% = **1.375"** max notch.

### Stud Boring (R602.6)

- **Bearing wall:** bored hole **<= 40%** of stud depth = **1.4"** (2x4) — and the edge of the hole must be **>= 5/8" from the stud edge**, and **no hole in the same section as a notch**.
- **Non-bearing OR doubled studs:** up to **60%** = **2.1"** (2x4), provided no more than **two successive doubled studs** are bored.
- Never bore and notch the **same cross-section**.

### Top Plate Notching/Boring (R602.6.1)

If you cut/notch/bore a **top plate more than 50%** of its width, you must install a **galvanized metal tie** — Simpson **RPTS** or a `0.054" x 1-1/2"` strap with **(8) 16d nails** each side — across the cut to restore the plate's continuity (especially in exterior/bearing walls). This is constantly violated when HVAC runs a duct through the top plate.

### Joists (R502.8) — Related

For sawn-lumber joists:
- Notches in the **top or bottom** must not exceed **1/6 the depth**, not in the middle third of span.
- Holes bored **>= 2" from edges**, diameter **<= 1/3 the depth**.
- **Engineered I-joists/TJI: follow Weyerhaeuser's hole chart ONLY** — never notch the flange.

### Field Enforcement

- Walk the rough-in after the trades. Flag over-notched studs.
- Repair an over-cut stud with a **stud shoe (Simpson SP/NS)** or a sistered stud, or a steel mending plate.
- Reinforce hacked top plates with the metal tie BEFORE sheathing/drywall covers it.

When in doubt, smaller holes centered in the stud, drilled (not sawn) are always safer. Document repairs for the framing inspection.

### Quick Reference Limits

```
2x4 bearing stud:   notch 7/8"   | bore 1-3/8"
2x4 non-bearing:    notch 1-3/8" | bore 2-1/8"
2x6 bearing stud:   notch 1-3/8" | bore 2-3/16"
Top plate cut >50%: install metal tie (Simpson RPTS / strap)
Joist (sawn):       hole <= D/3, >= 2" from edge, not mid-span third
```

### Plumbing Wall Strategy

For a wall carrying a `3"`/`4"` DWV stack, frame a **2x6 "wet wall"** even on a 2x4 layout so the stack fits without over-boring. A 4" cast-iron or PVC stack will gut a 2x4 plate every time. Coordinate with the plumber at layout, not after the holes are cut. Where a large duct must pass through a bearing top plate, design a **header/drop** rather than hacking the plate.

title: Balloon vs. Platform Framing: When & How
content:
## Two Wall-Framing Systems

Understanding both methods matters for renovations (old homes are balloon-framed) and for tall-wall new construction.

### Platform Framing (Standard Today)

Each floor is built as a **platform**: studs run only floor-to-floor, the subfloor and walls of each level sit on the level below.

- **Pros:** safer (work off a deck), faster, easier material handling, built-in fire blocking at each platform.
- Studs are **pre-cut** (92-5/8" for 8' walls, 104-5/8" for 9'). Top and bottom plates contain the cavity.
- The floor platform acts as a natural fire stop between stories.

### Balloon Framing (Legacy / Special Cases)

Studs run **continuously from sill plate to the top plate two stories up**; the second-floor joists hang off a **ribbon/let-in ledger board** notched into the studs.

- **Historically** used for masonry-veneer homes (reduced shrinkage so brick didn't crack).
- **Major drawback:** the continuous stud cavity is a **chimney** — fire races up unimpeded. This is why balloon-framed homes MUST have **fire blocking at every floor line** (IRC R302.11 retrofit when renovating).

### Modern Use of Continuous (Balloon-Style) Studs

We still use long continuous studs for:

- **Tall great-room / gable walls** where a platform break would create a hinge.
- **Stairwell walls** and **rake walls** that exceed one story.
- These require **engineered tall-stud design** (often LSL studs like **TimberStrand** or LVL studs, 2x6/2x8 at tighter spacing) and may need **mid-height blocking/strongbacks** for wind.

### Renovating Balloon-Framed Homes

- **Add fire blocking** at each floor level when walls are opened — code requires it.
- Watch for **let-in ribbons** carrying second-floor joists; don't cut studs without temporary shoring.
- Continuous studs make **load paths different** — a header you add must transfer load to a continuous post, not just a platform.

### Selecting

- Default to **platform** for nearly all residential work.
- Use **engineered tall-wall (continuous stud)** framing where a wall exceeds a single platform height — and design it: deflection under wind, mid-span bracing, and sheathing schedule all change.

Match the new framing method to the existing one at tie-ins, and never leave an unblocked vertical chase open through a floor.

title: Soffit, Fascia & Exterior Trim Framing
content:
## Building the Eave

The soffit/fascia assembly closes the underside of the roof overhang, carries the gutter, and controls attic ventilation. Sloppy framing here shows in every wavy fascia line.

### Rafter Tails & Sub-Fascia

- **Cut rafter tails to a consistent line.** Snap a chalk line across all tails (plumb cut and seat/tail cut) and trim with a circular saw so the fascia lands straight.
- Install a **sub-fascia** (2x6 or 2x8) nailed to the tail ends — this is the structural backer for the finish fascia and gutter. It must be **dead straight**; shim or plane high tails.

### Soffit Framing — Two Types

- **Open/sloped soffit:** finish runs up the underside of the rafters (no level soffit). Add lookouts only as needed.
- **Boxed (level) soffit:** install **lookouts** from the wall to the sub-fascia. Nail a **ledger to the wall** (laser-leveled off the fascia bottom), then run 2x4 lookouts at **16"–24" OC** between ledger and sub-fascia. This creates the flat plane for the soffit panel.

### Gable / Rake Overhang

- Frame the rake with a **ladder (outrigger) assembly**: 2x4 lookouts cantilevered over the gable-end top plate, tying the last common rafter to the **barge/fly rafter**. Keep overhang ≤ **16"–24"** unless engineered.

### Fascia & Trim

- Fascia board (1x or 5/4 PVC like **AZEK/Versatex**, or LP SmartSide) covers the sub-fascia. Hold the top to the roof sheathing for a drip edge.
- **Scarf-cut joints at 45°** and glue PVC with cellular-PVC cement so they don't telegraph.
- Fasten PVC with **stainless trim screws or ring-shank SS nails**, accounting for thermal movement (PVC moves a lot — gap long runs and use cortex-style fastening).

### Ventilation (Code)

- Provide **continuous or vented soffit** plus ridge/roof venting. IRC R806 requires net free vent area = **1/150** of attic area (or **1/300** with balanced high/low vents + vapor retarder).
- Maintain **baffles (insulation stops)** at the eave so insulation doesn't block airflow from the soffit into the attic.

### Quality Checks

- Sight down the fascia line — it should be laser straight.
- Soffit panels level and tight to the wall; J-channel or finish trim caulked.
- Confirm vent openings aren't blocked by framing or insulation.

Getting the sub-fascia straight is 80% of the job — everything finishes off that line.

title: Metal Connector Fastening Safety with Simpson SDS & SD Screws
content:
## The Right Fastener Saves Lives

Metal connectors are only as strong as their fasteners. Using the wrong screw or skipping holes turns a rated connection into a liability — and the install process has its own injury risks.

### Use the SPECIFIED Fastener — Always

- **Simpson SDS** (1/4" structural wood screws) — for hold-downs, beam hangers, ledger connections where the catalog calls SDS.
- **Simpson SD** (#9, #10 connector screws) — for face-mount hangers and straps; SD9112/SD10112 replace traditional N10/N16 nails in many connectors.
- **Simpson SDW** — for multi-ply beam assembly.
- **NEVER substitute drywall screws, deck screws, or generic structural screws.** Drywall screws are brittle and shear under load. The connector's published allowable load assumes the EXACT Simpson fastener and that EVERY hole is filled.

### Fill Every Hole

- A joist hanger rated for `1,000 lb` only achieves it with all nail/screw holes filled with the correct fastener. Half-filled = half-rated (or less).
- **Round holes** are mandatory (structural); **triangle/oblong holes** are for temporary positioning only unless the table says otherwise.

### Tool & PPE Safety

- Drive SDS/SDW with a **high-torque impact driver** (DeWalt DCF887/Milwaukee Fuel). Long structural screws generate strong reaction torque — **keep a firm two-hand grip / side handle** to avoid wrist injury and kickback.
- Wear **ANSI Z87 eye protection** — screw heads can cam-out and metal connectors throw chips.
- Wear **cut-resistant gloves**; connector edges are sharp and galvanized burrs cut deep.
- **Hearing protection** during repetitive impact driving.

### Galvanic & Treated-Lumber Compatibility

- On **ACQ/CA pressure-treated** wood, use **ZMAX/HDG or stainless** connectors AND matching coated/stainless fasteners. Mixing bright-steel screws with treated lumber causes rapid corrosion and connection failure.

### Installation Discipline

- **Don't pre-drill** unless the instructions allow it — SDS screws are self-drilling and pre-drilling can reduce withdrawal.
- Drive **flush, not overdriven** — stripping the head ruins the connection.
- Keep required **edge and end distances**; a screw too close to the end splits the wood and loses capacity.

### Final Check

Before covering: confirm correct connector model, correct fastener type, all holes filled, no stripped/spinning screws. Inspectors will pull the connector schedule and count fasteners. A documented, fully-fastened connection is the difference between a passing inspection and a structural recall.

title: Driveway & Approach Concrete Pour
content:
## Building a Driveway That Lasts

Driveways carry vehicle loads and live in the weather — thickness, subgrade, and jointing decide whether they last 30 years or crack in three.

### Subgrade & Base

- **Strip topsoil and organics.** Compact subgrade to **95% Standard Proctor**.
- Add **4" of compacted aggregate base** (3/4" minus / Class 5) over the subgrade, compacted in lifts with a plate compactor or roller. Good base prevents differential settlement.
- Slope the base for drainage — minimum **1-2% (1/8"-1/4" per foot)** away from structures.

### Thickness & Reinforcement

- **Passenger driveway:** `4"` minimum slab.
- **Heavy vehicles / RV / approach apron:** `5"-6"` thick.
- Reinforce with **#3 or #4 rebar @ 18" OC each way**, OR **6x6 W2.9xW2.9 welded wire** placed at mid-depth on chairs (not pulled up by hand mid-pour).
- Thicken the edges and the approach where vehicles transition off the street.

### Mix

- **4,000 psi, 4"-5" slump**, air-entrained **5-7%** in freeze-thaw climates (ASTM C260). Specify air on the ticket.
- Max **0.50 w/c ratio** for durability.

### Forming & Placing

- Form with straight 2x stock staked at 4' OC; set the grade with a string line for the cross-slope.
- Pour, screed with a straightedge, bull float, then wait for bleed water to leave before finishing.
- **Broom finish** for traction (mandatory on a sloped drive) — drag the broom perpendicular to traffic.

### Jointing (Critical for Crack Control)

- **Control joints** every **8'-12'** (rule of thumb: spacing in feet <= 2.5x slab thickness in inches; 4" slab -> ~10' max). Cut **1/4 of slab depth** deep with a groover or early-entry saw (within 6-12 hr).
- **Isolation joints** with 1/2" fiber-expansion material where the drive meets the garage slab, sidewalks, and foundation.
- Keep panels as close to **square** as possible; avoid long skinny rectangles (max length:width ~1.5:1).

### Curing & ROW Permit

- Cure 7 days — wet cure or apply a curing compound (W.R. Meadows **1100-Clear**).
- Keep vehicles off **7 days** (passenger), **10-14 days** for heavy loads.
- The **approach/apron in the public right-of-way** usually requires a municipal permit and may dictate thickness, jointing, and ADA detectable warnings at the sidewalk crossing — verify before you pour.

Proper base + correct joint spacing prevents 90% of driveway cracking complaints.

title: Stamped & Decorative Concrete Techniques
content:
## Concrete That Looks Like Stone

Stamped concrete mimics brick, slate, flagstone, or wood plank. Timing is everything — the window between too wet and too hard is short.

### Mix & Placement

- Standard **4,000 psi** mix, `4"-5"` slump. Air-entrain in freeze-thaw zones.
- Place, screed, bull float, and edge as normal. Get the slab flat — stamping won't hide a bad screed.

### Color Methods

- **Integral color:** pigment (Davis Colors, Solomon) added to the truck — colors the full depth, most durable for chips.
- **Color hardener (broadcast):** shake-on dry-shake hardener (Brickform, Increte) floated into the surface — richer color and a harder wear surface, but only skin-deep.
- **Release agent:** powder or liquid (antiquing release) prevents stamps from sticking AND adds secondary accent color in the grout lines.

### Stamping Sequence

- Apply color hardener and float in; then broadcast **release agent** over the surface.
- Wait for the right **thumbprint hardness** — you should be able to press and leave a ~`1/4"` impression that holds its edge. Too wet = mushy/no detail; too hard = no imprint and you'll wreck your stamps.
- Lay stamp mats in sequence, **tamp** evenly with a tamper, advance in rows keeping the pattern aligned. Use **flex/floppy mats** at edges and walls.
- "Detail" hard-to-reach spots with a texture skin or chisel by hand.

### Cutting Joints

- Still install **control joints** (saw-cut or hand-tooled into the pattern) at proper spacing — stamping doesn't eliminate the need to control cracking. Hide cuts in grout lines where possible.

### Wash, Seal & Cure

- After 24+ hours, **power-wash off the excess release** (and reveal the antique tone). Acid or pressure wash per the release type.
- Let dry, then apply a **solvent or water-based acrylic sealer** (2 coats) — gives color depth and protection. Add a **micronized polymer grit (anti-slip)** to the sealer for walking surfaces.
- Re-seal every **2-3 years**.

### Common Failures

- **Inconsistent stamping** from uneven set — pour smaller sections you can stamp in the window, or use a retarder in heat.
- **Fading/efflorescence** — proper sealer and a moisture barrier under the slab help.
- **Stamp slipping** — adequate release agent and correct timing.

Decorative work rewards a crew that has rehearsed the timing. Do a mock-up panel first to dial color and set time.

title: ICF Foundation Walls with Nudura & Fox Blocks
content:
## Insulated Concrete Forms

ICF stay-in-place forms give you an insulated, formed, and braced wall in one system — R-22+ continuous insulation around a reinforced concrete core. Done right they're fast; done wrong they blow out.

### System Basics

- **Nudura** and **Fox Blocks** are EPS form units with integral plastic webs (also the rebar chair and fastening strip).
- Core widths typically **4", 6", or 8"**; 6" core (`6" concrete`) is the residential standard for foundations.
- Webs are at **6"-8" OC** and double as **screw strips** for finishes — mark them.

### Footing & First Course

- Pour a level footing with a **keyway or rebar dowels** projecting up to tie the wall.
- Snap lines and set the **first course** dead level — everything stacks off it. Glue/foam the bottom block to the footing and brace it; a bad first course telegraphs the whole wall.

### Stacking & Rebar

- Stack courses **running bond**, interlocking the teeth. Stagger seams.
- Place **horizontal rebar** in the web chairs each course and **vertical rebar** per the engineer (commonly **#4 @ 12"-16" OC vertical, #4 horizontal each course**). Maintain cover per ACI.
- Cut openings for windows/doors and **buck them** (treated lumber or vinyl buck) with bracing to resist the pour pressure.

### Bracing & Alignment

- Install **engineered ICF bracing/scaffold** (Nudura/Fox bracing or Plumwall) every **~6'** — these also serve as work platforms and walkalignment turnbuckles. **This is the #1 safety/quality item.**
- Brace and plumb the wall; check alignment continuously during the pour.

### Pouring (Where Blowouts Happen)

- Use a **lower-slump-than-you-think... actually a flowable mix**: `6" slump` or self-consolidating, **3/8" pea-gravel aggregate**, 3,000-4,000 psi.
- **Pour in lifts of ~4' max**, going around the building, NOT filling one wall top to bottom. Lift height controls hydrostatic pressure on the forms.
- **Consolidate** with an internal pencil vibrator or by rodding — don't over-vibrate (causes blowouts).
- Keep a **blowout kit** (plywood, screws, bracing) on hand. Watch corners and bucks closely.

### After the Pour

- Set **anchor bolts / sill plate** while concrete is plastic (or use ICF top-of-wall anchors).
- Recheck plumb; the wall can drift before set.
- Damp-proof/waterproof the exterior below grade and install drainage board + footing drain per IRC R405.

Follow the manufacturer's pour-rate and bracing schedule exactly — that document is your blowout insurance.

title: Anchor Bolts, Embeds & Post-Installed Anchors (Simpson Titen HD & SET-XP)
content:
## Connecting Wood & Steel to Concrete

Anchorage is a code-governed, calculated connection. **ACI 318 Chapter 17** governs anchor design; misuse causes pull-out failures.

### Cast-in Anchor Bolts (Sill Plate)

Per **IRC R403.1.6**:

- **1/2" min anchor bolts** embedded **>= 7"** into concrete/grouted masonry.
- Spacing **<= 6' OC**, with a bolt **within 12" but not less than 7 bolt diameters** from each plate end. Min **(2) bolts per plate piece**.
- **Plate washers** `3" x 3" x 0.229"` required in many jurisdictions (and all seismic SDC D) — standard cut washers do not qualify.
- In high seismic/high wind, spacing tightens and larger diameters/holdowns are added per engineering.

### Cast-in Embeds

- Set **anchor bolt templates (Simpson SSTB, PAB, ABA/PB column bases)** in the wet pour for posts and Strong-Walls. Use a template so spacing matches the connector exactly.
- Maintain **edge distance and embedment** from the catalog — too close to an edge and the cone breaks out.

### Post-Installed Mechanical Anchors

- **Simpson Titen HD (THD)** — screw anchor for cracked and uncracked concrete; ICC-ES listed (ESR-2713). Drill the **specified bit diameter**, blow/brush the hole clean (3x), drive to embedment with an impact. No spacing/curing wait.
- Good for sill-plate retrofit, ledgers, equipment, and standoff bases.

### Post-Installed Adhesive Anchors (Epoxy)

- **Simpson SET-XP** (epoxy) or **AT-XP** (acrylic) for threaded rod/rebar dowels into hardened concrete.
- **Hole prep is everything:** drill to spec diameter/depth, then clean with the **brush-and-blow cycle (blow 2x, brush 4x, blow 2x typical)** — dust kills bond. Use a **wire brush of the correct diameter**.
- For **overhead/horizontal sustained-tension** installs, ACI 318 §17.8.2.4 requires a **certified ACI Adhesive Anchor Installer** and continuous special inspection.
- Observe **gel time and full cure time** (temperature dependent) before loading.

### Special Inspection

- Post-installed anchors in structural applications often require **special inspection** per IBC 1705 / ACI 318. Torque/proof-load testing may be specified.

### Field Discipline

- Match the anchor to **cracked vs. uncracked** concrete design.
- Verify embedment with a depth mark on the rod.
- Use **hydrogen-embrittlement-rated** anchors where required; correct corrosion class (HDG/SS) for exterior/treated lumber.

Never "wet-set" a bolt by shoving it into finished concrete and never field-substitute an anchor without the engineer's blessing.

title: Cold-Weather & Hot-Weather Concreting (ACI 306 & 305)
content:
## Temperature Is a Variable, Not an Afterthought

Concrete is a chemical reaction. Too cold and it won't hydrate (or it freezes and is destroyed); too hot and it flash-sets, cracks, and loses strength.

### Cold-Weather Concreting (ACI 306)

Applies when ambient is below **40°F** or expected to drop there within the protection period.

- **Minimum delivered temperature:** ~**55-65°F** for thin sections (ACI 306 Table); thicker sections can be cooler.
- **Protect from freezing** until the concrete reaches **500 psi** — about the first 24-48 hr. Freezing fresh concrete before this destroys it permanently (expanding ice disrupts the paste).
- Methods:
  - **Insulating blankets** over slabs; **insulated forms** for walls.
  - **Heated enclosures + ground heaters** (hydronic, like a Wacker Neuson, or hoarding with indirect-fired heaters — vent CO/CO2, never direct-fire into an enclosure carbonating the surface).
  - **Heated mix water/aggregate** at the plant.
- **Accelerators:** non-chloride accelerator (don't use calcium chloride near rebar/PT — corrosion). Type III high-early cement helps.
- **Don't place on frozen subgrade** — it'll settle when it thaws. Thaw or insulate the ground first.

### Hot-Weather Concreting (ACI 305)

Applies above roughly **90°F**, high wind, low humidity, or strong sun — anything accelerating set and evaporation.

- **Keep mix temp below ~90°F.** Use **chilled water or ice**, cool aggregates, shade the trucks.
- **Retarder / hydration stabilizer** (set-retarding admixture) extends working time.
- **Plastic shrinkage cracking** is the big risk — when evaporation rate exceeds **~0.2 lb/sq ft/hr** (use the ACns evaporation nomograph). Combat with:
  - **Evaporation retarder / monomolecular film** (Confilm) sprayed after screed.
  - **Fog spraying** the air above the slab (don't add water to the surface).
  - **Windbreaks and sunshades.**
- **Pour early morning or at night** in extreme heat.
- **Cure immediately** — start wet curing/curing compound as soon as finishing allows; hot concrete dries fast.

### Universal Rules

- **Have a written cold/hot weather plan** before the truck arrives; you can't improvise blanket coverage at 6 PM in a snow squall.
- **Monitor concrete temperature** with a probe, not just air temp.
- **Maturity meters / field-cured cylinders** confirm strength gain before stripping forms or loading.
- Don't strip forms or remove shoring until the concrete has the strength (per cylinders/maturity), which takes **longer in cold**.

Planning the temperature is as important as the mix design — the best 4,000 psi mix means nothing if it freezes overnight.

title: Concrete Pumping & Placement Methods
content:
## Getting Concrete Where the Truck Can't

Pumps move concrete to upper floors, over obstacles, and into ICF/wall forms. The two workhorses are boom pumps and line (trailer) pumps.

### Pump Types

- **Boom pump (truck-mounted):** articulating boom reaches **80-200+ ft**; best for slabs, decks, and high pours. Fast placement, fewer laborers.
- **Line pump / trailer pump:** ground-level hose lines for tight access, basements, ICF walls, and smaller pours. Slower but fits where a boom can't set up.

### Mix Considerations for Pumping

- **Pumpable mix:** adequate **fines and paste**, consistent gradation, **3/8"-3/4" max aggregate** depending on line size. Too-lean or gap-graded mixes **plug the line**.
- **Slump ~5"** or use a **superplasticizer** to flow without adding water (adding water weakens it).
- **Prime the line** with a grout/cement slurry (or a pump primer) before concrete — never pump dry; dispose of the priming slurry, don't place it.

### Setup & Safety (OSHA 1926.1431/Crane rules)

- **Boom = crane:** survey for **overhead power lines** (maintain min clearance, 10 ft+ per voltage), set **outriggers fully on cribbing/pads**, level the truck. Outrigger failure flips the truck.
- **Don't whip the boom** over workers; keep crew clear of the discharge.
- **Blowout hazard:** the line is under high pressure. A clog that suddenly clears can **whip the hose** or eject concrete. Never look into the hose end; secure the end hose; **relieve pressure before opening a coupling** to clear a plug.
- **Wear** hard hat, Z87 eye pro, gloves; concrete is caustic.

### Placing Technique

- Place **near final position** — don't use the pump to move concrete laterally across the slab (causes segregation). Move the hose, not the puddle.
- Place in **uniform lifts**, keep up with the finishers, and **consolidate** (vibrate walls/columns) as you go.
- For walls/ICF, **limit lift height** and let the pump fill in passes to control form pressure.

### Cleanup

- **Flush and clean the line** immediately after the pour with water and a sponge ball (catch the ball in a washout). A neglected line sets up solid and is scrap.
- Wash out into a **designated washout containment** — never into storm drains (EPA/SWPPP).

Coordinate truck timing so the pump isn't waiting (pump charges by time) and the line never sits long enough to set. Good pumping is rhythm: trucks, pump, placers, and finishers in sync.

title: Self-Leveling Underlayment Installation
content:
## Flat Floors Without the Float

Self-leveling underlayment (SLU) creates a flat, smooth substrate for tile, LVT, or hardwood over uneven concrete or wood subfloors. It flows out, but only if you prep correctly — it's a system, not a bag-and-water job.

### Product Selection

- Cement-based SLU: Mapei **Ultraplan/Novoplan**, Ardex **K15/Liquid Backerboard**, USG **Levelrock**, Sika.
- Choose the right product for the **substrate** (concrete vs. wood vs. over-radiant) and the **thickness** range (feather to ~1"+, with aggregate extension for deeper).

### Substrate Prep (Make or Break)

- **Clean** to sound substrate — grind/shot-blast off curing compounds, sealers, paint, glue. SLU won't bond to a sealed slab.
- **Profile** concrete to ~CSP 2-3.
- **Prime** with the manufacturer's primer (e.g., Ardex P51, Mapei Primer L). Primer prevents pinholing/outgassing and promotes bond. **Two coats over porous/wood**, let dry per spec. Skipping primer = bubbles and delamination.
- Over **wood subfloors:** ensure rigid, fastened deck; many systems require **lath/mesh** stapled down and a wood-rated primer; respect deflection limits (L/360+).

### Dam & Penetrations

- **Dam off** doorways and floor edges with foam strips or wood. SLU is liquid — it will run into the next room and down floor penetrations. Plug drains and core holes.

### Mixing

- **Exact water ratio** — too much water = weak, segregated, cracky; too little = won't flow. Use a calibrated jug.
- Mix with a **paddle on a low-RPM drill** (or barrel mixer for volume) to a lump-free pourable consistency. Mix **2 bags continuously** with a helper so it stays wet-edge.

### Placing

- **Work fast** — pot life is often **10-20 min**. Pour and spread with a **gauge rake/smoother** set to depth, then break surface tension with a **spiked roller** to release air and help flow/level.
- Maintain a **wet edge**; keep batches coming so seams don't cold-joint.
- Don't overwork — it self-levels; let it.

### Cure & Next Steps

- Walkable in **2-4 hours**, most go to floorcovering in **24 hours** (check moisture for vapor-sensitive finishes; some need a moisture mitigation membrane first).
- Don't add extra water to the surface; protect from fans/direct sun/draft during initial set to avoid fast skinning.

Measure your low spots with a straightedge first, calculate bag count by area x depth, and have enough product + labor staged — you cannot stop mid-floor.

title: Sidewalk & ADA Ramp Construction
content:
## Walkways That Pass Inspection

Public and commercial walkways must meet **ADA Standards (2010 ADAAG)** and **PROWAG** for accessibility — slope, width, and surface are code, not preference.

### Sidewalk Basics

- **Thickness:** `4"` standard, `6"` at driveway crossings.
- **Width:** ADA accessible route min **36"** clear (with **60" x 60" passing spaces** every 200 ft if under 60" wide). Most public walks are **48"-60"**.
- **Base:** 4" compacted aggregate over compacted subgrade.
- **Cross slope:** **<= 2% (1:50)** maximum — this is strict; even 2.1% can fail. Running slope <= 5% (1:20) without being a ramp.
- **Joints:** control joints at intervals ~ spacing in feet equal to the width (4-5' for a 4-5' walk), tooled or saw-cut **1/4 depth**; expansion joints at structures and ~ every 20-30'.
- **Finish:** broom finish for slip resistance (perpendicular to travel).

### ADA Ramps (Running Slope > 5%)

When the running slope exceeds **5%**, it's a **ramp** and must comply (ADA 405):

- **Max running slope 8.33% (1:12).**
- **Max cross slope 2%.**
- **Max rise 30"** per run before a landing.
- **Landings** at top and bottom, **60" long** min, level (<= 2% all directions); landings at direction changes **60" x 60"**.
- **Clear width 36"** between handrails.
- **Handrails** required when rise > 6": **34"-38"** height, both sides, with **12" extensions** at top and bottom, continuous gripping surface.
- **Edge protection** (curb/rail) to keep wheels on.

### Curb Ramps (ADA 406 / PROWAG)

- At street crossings: max slope **8.33%**, flared sides **<= 10%**.
- **Detectable warning surface (truncated domes):** required at the bottom, **24" deep** full width, contrasting color (safety yellow common). Use cast-in or surface-applied panels (ADA-compliant truncated dome plates).
- Bottom landing/transition flush with street, **<= 1/4" vertical** lip (or beveled to 1:2 up to 1/2").

### Surface & Tolerance

- Surface gaps **<= 1/2"**; vertical changes **<= 1/4"** (or beveled).
- Stable, firm, slip-resistant.

### Field Tips

- **Shoot grades with a level/laser** and verify with a **digital smart-level (Smart Tool)** during the pour — once it's hard, a 2.2% cross slope is a tear-out.
- Set the detectable warning panels while plastic or use surface-mount with the specified adhesive/anchors.

Accessibility violations are expensive to remediate. Measure slopes before AND after finishing.

title: Concrete Field Testing: Cylinders, Slump & Air (ASTM C39/C143/C231)
content:
## Proving the Concrete Meets Spec

Field testing documents that what arrived matches what was ordered. On commercial/structural work it's mandatory and tied to acceptance. A **certified ACI Field Technician Grade I** should perform these.

### When to Sample (ASTM C172)

- Sample from the **middle of the discharge** (not first or last). Take a composite per ASTM C172.
- Frequency (ACI 318 / IBC 1905): typically **one test set per 150 cu yd or per 5,000 sq ft of slab**, and at least one per day per mix design. "One test" = the average of **(2) cylinders at 28 days** (plus extras for 7-day and hold).

### Slump Test (ASTM C143)

- Fill the **slump cone in 3 layers**, each rodded **25 times** with the 5/8" rod.
- Strike off, lift the cone **straight up in 5±2 seconds**, measure the slump (drop from cone height) to the displaced center.
- Compare to the spec (e.g., `4" ± 1"`). Out-of-spec slump = grounds to **reject the load** (do NOT add water on site without re-tempering rules and approval).

### Air Content (ASTM C231 — Pressure Method)

- Use the **Type B pressure meter** (or C173 volumetric for lightweight/porous aggregate).
- Fill in 3 layers, rod and tap each, strike off, clamp the lid, add water, pump to pressure, read **% air**.
- Air-entrained exterior concrete typically **5-7%** for freeze-thaw durability (ASTM C260 admixture). Low air = scaling risk; high air = strength loss.

### Unit Weight & Temperature

- **ASTM C138** unit weight (density) and yield check.
- **ASTM C1064** concrete temperature — relevant for hot/cold-weather limits.

### Making Cylinders (ASTM C31)

- Standard **4x8 or 6x12** cylinders. Rod per layer count (4x8 = 2 layers x 25; 6x12 = 3 layers x 25).
- **Initial cure** on site at **60-80°F**, protected from moisture loss and disturbance for the first **24-48 hr** (insulated cure box in cold/heat). Then transport to the lab moist-cure room.

### Compressive Strength (ASTM C39)

- Lab breaks cylinders at **7 and 28 days**; report **psi** and **fracture pattern**.
- **Acceptance (ACI 318 §26.12):** every average of 3 consecutive tests **>= f'c**, AND no single test **> 500 psi below f'c** (for f'c <= 5,000). One low break triggers investigation/cores (ASTM C42).

### Documentation

- Record: mix ID, ticket #, truck #, time batched/sampled, slump, air, temp, ambient, cylinder IDs, location placed.
- File results with the inspector; they're part of structural acceptance.

Test early in the pour — if slump/air fails the first truck, you can correct or reject before the whole structure is placed.

title: Curing Compounds & Sealers with W.R. Meadows Products
content:
## Curing Is Not Optional

Concrete that dries before it cures loses up to **40% of potential strength** and the surface is weak, dusty, and scale-prone. Curing keeps moisture in for hydration; sealing protects the finished surface. They are different jobs.

### Why Cure (ACI 308)

- Maintain moisture and temperature for at least **7 days** (more in cold) so cement hydration continues.
- Proper curing improves **strength, abrasion resistance, reduced cracking, and freeze-thaw durability**.

### Curing Methods

- **Water curing:** wet burlap, soaker hose, ponding — best results but labor-intensive.
- **Membrane curing compounds:** spray-applied film that holds moisture in. The practical standard for slabs.

### Curing Compound Types (ASTM C309 / C1315)

- **W.R. Meadows 1100-CLEAR / 1200-WHITE** — membrane-forming curing compounds (ASTM C309). White-pigmented reflects heat on hot-weather slabs.
- **CS-309** for general curing.
- **VOCOMP-25** — water-based acrylic cure & seal (ASTM C1315), cures AND leaves a sealer film.
- **DUO-GUARD / SEALTIGHT** product lines for cure-and-seal in one.

**Caution:** A membrane curing compound can interfere with the **bond of flooring, coatings, or toppings** (tile thinset, epoxy). On floors getting a topping, either use a **dissipating-resin compound** (W.R. Meadows **1100 Series Dissipating**) or water-cure, then mechanically prep.

### Application

- Apply **immediately after finishing**, as soon as the surface sheen/bleed water is gone and won't mar.
- Spray a **uniform film** with a pump/airless sprayer at the **specified coverage** (e.g., ~300 sq ft/gal — check the TDS). Two perpendicular passes for full coverage.
- Don't over-apply or it puddles and won't dry; don't skip spots (leaves cure shadows).

### Sealers (After Cure)

- **Penetrating sealers** (silane/siloxane, W.R. Meadows **SEAL TIGHT / DECRA-SEAL**) repel water/chlorides without changing appearance — good for driveways, garage floors, freeze-thaw protection. Don't make the surface slippery.
- **Film-forming acrylic sealers** (CS-309/25) add sheen and "wet look," common on decorative/stamped — but can be slick (add anti-slip grit) and need periodic reapplication.
- **Densifiers** (lithium/sodium silicate) harden and dustproof interior slabs.

### Sequence & Timing

- Cure first (7 days), let the slab **dry/age** (penetrating sealers often want **28 days** and a dry surface), test moisture, then seal.
- Match the sealer to the service: chloride exposure -> silane; decorative -> acrylic; warehouse -> densifier.

Read the TDS, confirm compatibility with the next coating, and apply at the right window. A good cure plus the right sealer is the cheapest durability you'll ever buy.

title: Stem Walls & Grade Beams Construction
content:
## The Wall Between Footing and Floor

A stem wall sits on the footing and lifts the structure above grade; a grade beam spans between piers/piles to carry loads over poor or expansive soil. Both are reinforced concrete and follow **ACI 318 / IRC R404**.

### Stem Walls

- Built on a **spread footing** (see footing code R403). Typical residential stem wall **8" thick** on a **16"-24" wide x 8-10" footing**.
- Height set so the **top of stem is min 8" above grade** (IRC R404.1.6) and **6" above adjacent finished grade** for siding clearance.
- **Rebar:** dowels from the footing tie into vertical bars (commonly **#4 @ 24"-48" OC vertical**) and **(2) #4 horizontal** top and bottom continuous; lap splices **40 bar diameters** min. Maintain **3" cover** against earth, **1-1/2"** formed faces.
- **Anchor bolts** cast in the top per R403.1.6 (1/2" @ 6' OC, 7" embed) for the sill plate.
- Provide a **brick ledge / step** if supporting masonry veneer.

### Forming

- Form both faces, brace and align (form ties / she-bolts, plywood + walers, or modular forms like Symons). Keep forms **plumb and straight**; check diagonals.
- Set **bulkheads** at construction joints with a keyway or roughened surface + dowels.

### Grade Beams

- Used on **drilled piers, helical piles, or in expansive/soft soil** to span between bearing points so the beam carries the wall, not the soil directly.
- Often formed with a **void form (cardboard carton form, e.g., SureVoid)** under the beam in expansive clay so the swelling soil doesn't lift the beam.
- Heavily reinforced: top and bottom bar mats, stirrups (e.g., **#3 stirrups @ 12"**), continuous over piers with proper development length into pier cages.

### Pouring & Consolidation

- **3,000-4,000 psi**, `4"-5"` slump (or pump mix).
- **Consolidate with an internal vibrator** — stem walls and beams are tall, narrow, and congested with steel; vibrate to remove honeycomb but don't over-vibrate (segregation). Insert vibrator every **18-24"**, into the prior lift, withdraw slowly.
- Pour in **lifts**; control form pressure on tall walls.

### Strip, Cure, Backfill

- Strip forms after concrete has set enough (don't strip too early — green concrete spalls). Cure **7 days**.
- **Waterproof/damp-proof** below-grade faces and install **drainage + footing drain** (R405) before backfill.
- **Don't backfill until the floor framing/slab braces the wall** (or temporarily brace it) — unbalanced backfill can crack/push an unbraced stem wall, a classic failure.

Verify rebar, cover, anchor bolt layout, and wall plumb before the pour — these are inspected and hard to fix after.

title: Concrete Repair & Patching with Epoxy & Polymer Systems
content:
## Diagnose Before You Patch

A patch that doesn't bond or that's the wrong material pops out in a season. Identify the failure first: shrinkage crack, structural crack, spall, delamination, or surface scaling — each wants a different repair.

### Crack Repair

- **Non-moving structural cracks:** **epoxy injection** restores monolithic strength. Surface-seal the crack, set injection ports, and inject low-viscosity structural epoxy (Sika **Sikadur 35/52**, Simpson **CrackPac**) until it travels port to port. Bonds the crack stronger than the surrounding concrete.
- **Moving/active cracks:** do NOT epoxy (it'll just crack elsewhere). Rout and seal with a **flexible polyurethane sealant** that accommodates movement, or convert to a control joint.
- **Hairline shrinkage cracks:** route to a `1/4" x 1/4"` reservoir, clean, fill with polymer-modified or polyurethane crack filler.

### Spall & Surface Patch

- **Saw-cut the perimeter** square `1/2"` deep — never feather-edge a patch (feather edges crumble). Chip out to **sound concrete**, exposing/cleaning rebar if present.
- **Clean** thoroughly (no dust/laitance); the substrate must be **SSD (saturated surface-dry)** for cementitious repair, or dry for epoxy mortars.
- **Bonding:** scrub in a **bonding agent / cement slurry** or a polymer bonding bridge (Sika Armatec for rebar, SikaLatex / Quikrete Acrylic Fortifier in the mix).
- **Repair mortar:**
  - **Polymer-modified cementitious** (Sika **MonoTop**, Quikrete **FastSet Repair Mortar / Vinyl Concrete Patcher**, Ardex) for general spalls — good for thin to moderate.
  - **Epoxy mortar** for thin overlays, chemical exposure, fast return-to-service.
  - For **rebar corrosion** spalls, abrasive-clean the steel, coat with anti-corrosion primer (Sika Armatec), then patch.

### Resurfacing & Overlays

- For worn but sound slabs, a **polymer-modified overlay / micro-topping** (Ardex, Sika, Quikrete Re-Cap) re-levels the surface. Prep = mechanical profile + primer; respect minimum thickness.

### Vertical & Overhead

- Use a **sag-resistant repair mortar** built up in lifts; for overhead use products rated for it and a bonding/anti-corrosion system on exposed steel.

### Cure the Repair

- Patches are thin and **dry fast** — cure them (wet or curing compound) or they craze and debond. Protect from sun/wind.

### Why Patches Fail

- Feather edges, dusty/loose substrate, no bonding agent, wrong material (rigid patch over a moving crack), too dry/too wet substrate, or no curing. Prep is 80% of a durable repair.

Match the product to the cause and the exposure, prep aggressively, and cure the repair like you would new concrete.

title: Fire-Rated Gypsum Assemblies: UL Designs & GA-600 1-Hr/2-Hr Walls
content:
## Fire-Rated Gypsum Assemblies

Fire-rated walls and ceilings must be built **exactly** as the tested assembly specifies. You cannot mix substitutes. The two authoritative sources are **GA-600 (Gypsum Association Fire Resistance Design Manual)** and **UL Fire Resistance Directory** designs (e.g., **UL U419, U411, V417**). The IBC Section 703 and IRC R302 reference these.

### What Defines the Rating

A fire-resistance rating is achieved by the **complete assembly**, not just the board. Variables that cannot change:

- Board type and thickness: almost always `5/8" Type X` (USG Sheetrock Firecode C or National Gypsum Gold Bond Fire-Shield)
- Stud spacing (typically 16" o.c. or 24" o.c.)
- Fastener type, length, and spacing
- Number of layers per side
- Insulation requirement (some designs require mineral wool in the cavity)

### Common Designs

**1-Hour Wall (GA WP 3605 / UL U419):**
- One layer `5/8" Type X` each side of `3-5/8"` steel studs or 2x4 wood at 16" o.c.
- Screws `1-1/4" Type S` at 8" o.c. edges, 12" field
- Joints taped (Level 1 minimum)

**2-Hour Wall (GA WP 3820 / UL U411):**
- Two layers `5/8" Type X` each side
- Base layer screws `1-1/4"`, face layer `1-5/8" Type S` at 16" o.c.
- Stagger joints between layers

### Critical Field Rules

- **Type X vs Type C:** Type C contains additional glass fiber and vermiculite for less core shrinkage. Designs calling for Type C (Firecode C) **cannot** substitute standard Type X.
- Joints in multi-layer assemblies must be **offset** at least 16" between layers.
- All penetrations (boxes, pipes) require **firestopping** per UL through-penetration systems; back-to-back electrical boxes must be offset 24" or use a UL-listed putty pad (e.g., 3M Fire Barrier Putty Pad MPP+).
- Head-of-wall joints at rated partitions need a UL-listed top-of-wall system (e.g., deflection track with mineral wool + firestop sealant).

### Inspection & Documentation

- Keep the GA-600 design number or UL design number posted at the job and in submittals.
- Rated walls must extend to the deck (full-height), not stop at a dropped ceiling, unless the design specifically allows a fire-rated membrane ceiling.
- Label fire/smoke partitions above the ceiling per IBC 703.7 with stenciled lettering.

Never "improve" a tested assembly by adding material outside the listing without an engineering judgment (EJ) from the gypsum manufacturer's technical line.

title: Sound-Rated STC Assemblies: Resilient Channel & QuietRock
content:
## Building Sound-Rated Partitions

Sound Transmission Class (STC) measures airborne sound isolation per **ASTM E90** (lab) and **E336** (field, FSTC). A standard single-layer 2x4 wall is roughly STC 33-35 — you can hear normal conversation. Building codes (IBC 1206) require **STC 50** (45 field-tested) between dwelling units.

### Strategies That Actually Work

Four principles drive STC: **mass, decoupling, absorption, and damping.**

- **Mass:** Add layers of `5/8"` gypsum. Each doubling of mass adds roughly 5 STC.
- **Decoupling:** Break the vibration path with resilient channel, staggered studs, or a double-stud wall.
- **Absorption:** Fill the cavity with `R-13` mineral wool or fiberglass batts (mineral wool like Rockwool Safe'n'Sound performs best).
- **Damping:** Use constrained-layer damping board (QuietRock) or Green Glue between two layers.

### Resilient Channel (RC-1)

- Install RC-1 **horizontally** at 24" o.c., perpendicular to studs.
- Screw the channel to studs with `1-1/4"` screws through the mounting flange ONLY.
- Attach drywall to the channel with `1" Type S` screws — **screws must NOT touch the stud** or you "short-circuit" the channel and lose the rating.
- Keep drywall edges 1/4" off the floor and seal the gap with acoustical sealant.

### QuietRock

- **QuietRock EZ-SNAP (5/8")** can replace a multi-layer/Green Glue assembly with a single board. One layer over standard drywall yields up to STC 52 in tested assemblies.
- Score and snap like standard board, but use a heavier hand — it has a steel constrained layer.
- Use the manufacturer's published assembly (e.g., QR-510) to hit a target STC.

### Detailing That Makes or Breaks STC

- Apply a continuous bead of **acoustical sealant** (USG Sheetrock Acoustical Sealant or Tremco) at the perimeter — floor, ceiling, and abutting walls.
- Seal around all electrical boxes; never place outlets back-to-back. Offset by at least one stud bay and putty-pad them.
- Caulk all penetrations. Flanking paths through ductwork, shared top plates, and floor decking will defeat the wall.
- A double-stud wall with a 1" air gap, double `5/8"` each side, and mineral wool can exceed STC 60.

Field STC is always lower than lab STC — design 3-5 points above the requirement to be safe.

title: Suspended Drop-Ceiling Grid Installation: Armstrong & USG Donn
content:
## Installing a Suspended Acoustical Ceiling

A suspended grid (Armstrong Prelude XL or USG Donn DX) carries lay-in acoustical tile and provides a plenum for ducts and lighting. Precision layout is everything — crooked borders ruin the look.

### Layout & Height

- Drop the ceiling a minimum of **4" below the lowest obstruction** (more if recessed cans need clearance — typically 6-8").
- Snap a level line around the room for the **wall angle (molding)**. Use a laser level; a 1/4" error reads badly across a room.
- Calculate border tiles so opposite borders are **equal and at least half a tile wide**. Never leave a sliver border.

### Grid Components

- **Wall angle (L-molding):** fastened to walls at the layout line, fasteners 16" o.c.
- **Main tees:** run perpendicular to joists, spaced **48" o.c.**, supported by **12-gauge hanger wire every 48"** and within 8" of each end.
- **4' cross tees** snap into mains at 24" intervals; **2' cross tees** complete a 2x2 grid.

### Hanging the Grid

- Install hanger wires to structure (joists, deck inserts, or `eye-lag` screws). Wire must be wrapped a minimum of **3 full turns within 1-1/2"** per ASTM C636.
- Level each main as you go with a stretched string line; saddle-tie wires.
- Square the grid using the 3-4-5 method before locking cross tees.

### Seismic & Code

- In **Seismic Design Categories D, E, F**, follow ASTM E580: heavier 2" wall molding, perimeter clips, compression posts, and bracing wires at 12' o.c. Two adjacent walls are attached, two float on an oversized molding.
- Light fixtures and air diffusers must be **independently supported** with their own wires — never hang fixtures on the grid alone.

### Tile Installation

- Wear clean gloves; fingerprints show on acoustical tile.
- Cut border tiles face-up with a sharp utility knife and straightedge.
- For fire-rated lay-in ceilings, use the listed tile and hold-down clips per the UL design.

Double-check main-tee direction against joists before committing — re-leveling a finished grid is miserable.

title: Drywall Access Panels & Control Joints: Placement & Install
content:
## Access Panels and Control (Expansion) Joints

Two often-overlooked details prevent callbacks: providing maintenance access without hacking holes, and relieving stress before it cracks the finish.

### Access Panels

Provide access wherever a valve, cleanout, damper, or junction box needs future service.
