- Use a manufactured panel (Acudor, Babcock-Davis, or Karp) sized to the task — common `12x12`, `14x14`, `22x30`.
- For finished living areas, drywall-bead-flange panels (e.g., Acudor DW-5040) accept joint compound and disappear into the wall.
- Fire-rated locations require a **UL-listed fire-rated access door** matching the wall's rating, with self-closing, self-latching hardware.
- Frame a header and sill in the rough opening; the panel frame screws to framing, not just drywall.
- Locate panels logically and discreetly — inside a closet or above a drop ceiling when possible.

### Control Joints (per ASTM C840 / GA-216)

Gypsum expands and contracts with temperature and humidity. Control joints relieve that movement.

- **Interior partitions and ceilings:** install a control joint where wall or ceiling runs exceed **30 feet** (walls) or **50 feet** (ceilings without perimeter relief).
- **Ceilings WITHOUT perimeter relief:** maximum `2,500 sq ft`; **WITH perimeter relief:** `900 sq ft` for ceilings, joint spacing not over 30'.
- Place a joint where the ceiling changes dimension, at wings/ells, and where structural movement is expected.
- Always break drywall at the joint — the board must NOT be continuous across the control joint. Cut the board and isolate framing.

### Installing a Control Joint

- Use a roll-formed zinc control joint (USG Sheetrock No. 093 / Trim-Tex 8100 series).
- Cut the gypsum to leave a `1/4"-1/2"` gap; center the joint over the gap.
- Fasten flanges 9" o.c.; **do not** screw through the V-relief.
- Remove the protective tape only after finishing the surrounding compound.
- At fire-rated walls, pack the gap behind the joint with mineral wool/firestop to maintain the rating.

Proper joint placement is the difference between a wall that stays flat and one that telegraphs a crack every winter.

title: High-Build Level 5 Finish: Skim Coat & Spray Application
content:
## Achieving a Level 5 Finish

A **Level 5 finish (GA-214)** applies a thin skim coat over the entire surface after Level 4 taping. It's required under gloss/semi-gloss paint, severe critical (raking) lighting, and dark colors where any joint photographing is unacceptable.

### When Level 5 Is Specified

- Large unbroken walls hit by side light from windows
- Enamel, gloss, or high-sheen paints
- Deep accent colors
- High-end residential and commercial lobbies

### Two Approved Methods

**1. Hand/roller skim coat:**
- Thin all-purpose or a setting-type joint compound (USG Sheetrock Plus 3 or a lightweight) to a paint-like consistency.
- Roll on with a 1/2" nap, then immediately knock down flat with a wide (14"-24") skimming blade or a skimming squeegee (Level5 Tools / Columbia).
- Leave a tight, thin film — fill the paper texture and pinholes, not build thickness.

**2. Spray-applied skim (high-build):**
- Use a high-build drywall primer/surfacer (USG Tuff-Hide or Sherwin-Williams equivalent) sprayed with an airless rated for heavy material (Graco with a 0.025-0.035 tip).
- Tuff-Hide combines Level 5 skim + primer in one spray pass at roughly `8-10 mil` wet — it both fills and primes.
- Back-roll if specified for uniform texture.

### Technique That Matters

- Sand the Level 4 work to 150-grit and vacuum/wipe before skimming — debris telegraphs through.
- Work in manageable sections so the skim doesn't set before knock-down.
- Keep a wet edge and overlap passes slightly.
- Light the wall with a raking work light during application to catch every imperfection.

### Verification

- After it dries, inspect under the same raking light the room will see.
- A true Level 5 should show **uniform sheen and texture** with no visible joints, fastener spots, or trowel marks.
- Prime with a quality drywall primer/sealer before topcoat (unless Tuff-Hide already primed) so the finish paint flashes evenly between the porous skim and the denser joint compound.

Never sell Level 5 as just "extra sanding" — it is a full additional skim over 100% of the surface and should be priced as a separate scope.

title: Drywall Texture Types: Knockdown, Orange Peel & Popcorn
content:
## Applying and Matching Drywall Textures

Texture hides minor imperfections, adds character, and must be matched precisely for patches. The three workhorses are orange peel, knockdown, and acoustic (popcorn).

### Surface Prep (all textures)

- Finish joints to at least **Level 3** before texturing.
- Prime bare board first when possible — texture over raw paper vs. compound flashes differently and bonds inconsistently.
- Mask trim, floors, and adjacent surfaces; texture overspray travels.

### Orange Peel (Splatter)

- Thin all-purpose joint compound to a thick-cream consistency.
- Spray with a hopper gun (Graco/Marshalltown) at `25-35 psi`, larger orifice for heavier peel.
- Apply a light, uniform splatter and **leave it** — no knock-down.
- Common on walls; easy to repair.

### Knockdown

- Spray a heavier splatter than orange peel (mud thinned slightly less).
- Wait **10-15 minutes** until the peaks lose their wet sheen and begin to flatten.
- Drag an 18"-24" knockdown knife or flexible blade lightly across to flatten the peaks into flat "splotches."
- Timing is critical — too soon smears, too late won't flatten.

### Popcorn / Acoustic (Spray Texture)

- Mix bagged aggregated acoustic texture (USG/Homax) with water; polystyrene or vermiculite aggregate.
- Spray on ceilings with a hopper and large orifice; never roll.
- **WARNING:** Popcorn installed before **1980** may contain **asbestos** — test before scraping or disturbing. Removal of asbestos-containing texture is regulated under EPA/OSHA and often requires licensed abatement.

### Matching Existing Texture for Patches

- Identify the pattern and aggregate first.
- Practice on cardboard to dial in air pressure, mud consistency, and orifice.
- Feather the new texture slightly into the old; prime and paint the whole wall/ceiling plane when possible to blend sheen.

### Cleanup & Quality

- Flush hopper guns immediately — dried texture ruins them.
- Inspect under raking light; touch up bald spots before primer.
- Always prime textured surfaces before finish paint for uniform sheen and to lock down loose aggregate.

title: Moisture & Mold-Resistant Board: Green, Purple & USG Mold Tough
content:
## Specifying Moisture- and Mold-Resistant Gypsum

Standard gypsum's paper face feeds mold when wet. In wet and humid locations, use the right specialty board and pair it with the correct backer for tile.

### Board Types and Where They Belong

- **Green board (water-resistant, ASTM C1396):** treated paper face. Acceptable for **humid** areas (bathroom walls/ceilings not in direct water) but **NOT behind tile in showers/tub surrounds** per current code and TCNA.
- **Mold-resistant board (USG Mold Tough / Sheetrock Brand Mold Tough, National Gypsum XP, CertainTeed M2Tech):** treated core and face, scores **10 on ASTM D3273** mold-growth resistance. Use in bathrooms, basements, laundry, and behind kitchen casework.
- **Purple board (Gold Bond Purple XP):** mold- and moisture-resistant; some variants add abuse resistance.
- **Glass-mat board (Georgia-Pacific DensArmor Plus):** no paper face — fiberglass mat — for the highest mold/moisture exposure short of cement board.

### Code & Standard Rules

- **IRC R702.3.8 / R702.4.2:** Water-resistant gypsum backing board shall **not** be used in tile showers or tub-surround wet areas; use cement board (ASTM C1325) or a listed glass-mat/foam backer with the proper waterproofing.
- **IRC R702.7:** vapor retarders — be careful not to double-up vapor barriers that trap moisture in the wall.
- Ceilings over showers/tubs and high-humidity rooms: use mold-resistant board, and run the exhaust fan.

### Installation Best Practices

- Maintain a `1/4"` gap above tubs/floors so the board doesn't wick standing water.
- Use **corrosion-resistant fasteners** in wet areas.
- Finish with a mold-resistant setting compound or a moisture-rated joint compound; standard ready-mix in chronically damp areas can mold at the joints.
- Seal cut edges and penetrations at plumbing.

### Don't Confuse Mold-Resistant with Waterproof

Mold-resistant board resists mold growth — it is **not** a waterproofing layer. Showers still require a waterproof membrane (sheet or liquid like Schluter-KERDI or USG Durock membrane) over the appropriate backer. Specify each layer for its job.

title: Framing & Finishing Soffits and Bulkheads
content:
## Building Drywall Soffits and Bulkheads

Soffits (also called bulkheads or drop boxes) conceal ductwork, plumbing, and beams, and create architectural definition over cabinets and islands. Clean, straight, plumb boxes are a hallmark of skilled work.

### Layout

- Snap level lines on the ceiling and walls defining the soffit's depth (drop) and width (projection).
- Verify the soffit clears the obstruction (duct/pipe) with at least `1/2"-1"` margin plus board thickness.
- Check for level and plumb of existing surfaces — shim the framing, not the drywall, to correct.

### Framing Methods

**Ladder (L-frame) method:** Build two flat "ladders" — one fastened to the ceiling joists, one to the wall — then connect with cross blocks (rungs) at 16"-24" o.c. forming an L-section. Strong and accessible.

**Steel stud method:** For long runs and commercial work, frame with `1-5/8"` or `2-1/2"` steel studs and track. Lighter, straighter, and fireproof. Screw track to ceiling and wall, drop verticals, then a horizontal face track.

- Keep the bottom face track dead level — it sets the whole look.
- For wide soffits, add intermediate hangers to the structure above so the box doesn't sag.

### Hanging

- Hang the **bottom (soffit) face first**, then the vertical side, so the side board overlaps and hides the edge.
- Hold board `1/8"` off intersecting surfaces for clean joints.
- Use `5/8"` board on wide horizontal soffit bottoms to prevent sag, especially if textured.

### Finishing the Corners

- Outside corners are the focal point — use a quality bead. **No-Coat / Trim-Tex Mud-Set bullnose or square bead** gives crisp, ding-resistant edges and is easier to keep straight than metal on a long run.
- For the long bottom-to-side corner, a structural laminate bead resists cracking from movement.
- Tape inside corners normally; consider a flexible/tear-away bead where the soffit meets an uneven ceiling.

### Quality Checks

- Sight down each edge — bows show under lighting, especially cove or under-cabinet lighting.
- Confirm the box is square at corners with a framing square before hanging.
- Prime and inspect under the final lighting before painting.
estimated_time: Half to full day per run
materials_required: steel studs and track or wood

title: Drywall Patch & Water-Damage Repair
content:
## Repairing Drywall Holes and Water Damage

Done right, a patch disappears; done wrong, it telegraphs forever. Match the repair method to the damage size and always fix the cause of water damage first.

### Small Holes (under 6")

- For nail/screw holes and dings, use lightweight spackle or setting compound; two thin coats, sand, prime.
- For golf-ball-size holes, use a **self-adhesive aluminum mesh patch** (FibaTape) — apply, coat with setting compound, feather wide, sand.

### Medium to Large Holes (California / Butterfly Patch)

- Cut a clean square in the wall around the damage.
- Cut a drywall plug larger than the hole, score and snap the back gypsum leaving the face paper as flaps (the "butterfly").
- Butter the paper flaps with compound, insert the plug, and press the flaps flat. No backing needed.

### Large Holes (Backed Patch)

- Cut out to the nearest studs or insert wood/`1x` backing strips behind the opening, screwed to the existing board.
- Screw a new gypsum patch to the backing.
- Tape the seams with paper tape and setting compound; three coats, feathered 10"-12" wide; sand and prime.

### Water Damage — Fix the Source First

- **Stop the leak** (roof, plumbing, flashing) before any repair, or you'll do it twice.
- **Moisture-test** the area with a meter (Delmhorst/General). Drywall reading above ~`1%` MC equivalent / elevated readings means it's still wet.
- Cut out **all** soft, stained, or crumbling board plus a margin into sound material. Sagging or delaminated board must go.
- Inspect framing and insulation for mold. If mold covers more than ~10 sq ft or you see black growth, follow EPA mold guidance — contain, use N95/respirator, HEPA vacuum; large areas warrant remediation pros.
- Dry the cavity fully (fans/dehumidifier) before closing up.

### Stain Sealing

- Water stains bleed through latex paint. Seal with a **stain-blocking primer** — shellac-based (Zinsser B-I-N) or oil/alkyd (Kilz Original) — before topcoating, or the rusty halo returns.

### Finishing for an Invisible Repair

- Feather wider than you think you need; the wider the taper, the less it shows.
- Match surrounding texture before priming.
- Prime the patch and surrounding area so paint sheen blends.

title: Estimating Drywall: Sheets, Mud, Screws & Tape Takeoff
content:
## Drywall Material Takeoff and Estimating

Accurate takeoffs protect margin and prevent mid-job runs to the supply house. Estimate board, fasteners, tape, compound, and labor methodically.

### Board Quantity

- Calculate total wall + ceiling square footage. Divide by sheet area: a `4x8` = 32 sf, `4x12` = 48 sf.
- Add **10-15% waste** for cuts, openings, and breakage (more on cut-up jobs, less on big flat commercial).
- Subtract large openings (garage doors, storefronts), but count small windows/doors as full for waste.
- Prefer longer sheets (`4x12`) to reduce butt joints — fewer seams, faster finishing.

### Screws

- Rule of thumb: about **1 lb of screws per 100-200 sf**, or roughly **1,000 screws (≈5 lb) per 50 sheets**.
- Ceilings use more (12" o.c. field). `1-1/4" Type W` for wood, `1-1/4" Type S` for steel; `1-5/8"` for double-layer face.

### Joint Tape

- Estimate roughly **370 lf of tape per 1,000 sf** of board.
- One 500' roll of paper tape covers ~1,350 sf of board. Add corner bead by linear foot of every outside corner.

### Joint Compound

- Plan about **140 lb (≈2 to 2.5 buckets/boxes) of compound per 1,000 sf** for a standard Level 4, three-coat finish.
- Add more for Level 5 skim, heavy texture, or fire-taping. Setting compound for first coat/fills, ready-mix for fill/finish.

### Corner Bead & Accessories

- Count linear feet of outside corners; add control joints, bullnose, and L-trim per plan.

### Labor

- Hanging: an experienced crew hangs roughly **35-60 sheets per hanger per day** depending on complexity.
- Finishing is the bigger labor line — taping/finishing typically runs **1.5-2x** the hang labor for Level 4.
- Price texture, Level 5, high ceilings, and access scaffolding as separate line items.

### Build the Estimate

- Itemize: board, screws, tape, bead, compound, texture, primer, fasteners, plus labor by phase (hang, tape, sand, texture).
- Add margin and contingency for site conditions (high ceilings, demo, occupied space).
- Always note assumptions and exclusions on the proposal to avoid scope disputes.

title: Automatic Taping Tools: Bazooka, Boxes & TapeTech Workflow
content:
## Running Automatic Taping Tools

Automatic taping tools ("auto tools") — Bazooka, flat boxes, angle heads, and pumps from TapeTech, Columbia, Drywall Master, and Apla-Tech — apply tape and mud faster and more consistently than hand taping on production work.

### The Tool Set

- **Automatic taper (Bazooka):** applies paper tape with embedded mud to flats and inside corners in one pass.
- **Compound tube / loading pump:** fills the Bazooka and flat boxes from the mud bucket.
- **Flat boxes (7", 10", 12"):** apply and crown the coats over flats. Progress 7" first coat, 10", then 12" finish.
- **Angle head + corner applicator (corner roller/glazer + finisher):** apply and finish inside corners.
- **Nail spotter (2"-3"):** fills fastener rows fast.

### Mud Prep

- Thin all-purpose compound to a **smooth, lump-free, slightly soupy** consistency — too thick clogs tools, too thin runs and slumps.
- Mix with a paddle and screen out lumps; lumps jam the Bazooka cutter and box blades.
- Use a clean bucket and pump; grit ruins tools.

### Sequence (Production Workflow)

1. **Tape coat:** Run the Bazooka down all flats and inside corners. Wipe down tape with a wiper/taping knife to set it and remove excess mud.
2. **Roll & flush corners:** Use the corner roller then the angle head/finisher on inside corners.
3. **Coat fasteners** with the nail spotter; **bed/coat outside corner bead** with a knife or applicator.
4. **Fill coat:** 7" or 10" flat box over flats once the tape coat sets/dries.
5. **Finish coat:** 12" box for a wide, feathered crown; second angle-head pass on corners.

### Maintenance — Tools Are an Investment

- **Flush every tool thoroughly with water at the end of the day** — dried mud destroys seals and blades.
- Lubricate moving parts; check the Bazooka cutter, drive cord, and box blades for wear.
- Store boxes drained and gear racked. A neglected Bazooka can cost hundreds to rebuild.

### When to Use Them

Auto tools pay off on large, repetitive work (tract homes, commercial). For small patches and remodels, hand tools are faster. Master hand taping first — auto tools amplify good technique, not bad.

title: Drywall Lift Operation & Big-Ceiling Hang Safety
content:
## Safely Hanging Big Ceilings with a Drywall Lift

Lifting full sheets overhead is where drywall crews get hurt — back strains, falls, and dropped panels. A drywall lift (Telpro PanelLift 138, Troy DPH11) plus disciplined procedure prevents injuries and produces tighter ceilings.

### Setting Up the Lift

- Inspect the lift before each use: cables/straps for fraying, hooks, wheel locks, and the cradle/outriggers.
- Set it on a **level, solid floor**; lock all caster brakes before loading.
- Know the rated capacity — most handle `4x12` and up to ~`150 lb`. Do not overload.

### Loading and Lifting

- Load the sheet **finish-side down** with two people; tip the cradle to a comfortable angle.
- Crank steadily; keep hands and fingers clear of the cradle pivot and cable spool.
- Raise until the sheet is snug to the framing, then fine-position by hand.
- Stage the next sheet so you're not rushing the crank.

### Hang Sequence

- Run sheets **perpendicular to joists**, starting in a corner.
- Tack a few screws to hold, then lower the lift and finish fastening at `12" o.c.`
- Stagger butt joints and keep ends on framing.

### Working at Height Safely

- Use proper **stilts**, an OSHA-compliant scaffold, or a baker's scaffold — not buckets or wobbly ladders — for high ceilings.
- On stilts: clear the floor of scraps/cords, work on flat surfaces only, and never carry full sheets while wearing them. Many jurisdictions and OSHA-conscious GCs restrict stilt use — confirm site rules.
- Guardrails required on scaffolds per **OSHA 1926 Subpart L** above 10 ft.

### Ergonomics & PPE

- The lift exists so nobody muscles sheets overhead — use it; don't "just hold this one."
- Wear safety glasses (debris falls during overhead screwing), a dust mask/respirator, and a hard hat where overhead hazards exist.
- Keep two hands free for control; never reach overhead with a running screw gun and a sheet at once.

### Crew Communication

- One person calls the lift; the other spots. Agree on signals.
- Don't stand directly under a loaded lift longer than necessary.
- Lower and lock the lift when stepping away.

A $400 lift is cheaper than one back injury or a destroyed sheet.

title: Furring & Drywall Over Masonry and Concrete Walls
content:
## Drywalling Over Masonry, Block, and Concrete

Finishing basements and concrete/CMU walls requires furring or a stud wall plus moisture management. Get the assembly right or you'll trap water and grow mold.

### Moisture First

- Concrete and block walls move moisture vapor. Address bulk water (grading, drainage, sealing the exterior) **before** finishing.
- Apply a damp-proof coating or use a dimple membrane on chronically damp walls.
- Avoid creating a **double vapor barrier** that traps moisture between layers — follow IRC R702.7 and local code for basement wall vapor retarders. In many climates, closed-cell spray foam or rigid foam against the wall is the safest approach.

### Furring Methods

**1. Furring strips (1x3 wood or 7/8" hat channel/Z-furring):**
- Fasten vertical furring `16" o.c.` to masonry with masonry screws (Tapcon) or powder-actuated fasteners (Ramset/Hilti).
- Use **pressure-treated** or foam-isolated furring in direct contact with concrete to prevent wicking and rot.
- Shim to a flat plane — block walls are rarely flat.

**2. Z-furring with rigid insulation:**
- Set rigid foam (XPS/polyiso) between `7/8" or 1-1/2"` Z-channels; provides insulation + a fastening surface.

**3. Independent stud wall:**
- Frame a `2x4` wall just off the masonry, with a PT bottom plate on a sill gasket/foam, leaving a small gap for the foam/insulation. Cleanest for very out-of-plumb walls.

### Fasteners

- **Tapcon/masonry screws:** predrill with the matched carbide bit; don't over-torque.
- **Powder-actuated tools:** require training; wear eye and ear protection (OSHA 1926). Test-fire to set proper pin penetration.

### Hanging & Finishing

- Use **mold-resistant board** (USG Mold Tough) in basements — humidity is unavoidable.
- Keep board `1/2"` off the slab; never let drywall touch concrete (wicks water).
- Insulate the cavity appropriately for the climate and seal the top plate to limit air movement.

### Common Mistakes

- Furring strips fastened to a damp wall with no moisture break → mold and rot.
- Untreated wood on concrete → decay.
- Standard paper board in a basement → mold at the first humid season.

Plan the wall assembly as a system: drainage, vapor control, insulation, framing, then board.

title: Curved Drywall & Arches: Wetting, Bending & Double-Layer
content:
## Bending Drywall for Arches and Curved Walls

Curved walls, barrel ceilings, and archways require board that bends without cracking. Method depends on the radius.

### Know Your Minimum Bend Radius (Dry)

Per USG/GA data, the minimum DRY bend radius for standard board (lengthwise, perpendicular to framing):

- `1/4"` board: ~`5 ft` radius
- `3/8"` board: ~`7.5 ft` radius
- `1/2"` board: ~`10 ft` radius (`20 ft` widthwise)
- `5/8"` board: ~`15 ft` radius

Tighter radii than these require wetting, scoring, or special flexible board.

### Tight Curves — Use Flexible Board

- **USG Sheetrock Flexible** or **National Gypsum High Flex `1/4"`** bends to about a `15"` radius (double-layered) and is the easiest path for tight arches.
- Apply in **two `1/4"` layers** for strength on tight curves, staggering joints and laminating with screws/adhesive.

### Wet-Bending Technique

- Lightly wet the **compression (concave) face** with a sponge/roller — score the back paper for very tight bends if needed.
- Let water penetrate ~`1 hour` until the board is pliable.
- Bend gently around the framed form and fasten; let it dry in place to lock the curve, then it stiffens.
- Don't soak it — too much water destroys the core.

### Framing the Curve

- Build a curved framework: kerf-cut wood plates or **flexible track** (steel track with the flanges snipped to curve, e.g., Flex-C Trac).
- Space studs/blocking **closer (12" o.c. or tighter)** on curves so the board follows a smooth arc, not flat facets.
- The smoother the framing, the smoother the finished curve.

### Archways

- For the underside (intrados) of an arch, `1/4"` flexible board bends easily.
- Finish the curved outside corners with **flexible/archway corner bead** (Trim-Tex Magnum 360 flexible bead or vinyl arch bead) — metal bead won't follow the curve.
- Tape inside transitions with paper tape; mesh + setting compound on the bead.

### Finishing

- Skim the curve smooth; sand carefully to keep the arc fair (no flat spots).
- Inspect under raking light — facets and bumps show badly on curves.
- Prime and paint; gloss reveals every imperfection, so keep sheen low if the curve isn't perfect.
estimated_time: Half to full day per arch/curve

title: Cabinet Painting & Refinishing: Conversion Varnish & Urethane Enamel
content:
## Refinishing Kitchen Cabinets for a Factory Finish

Cabinets are the hardest interior finish to get right — they're touched constantly and viewed up close. The goal is a hard, smooth, durable film with no brush marks.

### Coating Choices

- **Waterborne urethane enamel (Sherwin-Williams Emerald Urethane Trim Enamel, Benjamin Moore Advance):** the best DIY/refinish-shop choice — self-levels, blocks well, cleans up with water, cures hard over ~2-3 weeks.
- **Conversion varnish / post-catalyzed lacquer (Sherwin ML Campbell, M.L. Campbell Krystal):** the true factory finish — extremely hard and chemical-resistant, but **2-component, high-VOC, requires spray + proper respirator (organic vapor) and ventilation**. Shop or controlled-spray only.
- **Pre-cat lacquer:** sprays fast, dries fast; less durable than conversion varnish but good for cabinet refinishing.

### Prep — 80% of the Job

1. Label and remove doors, drawers, and hardware.
2. Clean thoroughly with a degreaser (TSP substitute or Krud Kutter) — kitchen grease is the #1 cause of adhesion failure.
3. **Scuff-sand** all surfaces with 220-grit; on slick factory finishes, sand and use a **bonding primer**.
4. Fill grain/dents; sand smooth.
5. Prime with a **bonding/stain-blocking primer** (Zinsser BIN shellac for tannin-prone oak/knots, or STIX bonding primer for slick surfaces).

### Spraying for a Smooth Finish

- Spray with an **HVLP or fine-finish airless** (Graco with a fine-finish tip, e.g., 210-310) for the smoothest film.
- Set up a clean, dust-controlled spray area; horizontal racks for doors.
- Apply **2-3 thin coats**, sanding lightly (320-400) between coats; tack off dust each time.
- If brushing/rolling, use a fine microfiber roller + quality brush (Purdy) and a self-leveling enamel; mist with extender (Floetrol/water per product) sparingly.

### Curing & Reassembly

- Wait until the coating is **dry to handle** before flipping; full block resistance takes days to weeks (urethane enamels). Don't stack or close doors hard too soon.
- Add felt bumpers; reinstall hardware after cure.

### Safety

Conversion varnish and lacquers are flammable, high-VOC, and require an **organic-vapor respirator (NIOSH)**, eye protection, and strong ventilation; follow OSHA 1910.134 and product SDS.

title: Wood Staining & Sealing: Conditioner, Stain & Topcoat
content:
## Staining and Sealing Wood Trim and Doors

A great stain job is even, blotch-free, and protected by the right topcoat. Species and prep dictate the process.

### Sanding & Prep

- Sand progressively to **150-180 grit** for stain (finer than that can burnish and reduce stain uptake).
- Sand with the grain; remove all cross-grain scratches — they show as dark streaks after staining.
- Vacuum and tack off all dust.

### Wood Conditioner (Critical for Softwoods)

- **Pine, maple, birch, alder, and poplar blotch** badly. Apply a **pre-stain wood conditioner** (Minwax, Varathane) and stain within the product's window (often 15 min - 2 hr) for even color.
- Oak and walnut are more forgiving and usually skip conditioner.

### Applying Stain

- **Oil-based stain (Minwax, Old Masters):** long open time, easy to wipe even, rich color. Wipe excess **with the grain** after the dwell time stated on the can.
- **Gel stain:** sits on the surface — great for blotch-prone wood, fiberglass doors, and refinishing over existing finish.
- **Water-based stain:** low odor, fast dry, raises grain (sand lightly between).
- Test on a scrap or hidden area; layer coats for deeper color, allowing full dry between.

### Sealing / Topcoat

Choose by exposure and desired sheen:

- **Oil-based polyurethane (Minwax):** durable, amber-warm, slow dry — great for floors and trim.
- **Water-based polyurethane (Bona, Varathane):** clear/non-yellowing, fast dry — best where you want to keep the wood's true color.
- **Conversion varnish / pre-cat lacquer:** for sprayed cabinets and high-durability millwork.
- Apply **2-3 thin coats**, scuff-sanding with **320-grit** between coats; final coat un-sanded for the chosen sheen.

### Tips

- Maintain a wet edge and work in manageable lengths on long trim.
- Stir stain frequently — pigment settles and color drifts.
- For exterior wood, use exterior-rated penetrating stain/sealer (Sikkens/PPG ProLuxe, Cabot) and avoid film-forming interior poly outdoors.
- Dispose of oily rags safely — **lay flat to dry or submerge in water**; bunched oily rags self-combust.

title: New-Construction PVA Prime & Spray Production
content:
## Priming and Spraying New Construction

New drywall is thirsty and uneven in porosity. The standard production approach is to spray a **PVA drywall primer** to seal and equalize the surface, then spray finish coats.

### Why PVA Primer

- **PVA (polyvinyl acetate) drywall primer-sealer** is formulated for fresh gypsum: it seals the porous paper and joint compound so the topcoat lays out evenly and you avoid **joint banding/flashing** (shiny joints, dull field).
- Products: Sherwin-Williams ProMar 200 Latex Primer / PVA, PPG Speedhide PVA, Glidden PVA.
- **Note:** for critical-light walls, dark colors, or Level 5, upgrade to a high-build/quality acrylic primer — cheap PVA alone can let joints photograph.

### Spray Setup

- Use an **airless sprayer** sized for the job (Graco Ultra Max / Mark V) with the right tip: roughly a **`0.017-0.021` tip** for primer/wall paint.
- Strain the primer; keep filters clean to avoid tip spitting.
- Maintain `2,000-3,000 psi` as needed for a clean fan; adjust to eliminate tails.

### Production Sequence

1. Confirm drywall is finished, sanded, and **dust-wiped/vacuumed** — primer over dust = adhesion and texture problems.
2. Mask floors, windows, and pre-finished surfaces. In new construction, spray before trim/finish floors when possible.
3. **Spray ceilings first** (flat ceiling paint), then walls with primer.
4. **Back-roll** the primer where specified — back-rolling works primer into the texture, improves adhesion, and evens sheen.
5. Inspect under work lights; spot-prime repairs.

### Finish Coats

- After primer dries, spray two finish coats (or spray-and-back-roll) of the specified wall paint.
- Keep a wet edge; overlap fans 50%; consistent gun distance (`10-12"`) and speed prevent striping.
- Maintain adequate ventilation and temperature (most coatings need `>50°F` and surfaces dry).

### Quality & Efficiency

- Spraying is fast but produces overspray — contain it and protect adjacent trades.
- Box paint (intermix buckets) for color consistency across a large job.
- Wear a respirator for spray application (atomized mist); follow OSHA 1910.134 and product VOC/SDS.

title: Wallpaper Removal & Wall Prep for Paint
content:
## Removing Wallpaper and Prepping for Paint

Wallpaper removal is messy and unpredictable. Done carelessly, it gouges the drywall and leaves adhesive that ruins the new paint. Patience and proper sealing are everything.

### Identify the Paper and Wall

- **Strippable/peelable** modern papers may pull off dry — test a corner.
- **Plaster vs. drywall:** plaster tolerates water; **drywall is vulnerable** — too much water/soaking delaminates the paper face. Work in sections, don't flood it.
- Check whether the wall was primed before papering. Unprimed drywall makes removal much harder and damage more likely.

### Removal Methods

1. **Score** the surface with a scoring tool (Paper Tiger) so solution penetrates — light pressure; don't gouge the wall.
2. **Soak** with hot water + wallpaper remover (DIF gel/enzyme) or a steamer. Let it dwell to dissolve the adhesive.
3. **Scrape** with a 4"-6" broad knife at a low angle — lift, don't dig.
4. Work top-down in sections; re-wet stubborn spots rather than forcing.

### The Critical Step — Remove ALL Adhesive

- Leftover paste is glossy/slick and **reactivates under waterborne paint**, causing bubbling and poor adhesion.
- Wash the wall with hot water + a little remover or TSP substitute; squeegee and rinse until it **no longer feels slick** when dry.
- Run your hand across the dry wall — tacky/glossy = paste remains.

### Repair & Prime

- Skim-coat any torn paper face, gouges, or delaminated areas with joint compound; sand smooth.
- **Seal torn drywall paper** with an oil/shellac or specialty primer (Zinsser Gardz penetrating sealer is ideal over residual paste and torn paper — it locks down both).
- Apply an **oil or shellac-based primer (Zinsser Cover Stain / BIN)** if any adhesive residue or stains remain; latex over paste can bubble.

### Finish

- After primer, skim/sand any remaining flaws to the required level, then prime patches again.
- Topcoat with the specified wall paint. Inspect under raking light before painting — wallpaper jobs hide flaws until the paint goes on.

Never paint directly over wallpaper unless it's truly impossible to remove; if so, seal seams, skim, and prime with a stain-blocker, and warn the client of the risk.

title: Epoxy Garage Floor Coating Systems
content:
## Installing an Epoxy Garage Floor Coating

A garage floor coating is only as good as the concrete prep. Most failures (peeling, hot-tire pickup) come from skipping profiling or coating over moisture.

### Test the Slab First

- **Moisture test (ASTM D4263 plastic-sheet or calcium chloride):** tape a 2x2 plastic sheet down overnight; condensation underneath means the slab is too wet to coat. New slabs need to cure **28+ days**.
- **Check for prior sealer:** sprinkle water — if it beads instead of soaking in, a sealer is present and must be removed or the epoxy won't bond.

### Surface Preparation (the make-or-break step)

- **Mechanical profile** to a concrete surface profile of roughly **CSP 2-3** (ICRI guideline): diamond grinding or shot-blasting is the professional standard.
- **Acid etching** (muriatic/citric) is the minimum DIY method but inferior — it doesn't remove sealers and can leave residue. Grinding is strongly preferred.
- Repair cracks and spalls with an epoxy/polymer patch; degrease oil stains thoroughly.
- Vacuum to a dust-free surface.

### Coating System

A durable system is multi-coat, not a single big-box kit:

- **Primer/base coat:** penetrating epoxy primer for adhesion.
- **Build coat:** 100%-solids epoxy (high-solids commercial epoxy like Sherwin-Williams ArmorSeal, or a quality kit) — far more durable than water-based 1-part kits.
- **Broadcast** decorative flakes (optional) into the wet base for traction and looks; sweep excess after cure.
- **Topcoat:** clear polyaspartic or polyurethane for UV stability, chemical/abrasion resistance, and hot-tire resistance.

### Application

- Mix 2-part epoxy precisely by ratio; respect the **pot life** — mixed epoxy in the bucket heats and gels fast.
- Roll with a `3/8"` nap; maintain a wet edge; cut in edges first.
- Watch **temperature and humidity** windows per the product — too cold won't cure, too hot kills pot life.

### Cure & Safety

- Foot traffic typically `24 hr`, vehicle traffic `72 hr`+ (product-specific).
- Epoxies and solvents are irritants/sensitizers: wear nitrile gloves, eye protection, and an **organic-vapor respirator** with ventilation per OSHA 1910.134 and the SDS.
- Add anti-slip aggregate to the topcoat — cured epoxy is slick when wet.

title: Masonry & Elastomeric Coatings for Stucco and CMU
content:
## Coating Masonry, Stucco, and CMU

Masonry is alkaline, porous, and prone to cracking and efflorescence. Use coatings designed for it, and respect cure times on new concrete/stucco.

### Let It Cure and Check pH

- New concrete, stucco, and masonry must **cure ~28 days** before coating.
- Fresh masonry is highly **alkaline**; topcoats applied too soon can saponify/fail. Test pH (target generally below ~10) or use an alkali-resistant primer/block filler.

### Surface Prep

- Remove dirt, chalk, efflorescence, and loose material — wire brush, then wash (pressure wash where appropriate). See efflorescence remediation for salt deposits.
- Repair cracks: hairline cracks can be bridged by elastomeric; structural/moving cracks need proper sealant or routing-and-caulking first.
- Prime bare CMU/concrete block with a **block filler** (Sherwin-Williams PrepRite / Loxon Block Surfacer) to fill pinholes and pores before topcoat.

### Coating Choices

- **Acrylic masonry primer/sealer (Sherwin Loxon, Behr masonry primer):** alkali- and efflorescence-resistant primer for stucco/concrete.
- **Elastomeric coating (Sherwin Loxon XP, Behr Premium Plus Masonry, Sto):** a thick, flexible, high-build film (often `10-20 mil` dry) that **bridges hairline cracks** and waterproofs stucco walls. Excellent for crack-prone stucco.
- **Acrylic masonry paint:** breathable, durable standard topcoat where elastomeric isn't needed.

### When Elastomeric — and When NOT

- **Use** elastomeric on crack-prone stucco/EIFS and where waterproofing/crack-bridging is needed.
- **Avoid** trapping moisture: elastomeric is low-perm. On walls with moisture intrusion from behind (rising damp, no drainage), a thick elastomeric film can trap water and blister. Ensure the wall can dry, or use a more breathable acrylic.

### Application

- Apply by roller (heavy `1/2"-3/4"` nap) or spray-and-back-roll to achieve the **specified mil thickness** — elastomerics are sold by coverage rate to hit the film build; don't over-thin or over-spread.
- Two coats typical; respect recoat and temperature windows (`>50°F`, dropping overnight temps matter).
- Work cohesive areas to avoid lap marks on textured stucco.

### Safety

Wear eye protection and a respirator for spray; masonry coatings and washing chemicals are irritants — follow product SDS and OSHA respiratory guidance.

title: DTM & Rust-Prevention Metal Coatings
content:
## Coating Metal: DTM and Rust Prevention

Metal coatings fail without proper surface prep and the right primer. The standard for prep is the **SSPC/NACE** system; the topcoat workhorse for many jobs is a **DTM (Direct-to-Metal) acrylic**.

### Surface Preparation (SSPC Standards)

- **SSPC-SP1 Solvent Cleaning:** remove oil/grease first — always the first step.
- **SSPC-SP2/SP3 Hand/Power Tool Cleaning:** remove loose rust, mill scale, and old coating for mild service.
- **SSPC-SP6 Commercial Blast / SP10 Near-White Blast:** abrasive blasting for severe environments and industrial coatings — the gold standard for adhesion.
- Establish a surface **profile (anchor pattern)** so primer keys in.
- Feather sound existing coating edges; spot-prime bare metal.

### Treating Existing Rust

- Remove flaking rust mechanically (wire wheel, grinder, sandblast).
- For tight residual rust, use a **rust-converter** (phosphoric-acid based) or a **rust-inhibitive primer** (zinc-rich for steel in harsh service; Rust-Oleum, Sherwin Kem Kromik / Pro Industrial Pro-Cryl primer).
- Never coat over loose/active rust — it will lift the coating.

### Primers and Topcoats

- **Galvanized/aluminum:** these are slick and reactive — use a **galvanized/self-etching or DTM bonding primer**; ordinary alkyd primers saponify on galv.
- **DTM acrylic (Sherwin Pro Industrial DTM, PPG):** primer + topcoat in one for many railings, doors, and equipment — moderate corrosion resistance, easy cleanup.
- **Epoxy primer + urethane topcoat:** for severe/industrial corrosion (see commercial coatings).
- **Oil/alkyd enamels:** good leveling on metal trim/handrails but slower cure and higher VOC.

### Application

- Apply within the steel's clean window — bare blasted steel flash-rusts within hours; prime quickly.
- Respect **dew point**: surface temp must be at least `5°F above dew point` or moisture condenses under the film and causes failure.
- Hit the specified dry-film thickness (DFT); check with a gauge on industrial work.
- Two coats minimum for exterior/exposed metal.

### Safety

Blasting, grinding, and solvent coatings require eye/respiratory protection (silica/lead in old coatings is a hazard — test pre-1978 painted metal). Follow OSHA 1910.134, SSPC safety, and product SDS.

title: HVLP Fine Finishing & Spray Booth Technique
content:
## HVLP Fine Finishing for Doors, Cabinets, and Trim

HVLP (High Volume, Low Pressure) delivers the smoothest, most controlled finish with the least overspray — ideal for cabinets, doors, furniture, and fine millwork.

### HVLP vs. Airless

- **HVLP** atomizes at low pressure (`~10 psi at the cap`) with high air volume from a turbine or compressor — superior atomization, low overspray, excellent for fine finishes and small/medium work.
- **Airless** is faster for big square footage (walls, exteriors) but coarser atomization.
- For factory-smooth enamel and lacquer, HVLP (turbine units like Fuji Q-series, or a quality gravity gun) wins.

### Setup

- Match the **needle/nozzle (fluid tip)** to the coating viscosity: smaller tips (`1.0-1.3 mm`) for thin lacquers/sealers, larger (`1.4-1.8 mm`) for heavier enamels.
- **Thin/reduce** the material per the product to the gun's recommended viscosity (use a viscosity cup); waterborne enamels often need a little reducer/extender to spray glass-smooth.
- Set fluid, fan, and air controls; test on cardboard until the pattern is even with no fingers or spitting.

### Spray Technique

- Hold the gun **6-8"** from the surface, **perpendicular**, moving parallel — don't arc your wrist.
- **Overlap each pass 50%** and keep consistent speed.
- Trigger before the edge and release after — start/stop off the part to keep edges even.
- Apply **multiple light coats**, not one heavy coat; sand lightly (`320-400`) between coats and tack off.

### Spray Booth / Clean Environment

- Control dust and overspray — a booth or a clean, plastic-sheeted area with filtered exhaust.
- **Filtered intake and exhaust** keep dust out of the wet film; cross-draft or downdraft airflow carries overspray away from the work.
- Light the work well to see the wet film and catch runs.
- Rack doors/parts horizontally to avoid sags while flashing off.

### Maintenance

- Clean the gun immediately and completely after use — disassemble the tip/needle/cap; dried finish ruins atomization.
- Keep air caps free of buildup (a clogged cap causes pattern distortion).

### Safety

Atomized coatings and solvents demand an **organic-vapor respirator** (or supplied air for lacquers/CV), eye protection, and adequate ventilation. Spray booths must meet fire/electrical codes (explosion-proof fixtures, NFPA 33). Follow OSHA 1910.107/1910.134.

title: Lead-Safe RRP Practices for Pre-1978 Homes (EPA)
content:
## Lead-Safe Renovation, Repair & Painting (RRP)

Disturbing paint in homes built **before 1978** can release lead dust — a serious neurotoxin, especially to children. The **EPA RRP Rule (40 CFR Part 745, Subpart E)** legally governs this work.

### When the Rule Applies

- Renovation, repair, or painting that **disturbs more than 6 sq ft of interior** or **20 sq ft of exterior** painted surface, or any window replacement, in pre-1978 housing and child-occupied facilities.
- The firm must be **EPA Lead-Safe Certified**, and at least one **Certified Renovator** must be on site or available to direct the work.
- Provide the **EPA "Renovate Right"** pamphlet to owners/occupants before starting.

### Testing

- Use EPA-recognized **lead test kits** (3M LeadCheck, D-Lead) or have an inspector test with XRF.
- If you don't test, you must **assume lead is present** and follow RRP fully.

### Lead-Safe Work Practices

1. **Contain the area:** post signs, plastic sheeting on floors/surfaces, seal doorways and HVAC vents. Exterior: ground cover extending out from the wall, vertical containment near neighbors.
2. **Control dust — no prohibited practices:** **NO open-flame burning/torching, NO power sanding/grinding/planing without HEPA attachment, NO heat guns above 1,100°F.** These are banned by RRP.
3. Mist surfaces before scraping; use **HEPA-filtered** tools with shrouds for any power removal.
4. Keep workers and bystanders (especially kids/pregnant women) out of the work area.

### Cleanup & Verification

- HEPA-vacuum all surfaces, then wet-wipe, then HEPA-vacuum again.
- Perform the **cleaning verification** (white disposable cloth vs. EPA verification card) before re-occupancy.
- Bag waste in heavy plastic, goose-neck sealed; dispose per local regulations.

### Worker Protection (OSHA 1926.62)

- Wear a **NIOSH respirator (P100)**, disposable coveralls, and gloves; remove/launder separately to avoid take-home lead.
- No eating, drinking, or smoking in the work area; wash hands/face before breaks.
- OSHA may require **blood-lead monitoring** depending on exposure.

### Recordkeeping

Keep certification, the signed pamphlet receipt, and documentation of lead-safe practices for **3 years**. Penalties for non-compliance are steep. When in doubt on a pre-1978 home, test or assume lead and work safe.

title: Caulking & Sealant Selection for Paint Work
content:
## Choosing and Applying the Right Caulk and Sealant

The wrong caulk cracks, shrinks, or won't take paint — a callback waiting to happen. Match the sealant to the joint, the movement, and whether it gets painted.

### Sealant Types

- **Acrylic latex caulk:** general interior trim gaps; cheap, easy, paintable, water cleanup — but limited movement and not for wet areas.
- **Siliconized acrylic / "painter's caulk" (DAP Alex Plus, Sherwin):** the interior workhorse — paintable, decent flexibility for trim, baseboards, and crown.
- **Elastomeric acrylic/urethane hybrid (Sherwin SherMax, DAP Dynaflex, Big Stretch):** high movement (`±25-50%`) for exterior siding gaps, large joints, and crack-prone areas; paintable, durable. Best exterior painter's sealant.
- **Polyurethane sealant (Sikaflex, NP1):** very durable, high movement, excellent adhesion for exterior structural joints — paintable, but slower cure and messier.
- **100% silicone:** best for tubs, showers, and plumbing — but **NOT paintable**; never use silicone where paint must adhere.
- **Backer rod + sealant:** for joints over `~1/4"` wide/deep, install closed-cell backer rod first to control depth and avoid 3-sided adhesion.

### Where Each Goes

- **Interior trim/baseboard/crown:** paintable siliconized acrylic.
- **Exterior siding, trim, and corner gaps:** elastomeric/urethane hybrid for weather and movement.
- **Tubs/showers/sinks:** 100% silicone (mildew-resistant), never painted.
- **Dynamic joints (siding to brick, large gaps):** polyurethane with backer rod.

### Application

- Cut the tip small (`1/8"`) for trim; size to the bead you need.
- **Tool the bead** with a wet finger or caulk tool immediately for adhesion and a clean concave profile.
- Caulk gaps before painting (paintable types); caulking after paint leaves a shiny line.
- Don't over-caulk weep holes, drainage gaps, or the bottom of horizontal siding laps — those need to drain.

### Cure Before Paint

- Let caulk **skin/cure** per the label before painting (latex types accept paint quickly; some need hours).
- Painting too soon can cause cracking and adhesion issues.
- In cold weather, use a sealant rated for the temperature; many caulks won't cure below `40°F`.

Good caulking is invisible and lasts; sloppy caulking telegraphs and fails first.

title: Estimating Paint: Coverage, Coats & Labor
content:
## Estimating Paint Quantities and Labor

Accurate estimates protect margin and credibility. Calculate paintable area, apply realistic coverage and coat counts, then build labor and add for prep.

### Measure Paintable Area

- **Walls:** perimeter x wall height. Subtract large openings (doors ~`21 sf` each, average windows ~`15 sf`) — or leave them in as a cushion for cut-in time on small jobs.
- **Ceilings:** length x width.
- **Trim:** estimate by linear foot; convert to area or use a per-LF labor rate.
- Don't forget closets, stairwells (extra height/access), and accent walls.

### Coverage Rates

- Quality interior paint covers roughly **350-400 sq ft per gallon** on smooth, primed drywall.
- **Textured, porous, or rough surfaces** (stucco, popcorn, block) drop to `200-300 sf/gal` or less — increase your estimate.
- **Primer** coverage is similar but rougher surfaces eat more.
- Always check the **manufacturer's spread rate** on the can and adjust for surface.

### Coats

- Plan **2 finish coats** as the standard for a quality, uniform job.
- Add a **primer coat** for new drywall, bare wood, repairs, stain-blocking, and drastic color changes.
- **Deep/saturated colors and white-over-dark** often need an extra coat or a tinted primer — budget for it.

### The Formula

- Gallons = (total paintable area x number of coats) ÷ coverage rate. Round up and add a partial gallon for touch-ups.
- Box (intermix) paint across a job for color consistency.

### Labor

- Estimate by production rate or square foot. Cutting in, rolling, prep, and masking are separate time drivers.
- **Prep is the variable that wrecks bids** — sanding, patching, caulking, washing, and wallpaper/old-finish removal can exceed painting time. Walk the job and price prep honestly.
- Add for **height/access** (scaffold, lifts, stairwells), trim detail, dark colors (extra coats), and protection/masking of finished spaces.

### Build the Bid

- Line items: materials (paint, primer, sundries — tape, plastic, caulk, sandpaper), labor by task, access equipment, and overhead/margin.
- State assumptions, number of coats, and exclusions clearly on the proposal.
- Add **contingency** for unknown substrate conditions on repaints.

title: Deck Staining & Restoration
content:
## Staining and Restoring Wood Decks

Decks take brutal UV, moisture, and foot traffic. The keys to a lasting finish are thorough cleaning, correct stain type, and never over-applying film on a horizontal walking surface.

### Assess and Clean

- **Strip old failing finish:** peeling/film-forming stains must come off with a deck stripper and stiff brush/pressure wash, or the new coat won't bond.
- **Clean** the wood with a deck cleaner (oxygenated or percarbonate) to remove dirt, mildew, and graying.
- **Brighten:** after cleaning (especially after stripping), apply an **oxalic-acid wood brightener** to neutralize, restore pH, and open the grain for better stain penetration.
- **Sand** rough spots and feathered edges; remove splinters.

### Critical: Let It Dry

- The deck must be **dry (typically 24-48 hr of dry weather, MC below ~15%)** before staining. Staining wet wood traps moisture and causes peeling.
- Test by sprinkling water — if it soaks in, the wood is dry and ready; if it beads, an old sealer remains.

### Choose the Right Stain

- **Penetrating/transparent or semi-transparent oil stains (TWP, Penofin, Cabot, Sikkens/PPG ProLuxe):** soak into the wood, show the grain, wear by fading rather than peeling — **best for horizontal deck boards**.
- **Semi-solid/solid stains:** more pigment, more protection and hide, but more prone to peeling on high-wear walking surfaces; better on railings/vertical and weathered wood.
- **Avoid film-forming "deck paints" on walking surfaces** unless using a true deck-resurfacing product — they peel under traffic.

### Application

- Apply with a stain pad, brush, or sprayer **+ back-brush** to work it into the grain.
- **Maintain a wet edge** and do **full boards end-to-end** (board by board) to avoid lap marks.
- **Don't over-apply penetrating stain** — wipe excess that doesn't absorb within the product's window, or it gets sticky/shiny and fails.
- Coat the end grain and between boards where water sits.

### Conditions & Maintenance

- Stain in mild weather (`50-90°F`), out of direct hot sun, no rain for 24-48 hr.
- Reapply penetrating stain every `1-3 years` on horizontal surfaces (sun exposure dependent).
- Sweep and clean annually; spot-recoat high-wear paths.

### Safety

Oily stain rags self-combust — **dry flat or submerge**. Wear gloves/eye protection for strippers, brighteners (acids), and cleaners; follow SDS.

title: Mildew & Efflorescence Remediation Before Painting
content:
## Removing Mildew and Efflorescence Before You Paint

Two common surface problems guarantee paint failure if painted over: **mildew** (living fungus) and **efflorescence** (mineral salts). Neither can be sealed in — both must be removed and the cause addressed.

### Mildew — Identify First

- Mildew looks like dirt but is **black/green/gray fungal growth**, common in shaded, humid, north-facing, and bathroom areas.
- **Test:** dab household bleach on a spot — if it **lightens/disappears**, it's mildew; if it stays, it's dirt.
- **Painting over mildew = it grows right back through the new paint.**

### Removing Mildew

- Wash with a **mildewcide solution**: roughly 1 part household bleach to 3 parts water (or a commercial mildew remover like Jomax/Concrobium). Wear gloves and eye protection; never mix bleach with ammonia.
- Scrub, let dwell, rinse thoroughly, and let dry completely.
- **Fix the moisture source:** improve ventilation (bath fan), correct gutters/drainage, trim vegetation for sun and airflow.
- Repaint with a paint containing a **mildewcide / mildew-resistant additive** (Sherwin Emerald, BM Aura Bath & Spa, or add a mildewcide to the can).

### Efflorescence — White Salt Deposits

- Efflorescence is a **white, powdery/crystalline crust** on masonry, brick, concrete, and stucco — soluble salts carried to the surface as water evaporates.
- It signals **moisture moving through the masonry** — paint applied over it will be pushed off as more salts crystallize beneath.

### Removing Efflorescence

- Brush off dry deposits with a **stiff (non-metallic) brush**; light cases can be dry-scrubbed.
- For stubborn deposits, wash with water; if needed, use a **diluted muriatic acid** masonry cleaner per directions — **always add acid to water, wear acid-resistant gloves/goggles/respirator**, pre-wet the wall, and neutralize/rinse thoroughly afterward.
- **Address the water source** — the salts return until moisture intrusion stops (sealing exterior, fixing leaks, drainage).
- Allow the masonry to dry, then prime with an **alkali-/efflorescence-resistant masonry primer** (Sherwin Loxon) before topcoat.

### Don't Just Paint Over It

The #1 mistake is coating over mildew or efflorescence to "hide" it. Both are symptoms of moisture. Remediate the growth/salts, **fix the underlying moisture**, then prime with the correct product and topcoat. Otherwise you'll repaint the same failure within a season.

### Safety

Bleach and acid washes are hazardous — eye/skin/respiratory protection, ventilation, and SDS compliance (OSHA 1910.132/1910.134). Never combine cleaning chemicals.

title: Commercial & Industrial Coating Systems
content:
## Specifying Commercial and Industrial Coatings

Commercial and industrial environments demand coatings engineered for chemical, abrasion, corrosion, and sanitation requirements far beyond residential paint. The system (primer + intermediate + topcoat) matters more than any single product.

### Match the Coating to the Environment

- **High-traffic walls (corridors, schools, hospitals):** waterborne **epoxy** or acrylic-epoxy (Sherwin Pro Industrial Pre-Catalyzed Epoxy / Water-Based Catalyzed Epoxy) — scrubbable, durable, tile-like.
- **Wet/sanitary areas (kitchens, locker rooms, food processing):** catalyzed epoxy for moisture and frequent washdown; meet **USDA/FDA** incidental-contact requirements where food is present.
- **Steel structures/equipment (corrosion service):** **zinc-rich primer + epoxy intermediate + polyurethane/polyaspartic topcoat** — the classic 3-coat industrial system for severe environments.
- **Floors:** epoxy/polyaspartic systems (see garage floor article) sized to the chemical/traffic load.
- **Tank linings/immersion service:** specialized immersion-grade epoxies/novolacs — manufacturer-specified only.

### Surface Prep Drives Performance

- Follow **SSPC/NACE** standards: SP1 solvent clean, then SP6 commercial blast or SP10 near-white blast for steel in aggressive service.
- Establish the specified **anchor profile**; coat blasted steel before flash-rust.
- Concrete: profile to the required **ICRI CSP**, address moisture and laitance.

### Application Controls

- Hit the specified **dry-film thickness (DFT)** per coat — measure with a wet-film gauge during application and a DFT gauge after cure on industrial work.
- Respect **dew point** (surface `≥5°F above dew point`), temperature, humidity, and recoat windows; out-of-window recoats need a tie-coat or abrading.
- Mix 2-component products by exact ratio; honor **pot life** and induction time.
- Maintain coating data sheets and a QC log (DFT readings, ambient conditions) — owners/specs often require documentation.

### Project & Code Considerations

- **Low-VOC compliance:** many commercial specs and jurisdictions cap VOCs (SCAQMD, OTC, 40 CFR 59); specify compliant products.
- Schedule around facility operations — odor, overspray, and cure times affect occupied buildings.
- Coordinate containment and ventilation; many industrial coatings require forced air and confined-space procedures.

### Safety

Industrial coatings carry serious hazards: isocyanates (urethanes), solvents, blasting silica, confined spaces. Require **supplied-air or proper organic-vapor respirators**, monitoring, and OSHA compliance (1910.134, confined-space 1910.146). Always work to the SDS and the coating manufacturer's published system.

title: Installing Standing-Seam Metal Roofing (McElroy/Englert)
content:
## Standing-Seam Metal Roof Installation

Standing-seam systems run vertical panels with raised, interlocking seams that hide all fasteners. This guide covers mechanically-seamed and snap-lock systems from **McElroy Metal (Maxima, Medallion-Lok)** and **Englert (Series 1300/2500)**.

### Panel Selection & Specs

- **Snap-lock** (Medallion-Lok, Englert 1300): field-formed clip engagement, ideal for slopes **3:12 and steeper**.
- **Mechanical seam** (McElroy Maxima 180/360, Englert 2500): for low slope down to **1/4:12** when seams are field-crimped 90 or 180 degrees.
- Standard panel: **24-gauge** Galvalume AZ50/AZ55, 16 in. or 18 in. on-center seams, Kynar 500 PVDF finish.
- Verify **UL 580 Class 90** uplift rating and **ASTM E1592** structural performance for the project wind zone.

### Prep & Underlayment

Metal demands a clean, dry deck. Install a **high-temp self-adhered underlayment** (rated to 240F) such as ice-and-water at eaves/valleys per `R905.1.1`, then a synthetic over the field. Snap a chalk line square to the eave; metal magnifies any deck irregularity, so shim humps.

### Installation Sequence

- Set **eave trim/cleat** and hem the panel bottom over it for wind resistance.
- Lay the first panel dead-square; misalignment compounds across the roof.
- Fasten **concealed clips** at every purlin/spacing (typ. 12-24 in. O.C.) with `#10` pancake screws. Use **floating clips** on runs over 30 ft to allow thermal movement (steel moves ~1 in. per 100 ft per 100F swing).
- Engage the next panel's female leg over the male; snap-lock by foot pressure, mechanical by electric seamer (D.I. seamer for Maxima).
- **Do not face-fasten** field panels. Pin panels at one end only (typ. the ridge end) so they expand toward the eave.

### Penetrations & Closures

Use **Dektite/EPDM pipe boots** rated for metal. At ridge, install closed-cell **foam closures** and a vented ridge cap. Hem and seal endwall/headwall flashings; never rely on sealant alone — sealant is a backup to a hemmed mechanical lap.

### Best-Practice Notes

- **Never walk** in the pan center; step in the flat near seams over supports.
- Leave the strippable film on until the day of install; UV bakes it on.
- Use **stainless or coated fasteners** to avoid galvanic corrosion; never mix copper or treated-lumber contact with bare Galvalume.
- Field-cut with shears or a nibbler — **never an abrasive blade**, which throws hot swarf that rusts and voids finish warranty.

A properly clipped standing-seam roof carries a 30-50 year service life and qualifies for `ASTM D3161`/UL 580 wind documentation for insurance and code submittal.

title: Concrete & Clay Tile Roof Installation
content:
## Concrete & Clay Tile Roofing

Tile roofs offer 50+ year life but impose **9-12 psf (concrete)** to **6-10 psf (clay)** dead loads, so structural verification is the first step. Confirm the framing is rated for tile per the truss/engineering documents before tear-off.

### Underlayment & Code

Tile is **water-shedding, not waterproof** — the underlayment is the true water barrier. Per `IRC R905.3`, minimum slope is **2.5:12** (with double underlayment) or **4:12** single-layer. Use a reinforced **30# felt or self-adhered high-temp** membrane. In high-wind/hurricane zones follow Florida `TAS 100` and the FRSA/TRI manual.

### Battens & Layout

- Install **1x2 wood battens** (or elevated/counter-battens for ventilation) on `4:12+` slopes; batten spacing equals the tile gauge (typ. 13.5-14.5 in. for flat/profile tile).
- **Counter-battens** create a drainage plane and prevent water damming behind tiles — strongly recommended.
- Set **eave riser/anti-ponding** trim and bird stop at the eave course.

### Setting Tile

- Load tile in stacks distributed over rafters, never concentrated.
- Each field tile is hung on the batten lug and **fastened per the wind zone**: typically one `8d` corrosion-resistant nail or screw per tile; perimeter and high-wind areas may require **two fasteners plus a foam/clip**.
- Maintain **3 in. headlap** on profile tile.
- **Mortar or mechanically attach** hip/ridge tiles over a ridge board, using weather-blocking and flexible ridge venting where required.

### Flashing & Valleys

Use **W-profile open metal valleys** (min. 0.019 in. or 26-ga, often 24-ga painted) with 11 in. each side. Pipe penetrations get lead or malleable flashing dressed to the tile profile. Headwall/sidewall flashings must be **counter-flashed** into masonry.

### Safety & Handling

- Tile is heavy and brittle — use **roof hooks/ladder hoists**, never free-climb with armloads.
- Walk on the **lower third** of each tile (over the batten/headlap) to avoid cracking.
- Cracked tiles must be replaced, not sealed; cull breakage before it becomes a leak.

### Common Failures

- Underlayment failure (the real lifespan limiter) — spec a premium membrane.
- Slipped tiles from missing lugs/fasteners.
- Mortar-only ridges cracking — modern best practice is **dry ridge systems** with mechanical fixing and roll vent.

### Hip, Valley & Eave Closures

Close the gaps under barrel and S-profile tile at eaves, hips, and rakes with **mortar-bedded closures or weather-blocking foam/eave closures** so wind-driven rain and birds cannot enter the batten cavity. Use **rake/gable trim tile** or metal rake to finish edges cleanly.

### Walk Boards & Maintenance Access

Plan permanent **walk boards or step zones** for HVAC and chimney access so service techs do not crack random field tile. Keep a stock of matching tiles on site for breakage replacement throughout the building's life.

title: Cedar Shake & Wood Shingle Roofing
content:
## Cedar Shake & Wood Shingle Installation

Western red cedar shakes (split, thick) and shingles (sawn, tapered) breathe and need airflow. Follow the **CSSB (Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau)** application standards, which `IRC R905.7/R905.8` reference.

### Grades & Slope

- Use **No. 1 Grade (Blue Label)** 100% heartwood, clear, edge-grain for roofs.
- Minimum slope: **4:12** for shakes, **3:12** for shingles per `R905.7.1`.
- Common shakes: **18 in. or 24 in. medium/heavy** hand-split & resawn.

### Ventilated Deck

Cedar must dry from both sides. Best practice is **spaced sheathing (1x4 or 1x6 boards)** spaced to the weather exposure, or a **mesh ventilation mat (Cedar Breather)** over solid sheathing. Solid decks without a vent mat trap moisture and rot the shakes prematurely.

### Underlayment & Interlayment

- Apply **30# felt** at the eave starter.
- For **shakes**, weave an **18 in. felt interlayment** between each course, set up the roof at twice the exposure — this is the signature shake detail that sheds wind-driven water.

### Application

- Double (or triple) the **starter course** at the eave.
- Exposure: **5.5 in.** for 18 in. shakes, **7.5 in.** for 24 in. shakes; **3.75-5 in.** for shingles.
- Maintain a **1/4 to 3/8 in. gap** between adjacent shakes/shingles for expansion.
- **Offset joints** at least 1.5 in. between courses; no joint aligns within three courses.
- Use **two hot-dipped galvanized or stainless ring-shank nails** per piece, placed ~1 in. from each edge and ~1-2 in. above the exposure line — never face-nail in the weather.

### Hips, Ridges, Valleys

Use **factory or site-built mitered hip/ridge units** with alternating overlaps. Valleys get **W-metal, min. 24-ga or 0.019 in.**, with cleats — never close-cut wood valleys.

### Fire & Maintenance

- Many jurisdictions require **Class B/C pressure-impregnated fire-treated** shakes (CSSB Certi-Guard).
- Keep the roof clear of debris; trapped organic matter holds moisture and breeds rot/moss.
- Expect periodic maintenance and a ~30-year life with proper ventilation.

### Preservative & Service Life

Untreated cedar grays naturally; **CCA/borate preservative treatments** and periodic oil/UV treatments extend life and resist rot and insects. Re-treat every few years in damp climates.

### Inspection Points

- Watch for **cupping, splitting, and missing fasteners** at exposed butts.
- Keep valleys and keyways clear of needles and leaves — trapped debris holds moisture against the wood and is the leading cause of premature rot.
- Verify the **vent mat or spaced sheathing** stays unobstructed so the underside can dry; blocked ventilation halves the roof's life.

title: Natural Slate Roof Installation
content:
## Natural Slate Roofing

Genuine quarried slate is the longest-lived roof covering — **75 to 150+ years** for hard S1 slate. It is unforgiving of poor detailing, so layout, fastener metallurgy, and flashing discipline are everything.

### Material & Grade

- Specify **ASTM C406 Grade S1** for maximum service life; thickness typically **3/16 to 1/4 in.** (standard) up to **3/4 in.** for graduated roofs.
- Sources: Vermont/New York (Buckingham, Vermont Structural Slate), Spanish, and Welsh slate.
- Confirm framing supports **8-15+ psf** dead load before proceeding.

### Slope & Deck

Minimum **4:12** per `IRC R905.6`; steeper is better. Install over **solid wood sheathing** (kiln-dried, min. 15/32 in.) with **30# felt** underlayment. Self-adhered ice-and-water at eaves and valleys.

### Headlap — The Critical Number

Slate sheds by headlap, not sealant. Required headlap depends on slope:

- **3 in. headlap** for 8:12 and steeper
- **4 in. headlap** for 6:12 to 8:12
- More for lower slopes

Exposure = `(length - headlap) / 2`. Snap horizontal chalk lines for every course.

### Fastening

- Use **copper or stainless steel slate nails** only — never electro-galvanized, which rusts long before the slate fails ("nail-sick" roofs).
- **Hang, do not crush**: drive nails so the head just kisses the slate. Over-driving cracks the slate and causes it to hang on the nail shank.
- Two nails per slate near the shoulders.

### Flashing & Valleys

- Use **16-20 oz copper** for valleys, step flashing, and pipe collars. Open valleys with **4 in. minimum** clearance widening toward the eave.
- Step-flash sidewalls; never use roofing cement as primary flashing.

### Repair & Walking

- Replace broken slate with a **slate ripper** and a **copper bib/hook** — never face-nail a replacement.
- Use **roof ladders/hooks and staging**; slate is slippery and breaks under careless footing. Distribute weight; walk over headlaps near supports.

A slate roof outlives the building; budget and detail it accordingly.

### Layout & Coursing Discipline

- Sort slate by **thickness** before loading; mixing thick and thin slate telegraphs as lippage and breaks the watershed plane.
- Maintain a consistent **joint offset of at least 3 in.** so no joint stacks within two courses below — stacked joints are direct leak paths.
- Start with a **canted starter course** at the eave so the first course springs to the correct angle and butts line up.
- Snap **vertical control lines** in addition to horizontals on hip and valley roofs to keep coursing true around the geometry.

A properly laid slate roof outlives the building; budget and detail it accordingly.

title: Modified-Bitumen & Built-Up Roofing (Commercial Low-Slope)
content:
## Modified-Bitumen (Mod-Bit) & Built-Up Roofing (BUR)

For commercial low-slope decks, multi-ply asphaltic systems remain a workhorse. **Mod-bit** is a factory-reinforced SBS/APP membrane; **BUR** is built up in the field from felt plies and bitumen. Both fall under `IRC R905.9/R905.11`.

### System Types

- **SBS modified** — rubberized, flexible in cold; applied by **hot asphalt mop**, **cold adhesive**, or **self-adhered (SA)**.
- **APP modified** — plastic-modified; applied by **torch (heat-weld)**.
- **BUR** — alternating plies of **fiberglass ply felt (ASTM D2178)** in **Type III/IV asphalt**, topped with gravel or a cap sheet.

### Assembly (typical 2-ply SBS)

- Mechanically fasten or adhere a **base sheet** to the deck/insulation.
- Set the **smooth interply/base ply**, fully bonding to the substrate.
- Apply the **granulated cap sheet** with staggered, half-lapped seams; roll all laps to bleed-out a continuous bitumen bead.
- Provide a **3/4 to 1 in. bleed-out** at every lap as the watertight check.

### Flashings & Details

- **Cant strips** at all wall/curb transitions to avoid sharp 90s.
- Base flashing carried **8 in. min. up walls**, with a separate cap/counter-flashing or termination bar and sealant.
- Use **flashing-grade (woven/reinforced) membrane** at corners, drains, and penetrations; target the membrane manufacturer's detail (GAF, Johns Manville, Soprema, Carlisle).

### Slope & Drainage

Minimum **1/4:12** positive slope per `R905.9.1`. Tapered ISO insulation builds slope to drains; **no ponding** beyond 48 hours.

### Safety — Torch & Kettle

- **Torch-applied APP** requires a fire watch, hot-work permit, and an extinguisher within reach; **2-hour post-job fire watch** is standard practice to catch smoldering.
- Hot asphalt kettles: maintain temp below the flash point, use the **EVT (equiviscous temperature)** range, full PPE (face shield, gauntlet gloves, long sleeves) — asphalt burns are severe.
- Never torch directly against combustible walls or wood; use a non-combustible base ply transition.

Properly installed, mod-bit/BUR delivers a redundant, puncture-tough 20-30 year roof.

### Drains, Scuppers & Edge Metal

Strip-in all **roof drains and scuppers** with reinforcing flashing membrane and clamp the drain ring over the field plies. Install **gravel stop / fascia edge metal (ES-1 rated)** at perimeters and seal the membrane up and over the edge.

### Quality Checks

- Probe **all seams** with a trowel after cooling; rework any unbonded lap.
- Confirm **no fishmouths or wrinkles** at laps; cut, patch, and reflash.
- Verify positive drainage with a hose test — standing water voids many warranties.

title: Roof Tear-Off & Deck Inspection
content:
## Roof Tear-Off & Deck Inspection

A reroof is only as good as the deck under it. `IRC R908` governs reroofing — and prohibits new coverings over deteriorated or water-soaked decks. Plan tear-off for clean, dry weather with the dumpster staged at the eave.

### When Tear-Off Is Required

Per `R908.3`, you must remove existing roofing when:

- The existing roof is **water-soaked or deteriorated**.
- There are already **two layers** of any roof covering.
- The existing covering is **wood shake, slate, clay/cement tile**, or any base for new metal.
- The deck cannot support the dead load of an additional layer.

### Tear-Off Sequence

- Protect landscaping, AC units, and windows with tarps/plywood.
- Strip from the **ridge down** with tear-off shovels/spades; pull all nails or drive flush.
- Remove **all** old underlayment, drip edge, and flashings — reusing old flashing is a top leak source.
- Sweep magnetically for nails around the perimeter at end of day.

### Deck Inspection Checklist

- **Sheathing thickness/type:** verify min. **15/32 in.** plywood or **7/16 in.** OSB on 24 in. rafters; replace anything spongy.
- **Rot/delamination:** probe around penetrations, valleys, eaves, and chimneys — the usual wet spots.
- **Fastener pull:** re-nail loose sheathing to rafters with `8d` ring-shank; many codes now require **enhanced edge nailing** for wind.
- **Plane & sag:** sight along rafters for dips; check for over-spanned or notched rafters.
- **Spacing:** maintain a **1/8 in. gap** between panels for expansion; close gaps over 1/8 in. with H-clips if needed.

### Replacement & Documentation

- Replace damaged sheathing full-span to bear on rafters at each end.
- Photograph all rot and repairs for the owner/insurer before covering.
- Once dry and sound, immediately dry-in with underlayment per `R905.1.1` — never leave a bare deck overnight in changeable weather.

### Safety

Tear-off is the highest-fall-exposure phase: **PFAS anchors and harnesses** per OSHA 1926.501, eye protection against flying nails, and roof jacks/toe boards on steep slopes.

### Staging & Weather Windows

Never tear off more roof than you can **dry-in the same day**. Track the forecast hourly; a surprise shower on an open deck soaks insulation and framing. Stage underlayment and a tarp kit on the roof before stripping.

### Documentation for Code & Insurance

Record the **number of existing layers**, deck type/thickness, and every rot repair with dated photos. `R908.3` decisions (overlay vs. full tear-off) must be defensible to the inspector, and insurers require proof of decking condition before approving the new system.

title: Drip Edge & Gutter Apron Code Requirements (R905.2.8.5)
content:
## Drip Edge & Gutter Apron — Code & Best Practice

Drip edge is no longer optional. Since the 2012 IRC, `R905.2.8.5` **requires drip edge at eaves and rakes** for asphalt shingle roofs. Proper edge metal directs water off the fascia and protects the deck edge from rot.

### What Code Requires

- **Material:** corrosion-resistant metal, **min. 0.019 in.** thick (24-ga steel or 0.024 in. aluminum is common).
- **Profile:** drip edge must extend **min. 1/4 in. below the sheathing** and back onto the deck **min. 2 in.**
- **Overlap:** end laps **min. 2 in.**
- **Fastening:** nailed to the deck **max. 12 in. on-center**.
- **Layering — this is the part crews get wrong:**
 - At **eaves**, drip edge goes **UNDER** the underlayment so water on the membrane sheds over the metal. (Where ice-and-water is used, the membrane laps over the eave drip edge per local practice — follow the manufacturer detail.)
 - At **rakes**, drip edge goes **OVER** the underlayment.

### Drip Edge vs. Gutter Apron

- **Drip edge (D-style/L-style):** short vertical leg; standard eave/rake metal.
- **Gutter apron (extended L/F-style):** a longer, kicked-out leg that reaches **into the gutter**, so water can't wick behind the gutter and rot the fascia. Use gutter apron at eaves that have gutters — it is the single best detail against fascia rot.

### Installation Notes

- Lap pieces **shingle-fashion** (upper over lower) so water never runs into a seam.
- Miter outside corners cleanly; hem cut edges to stiffen and avoid oil-canning.
- Color-match aluminum drip to the gutter/fascia for appearance.
- Set **starter strip** flush to the drip edge, not overhanging more than the manufacturer allows (typ. 1/4-3/4 in.).

### Common Failures

- No gutter apron → water wicks behind gutter, soaks fascia and soffit.
- Drip edge nailed too sparsely → wind flutter and rake leaks.
- Wrong layering at eave vs. rake → reverse-lap leaks.

Get edge metal right and you eliminate the most common cause of eave/fascia rot in shingle roofs.

### Coordination with Ice-and-Water

In cold climates, sequence the eave so the **ice-and-water membrane laps over the eave drip edge** (per the membrane manufacturer) while the **rake drip edge laps over** the field underlayment — this keeps every transition shingle-lapped against gravity-fed water.

### Material & Corrosion Notes

Match metal to environment: **galvanized steel** inland, **aluminum or coated steel** in coastal/salt air to avoid rust streaks on fascia. Avoid direct contact between dissimilar metals (galvanic corrosion). Hem the drip leg for rigidity and a clean shadow line.

title: Skylight Installation & Flashing (Velux)
content:
## Skylight Installation & Flashing (Velux)

Skylights leak when the **flashing kit** is skipped or improvised. Velux deck-mounted units ship a model-specific **EDL (step-flashing) kit for shingles** or **EDW (high-profile)** for tile/shake — use the matching kit and the leak risk drops to near zero.

### Unit Types & Slope

- **Deck-mounted (D-series)** — lowest profile, integral gutter; for **14-85 degree** slopes (verify model).
- **Curb-mounted (C-series)** — sits on a site-built 2x curb; common on low-slope.
- **Fixed (FS), manual venting (VS), solar/electric (VSS/VSE)** — for fresh-air units, plan wiring/condensation.
- Confirm **Energy Star** Low-E3 laminated glass for code/comfort.

### Rough Opening & Mounting

- Frame the **rough opening** per the model chart (deck-mounted units mount directly to the deck with integral brackets).
- Set the unit square; fasten brackets to the deck/rafters.
- Slope-side, install **ice-and-water shield** wrapping up the curb/frame onto the roof a min. 6 in. — this is the secondary line of defense.

### Flashing Sequence (EDL kit, shingles)

- Shingle up to the **bottom (sill) flashing**; install it over the course below so water sheds onto shingles.
- Install **side step-flashing pieces** woven course-by-course with the shingles — each step laps the one below, just like sidewall step flashing.
- Install the **head (top) flashing** under the upslope shingles and a **counter-deflector/saddle** to divert water around the unit.
- Snap the **cladding/cover pieces** over the flashing to finish.

### Critical Rules

- **Never rely on sealant** as the waterproofing — the kit's stepped metal is the system; sealant is only a supplement at laps.
- Maintain a clear **water diverter at the head** so upslope runoff splits around the curb.
- For two skylights stacked vertically, use a **factory channel/saddle** between them.

### Curb-Mounted Note

Build the curb **min. 4 in. above the roof plane**, wrap with self-adhered membrane, then apply step and head flashing as above before setting the unit on butyl.

### Safety

Open holes in a deck are a fall hazard — **cover or guard the opening** whenever the crew steps away, and tie off per OSHA 1926.501.

### Condensation & Glazing

Spec **Low-E3 laminated glass** and verify the unit's **U-factor/SHGC** for the climate; cheap single-pane domes sweat and drip indoors. In humid rooms (baths, kitchens), choose a venting unit to shed moisture.

### Final Verification

After install, **hose-test from the bottom up** before closing the interior. Confirm cladding caps fully cover the stepped flashing and that the head diverter sheds upslope water around the curb.

title: Chimney Flashing with Cricket / Saddle
content:
## Chimney Flashing & Cricket (Saddle)
